cases.complaint: A 16-year-old girl is brought in by her parents, wheezing and too breathless to finish a sentence.

clues.history: She has had asthma since age 6 and has had a cold for three days. Tonight her chest got very tight and her blue reliever inhaler only helps for about 20 minutes. She has been using it a lot more this week and often forgets her brown preventer inhaler. She also has hay fever and eczema. One previous hospital admission for asthma, never in intensive care.
clues.vitals: Temp 37.6 °C, HR 124/min, BP 118/72 mmHg, RR 30/min, SpO2 93% on room air.
clues.exam: Sitting forward, using her neck muscles to breathe, speaking in 2–3 word phrases. Widespread high-pitched expiratory wheeze on both sides with a long expiration. Air entry still reasonable (the chest is not silent). Alert and not drowsy. Peak flow 42% of her best.
clues.labs: Arterial gas on oxygen: pH 7.46, PaO2 9.8 kPa, PaCO2 4.1 kPa (low, as expected from fast breathing). Potassium 3.6 mmol/L (watch it, as reliever treatment lowers potassium). WBC 9.8 ×10^9/L. A normal or rising PaCO2 would be a danger sign of exhaustion.
clues.imaging: Chest X-ray: hyperinflated lungs with flattened diaphragms; no pneumothorax and no consolidation. ECG: sinus tachycardia.

explain.patho: Asthma is chronic inflammation of the airways, often driven by an allergic (type 2) immune response with eosinophils, mast cells and IgE. A trigger such as a viral cold or allergen makes the airways react strongly: the smooth muscle around the bronchi contracts (bronchospasm), the airway lining swells and thick mucus plugs the small airways. Narrow airways mean air can still get in but struggles to get out, so air is trapped, the chest hyperinflates and breathing out is long and wheezy. Early in an attack, fast breathing blows off carbon dioxide so PaCO2 is low. As the patient tires, or the airways become critically narrow, PaCO2 climbs back to normal and then high, which signals impending respiratory failure. A 'silent chest' means so little air is moving that wheeze can't be heard.
explain.confirm: Acute asthma is diagnosed clinically from known asthma, wheeze and breathlessness, and severity is graded by peak flow, the ability to speak, heart and breathing rate, oxygen saturation and blood gases. Peak flow of about a third to a half of best predicted, inability to finish sentences or a fast heart rate mark a severe attack; a silent chest, exhaustion, confusion or a normal or high PaCO2 mark a life-threatening one.
explain.treat: Oxygen, repeated or continuous nebulised short-acting bronchodilators (a beta-agonist plus an anticholinergic) and early steroids by mouth or vein to calm the inflammation. Severe attacks not responding get intravenous magnesium and senior or intensive care review, and some need ventilation. Before going home she needs her inhaler technique checked, a written action plan and a regular inhaled steroid-containing preventer.

near.anaphylaxis: Wheeze can happen in anaphylaxis, but there's no rash, swelling or allergen exposure, and she has a long history of this.
near.copd exacerbation: COPD is a disease of older long-term smokers; in a teenager with eczema and hay fever think of something else.
near.pneumonia: She has a cold, but the chest X-ray shows no consolidation and the wheeze is everywhere.

cases.pearl: A 'normal' CO2 in a breathless asthmatic is not reassuring: it means they are tiring out.

cases.dx: Acute decompensated heart failure with pulmonary oedema
cases.complaint: A 74-year-old man is brought in at 3 a.m. because he woke up gasping for breath and can't lie down.

clues.history: Over two weeks he has needed more pillows to sleep and has woken several times choking for air, easing when he sits on the edge of the bed. His ankles have swollen and he has gained 4 kg. He had a heart attack six years ago. Tonight he is coughing up frothy, pink-tinged sputum. He ran out of his water tablets and heart tablets ten days ago.
clues.vitals: Temp 36.5 °C, HR 116/min, BP 168/98 mmHg, RR 30/min, SpO2 86% on room air.
clues.exam: Sitting bolt upright, sweaty, speaking in short phrases. JVP raised to the earlobe. Fine crackles across both lungs up to the mid-zones. Extra third heart sound (gallop rhythm). Pitting oedema to both knees. Cool peripheries.
clues.labs: NT-proBNP 9,800 ng/L (strongly raised). Troponin T 32 ng/L, stable on repeat. Sodium 133 mmol/L, potassium 4.8 mmol/L, creatinine 148 µmol/L, urea 11.2 mmol/L. Haemoglobin 131 g/L. Arterial gas on air: pH 7.32, PaO2 7.4 kPa, PaCO2 5.9 kPa, lactate 2.1 mmol/L.
clues.imaging: Chest X-ray: enlarged heart, fluffy shadowing spreading out from both hila ('bat's wing'), short horizontal lines at the lung edges (Kerley B lines), enlarged blood vessels to the upper lobes, small fluid collections at both bases. ECG: sinus tachycardia with old Q waves in V1–V4. Echo: left ventricle dilated and squeezing poorly, ejection fraction about 30%.

explain.patho: After his old heart attack, scarred heart muscle left the left ventricle weak and dilated, with a reduced ejection fraction. When the pump can't move blood forward, pressure backs up into the left atrium and the veins of the lungs. Once the pressure in the lung capillaries is high enough, fluid is pushed out into the tissue between the alveoli and then into the air sacs themselves, so oxygen can't cross easily: this is pulmonary oedema. Lying flat moves more blood back to the chest, which is why he wakes up breathless and has to sit up. The body senses low output and switches on the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system and the sympathetic system, holding on to salt and water and tightening blood vessels, which loads the failing heart further. Stopping his diuretics and heart medicines tipped him over the edge.
explain.confirm: A clinical diagnosis backed by a raised BNP or NT-proBNP, a chest X-ray showing congestion, and an echocardiogram showing the cause (here a weak left ventricle). It is also important to look for a trigger such as a new heart attack, an arrhythmia, infection or missed medications.
explain.treat: Sit the patient up and give oxygen, with CPAP or other non-invasive ventilation if breathing is failing. Intravenous loop diuretics remove fluid, and nitrates lower the pressure the heart pumps against when blood pressure allows. Once stable, long-term treatment for a weak heart combines ACE inhibitors or ARNIs, beta-blockers, mineralocorticoid antagonists and gliflozins (SGLT inhibitors), plus a salt and fluid plan, daily weights and sometimes a defibrillator or pacing device.

near.pneumonia: There's no fever and the crackles are on both sides with a high JVP and leg swelling, so the fluid is coming from the heart, not infection.
near.copd exacerbation: Breathless and hypoxic, yes, but think about why he can't lie flat, why the JVP is high and why BNP is so raised.
near.stemi: Old Q waves and a stable troponin suggest an old injury, not a new blocked artery.

cases.pearl: A third heart sound in an adult is the sound of blood slamming into an overfilled, stiff ventricle: a classic sign of heart failure.

cases.complaint: A 24-year-old man is brought to the ED faint, vomiting and with very low blood pressure after a two-day stomach bug.

clues.history: For several months he has felt increasingly tired and weak, has lost weight, gets dizzy when he stands up, and has been craving salty crisps. Friends commented that he looks tanned though he hasn't been on holiday. Two days ago he developed vomiting and diarrhoea, and today he collapsed. He has vitiligo and takes no regular medicines.
clues.vitals: Temp 37.8 °C, HR 124/min, BP 78/44 mmHg (does not improve much with an initial fluid bolus), RR 24/min, SpO2 98% on room air.
clues.exam: Drowsy and confused. Very dry mouth. Patchy dark pigmentation of the skin creases of his palms, his knuckles, an old scar and the inside of his cheeks, alongside pale patches of vitiligo on his hands. Diffuse mild abdominal tenderness without guarding.
clues.labs: Sodium 122 mmol/L (low), potassium 6.2 mmol/L (high), glucose 2.9 mmol/L (low), urea 14.5 mmol/L, creatinine 148 µmol/L. Random cortisol 40 nmol/L (very low for someone this sick; a stressed body should make a lot). ACTH 620 ng/L (very high; normal under about 50). Renin high; 21-hydroxylase antibodies positive.
clues.imaging: ECG: sinus tachycardia with tall, peaked T waves from the high potassium. Chest X-ray normal. A later CT of the abdomen shows small, thin adrenal glands without masses or calcification, consistent with autoimmune destruction rather than infection or cancer.

explain.patho: The adrenal cortex makes cortisol, which keeps blood pressure and blood sugar up during stress, and aldosterone, which makes the kidneys keep sodium and get rid of potassium. In Addison's disease, most commonly autoimmune in developed countries, antibodies against the enzyme 21-hydroxylase destroy the cortex, so both hormones fall. Without aldosterone, salt and water are lost in the urine and potassium builds up; without cortisol, blood vessels respond poorly to adrenaline and the liver cannot keep glucose up. The pituitary senses low cortisol and floods out ACTH; ACTH is made from a larger molecule that also produces melanocyte-stimulating hormone, which darkens the skin. A stress such as an infection or a tummy bug, when the body needs far more cortisol than it can make, tips the chronic illness into a crisis with shock.
explain.confirm: In a crisis, blood for cortisol and ACTH is taken before treatment but treatment is never delayed for results. A low cortisol with a high ACTH confirms primary adrenal failure. Later, a short Synacthen test (cortisol fails to rise after synthetic ACTH) confirms it, and adrenal antibodies identify the autoimmune cause.
explain.treat: Emergency intravenous hydrocortisone straight away, with rapid intravenous saline and glucose to correct shock and hypoglycaemia; the potassium usually corrects with this. The trigger is treated. Long-term he needs daily steroid replacement (hydrocortisone for cortisol and fludrocortisone for aldosterone), 'sick day rules' to increase steroids during illness, an emergency injection kit and a medical alert card.

near.gastroenteritis: The bug was the trigger, but months of tiredness, a tan and a high potassium point to a hormone failure underneath.
near.septic shock: Shock with fever fits, but the low sodium, high potassium, low glucose and dark skin creases point to a gland.
near.hypothyroidism: Tiredness fits, but low blood pressure with high potassium and dark skin creases point to a different endocrine gland.

cases.pearl: Low sodium plus high potassium plus low glucose in a shocked patient: give steroids first and ask questions later.

cases.dx: Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response
cases.complaint: A 71-year-old woman comes to the ED with a racing, fluttering heartbeat and breathlessness that started this morning.

clues.history: She woke feeling her heart 'flapping like a fish' and gets out of breath walking to the bathroom. She feels light-headed but did not faint. She has high blood pressure and no known thyroid problems. No chest pain. She has had brief, similar episodes over the past month that stopped on their own.
clues.vitals: Temp 36.9 °C, HR 148/min and irregular, BP 118/76 mmHg, RR 20/min, SpO2 96% on room air.
clues.exam: Pulse irregularly irregular, and the rate at the wrist is lower than the rate heard at the heart (pulse deficit). Varying intensity of the first heart sound. No murmur. Mild crackles at both lung bases. No leg swelling. Thyroid not enlarged.
clues.labs: TSH 1.8 mIU/L (normal), free T4 normal. Potassium 4.2 mmol/L, creatinine 88 µmol/L, haemoglobin 134 g/L. Troponin T 15 ng/L, flat on repeat. Glucose 6.0 mmol/L.
clues.imaging: ECG: irregularly irregular narrow-complex rhythm at about 150/min, no P waves, a wavy, chaotic baseline. No ST elevation. Echo: enlarged left atrium, normal left ventricular function, no significant valve disease. Chest X-ray: mild congestion only.

explain.patho: In atrial fibrillation, many tiny chaotic electrical wavelets spin around the atria instead of one organised beat from the sinus node, often triggered by bursts from muscle sleeves inside the pulmonary veins. The atria quiver at hundreds of times per minute and stop contracting properly. The AV node acts as a gatekeeper and only lets some impulses through, at random, so the ventricles beat irregularly; when many get through, the ventricular rate is fast (rapid ventricular response). A fast heart has little time to fill, so output drops and pressure backs up into the lungs. Age, high blood pressure and a stretched left atrium are the main risk factors. Blood pools in the left atrial appendage, where clots can form and travel to the brain, which is why AF raises stroke risk about five-fold.
explain.confirm: A 12-lead ECG showing an irregularly irregular rhythm with no P waves confirms it. Tests then look for causes and triggers (thyroid function, electrolytes, echo) and stroke risk is estimated with the CHA2DS2-VASc score, weighed against bleeding risk.
explain.treat: If the patient is unstable (shock, fainting, heart failure or ischaemia) the rhythm is reset urgently with synchronised electrical cardioversion. If stable, rate control with beta-blockers or certain calcium channel blockers is first, and rhythm control (medicines, cardioversion or catheter ablation) is chosen for some patients. Long-term anticoagulation, usually with a direct oral anticoagulant, is given to those with enough stroke risk.

near.supraventricular tachycardia: SVT is fast and narrow but perfectly regular; this rhythm is irregularly irregular with no P waves.
near.atrial flutter: Flutter shows sawtooth waves and usually a regular rate; this baseline is chaotic and the rhythm totally irregular.
near.hyperthyroidism: A good cause to check, but the thyroid tests are normal.

cases.pearl: Irregularly irregular plus no P waves equals AF; the danger isn't just the fast rate, it's the clot in the left atrial appendage.

cases.complaint: A 4-year-old girl is brought to her doctor because for three weeks she has been pale, tired, bruising easily and refusing to walk some mornings.

clues.history: Her parents noticed she has lost her energy and naps again, gets fevers that come and go, and has bruises on her legs and back that she can't explain. She has had two nosebleeds this week. Some mornings she cries that her legs hurt and won't walk, then limps around later. Before this she was a healthy, active child.
clues.vitals: Temp 38.0 °C, HR 138/min, BP 94/58 mmHg, RR 26/min, SpO2 98% on room air.
clues.exam: Pale. Scattered bruises on the shins and back, and pinpoint red-purple spots (petechiae) on her chest that don't fade when pressed. Painless, rubbery lymph nodes in the neck and armpits. The liver is felt 4 cm and the spleen 5 cm below the ribs. Tenderness when the long bones of the legs are pressed, but no swollen joints.
clues.labs: Haemoglobin 66 g/L, platelets 18 ×10^9/L (normal 150–400), WBC 46 ×10^9/L with very few neutrophils (0.4 ×10^9/L). Blood film: many large immature cells with scant cytoplasm (lymphoblasts). Uric acid 0.52 mmol/L and LDH raised from rapid cell turnover; potassium 4.9 mmol/L, phosphate 1.9 mmol/L. Bone marrow: over 80% lymphoblasts; flow cytometry shows CD19, CD10 and TdT, an early B-cell pattern.
clues.imaging: Chest X-ray: no mass in the middle of the chest (a mediastinal mass would suggest a T-cell type and could press on the airway). Abdominal ultrasound confirms an enlarged liver and spleen. Lumbar puncture (done at the start of treatment) shows no leukaemia cells in the spinal fluid.

explain.patho: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia is a cancer of the earliest lymphocyte precursors in the bone marrow. Genetic changes in one precursor cell, often a first change very early in life followed by a second 'hit' later, stop it maturing and let it divide without control, producing a flood of useless lymphoblasts. These blasts crowd out normal marrow, so the child cannot make enough red cells (pallor, tiredness), platelets (bruising, petechiae, nosebleeds) or working neutrophils (fevers and infections), even though the total white count may be high. Blasts packed into the marrow cavity stretch the bone lining, causing bone pain and limping. They spread to the lymph nodes, liver and spleen and can enter the brain and spinal fluid, which is why treatment must also reach the central nervous system. When treatment kills large numbers of cells at once, their contents (potassium, phosphate, uric acid) can flood the blood and damage the kidneys (tumour lysis syndrome).
explain.confirm: A blood count and film raise the suspicion; a bone marrow aspirate showing at least 20% lymphoblasts confirms acute leukaemia. Flow cytometry identifies the cell type (B or T) and genetic tests on the leukaemia cells guide risk and treatment. A lumbar puncture checks whether the central nervous system is involved.
explain.treat: Treatment in a specialist children's cancer centre with combination chemotherapy given in phases (induction, consolidation and a long maintenance phase), including medicine delivered into the spinal fluid to protect the brain. Supportive care is crucial: fluids and uric acid-lowering drugs to prevent tumour lysis, blood and platelet transfusions, and rapid treatment of infections. For relapsed or high-risk disease, options include immunotherapy such as CAR-T cells and bone marrow transplant.

near.idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura: ITP gives bruising and low platelets, but the haemoglobin and white cells are normal and there are no big organs or blasts.
near.infectious mononucleosis: That can cause big nodes and spleen with odd lymphocytes, but not severe anaemia, very low platelets and blasts filling the marrow.
near.juvenile idiopathic arthritis: Limping and bone pain can mimic arthritis, but there are no swollen joints and the blood count is badly abnormal.
near.leukaemia: Right idea! Be specific: which type of acute leukaemia is the commonest cancer in young children?

cases.pearl: Bone pain or limping plus pallor, bruising and fevers in a young child: check a full blood count and film. Cure rates for childhood ALL are now around nine in ten.

cases.complaint: A 57-year-old man has had a weak right hand for eight months and now his speech is slurring and he coughs when he drinks.

clues.history: It started with trouble turning keys and doing up buttons with his right hand. Since then he has noticed rippling twitches under the skin of his arms and thighs, painful cramps at night and, more recently, slurred speech and choking on thin liquids. He has lost 6 kg. He has no numbness or tingling, his vision is normal and his bladder works normally. No neck pain.
clues.vitals: Temp 36.7 °C, HR 80/min, BP 130/78 mmHg, RR 16/min, SpO2 95% on room air.
clues.exam: Wasting of the right thenar eminence and the first dorsal interosseous muscle, with weak grip. Visible fasciculations in both arms, the thighs and the tongue, which is also wasted. Yet the reflexes in those same wasted limbs are brisk, with a positive Hoffmann sign, upgoing plantars and a brisk jaw jerk. Sensation is completely normal. Eye movements normal. Slurred, slow, strained speech.
clues.labs: CK mildly raised at 380 U/L (from denervated muscle). Vitamin B12, thyroid tests, calcium and protein electrophoresis normal. Anti-GM1 antibodies negative (makes multifocal motor neuropathy less likely). Forced vital capacity 72% of predicted.
clues.imaging: MRI brain and cervical spine: no spinal cord compression and no structural lesion (rules out cervical myelopathy). EMG: active denervation (fibrillations and fasciculation potentials) with chronic reinnervation in the arm, leg and tongue muscles. Nerve conduction studies: sensory nerves normal.

explain.patho: ALS is a degenerative disease of motor neurons, affecting both the upper motor neurons in the motor cortex and corticospinal tracts and the lower motor neurons in the brainstem and the anterior horn of the spinal cord. That combination is the signature: wasting and fasciculations from lower motor neuron loss sit side by side with brisk reflexes and upgoing toes from upper motor neuron loss, sometimes in the same limb. In most patients, the protein TDP-43 misfolds and clumps inside neurons; around one in ten cases is inherited, with genes such as SOD1 and C9orf72. Glutamate excitotoxicity, mitochondrial failure and problems clearing damaged proteins all contribute to neuron death. Sensory neurons, eye movement neurons and bladder control are usually spared. As the breathing muscles weaken, respiratory failure becomes the main threat.
explain.confirm: Diagnosis is clinical: progressive upper and lower motor neuron signs spreading across body regions (using the Gold Coast or revised El Escorial criteria). EMG confirms widespread denervation, and MRI and blood tests rule out treatable mimics such as cervical cord compression or multifocal motor neuropathy.
explain.treat: There is no cure. Riluzole, which reduces glutamate release, modestly prolongs survival, and gene-targeted treatment exists for one inherited form. Care is multidisciplinary: non-invasive ventilation for weak breathing, a feeding tube (gastrostomy) when swallowing becomes unsafe, speech and communication aids, physiotherapy and palliative care focused on quality of life.

near.cervical myelopathy: Spinal cord compression would usually affect sensation and show on the MRI; his sensation and MRI are normal.
near.myasthenia gravis: Myasthenia fluctuates and doesn't cause wasting, fasciculations or brisk reflexes.
near.guillain-barre syndrome: GBS develops over days with lost reflexes and tingling; this has crept up for months with brisk reflexes.
near.multifocal motor neuropathy: Good mimic, but his reflexes are brisk and anti-GM1 is negative.

cases.pearl: Upper and lower motor neuron signs in the same limb, with normal sensation and normal eye movements: that combination is the signature of ALS.

cases.complaint: A 15-year-old boy collapses at a birthday party a few minutes after eating a cookie, with a blotchy rash and noisy breathing.

clues.history: About ten minutes after eating a homemade cookie he said his mouth was itchy and tingling, then his lips swelled, his voice went hoarse and he felt like his throat was closing. He then felt faint and was sick once. He reacted to peanut butter as a toddler with hives but has avoided peanuts since and wasn't carrying an adrenaline auto-injector. The cookie turned out to contain ground peanuts. He has asthma.
clues.vitals: Temp 36.9 °C, HR 136/min, BP 74/40 mmHg, RR 30/min, SpO2 89% on room air.
clues.exam: Raised, itchy red wheals (hives) over the face, chest and arms. Swollen lips and tongue. A high-pitched noise on breathing in (stridor) and wheeze on breathing out. Pale, sweaty and drowsy when sitting up, better lying flat with legs raised. Warm hands at first, now cooling.
clues.labs: Treatment must come first. Mast cell tryptase taken after treatment is clearly raised and is repeated later to compare with his baseline. Arterial gas: pH 7.29, lactate 4.6 mmol/L. Glucose 6.4 mmol/L. Haemoglobin 152 g/L (concentrated as fluid leaks out of vessels).
clues.imaging: Not needed for the diagnosis, which is clinical. ECG: sinus tachycardia, no ischaemia. A chest X-ray, if done after stabilisation, would be normal or show hyperinflation from bronchospasm.

explain.patho: In someone already sensitised, IgE antibodies against peanut proteins coat the surface of mast cells and basophils. When the peanut protein enters the body again, it cross-links these IgE antibodies and makes the cells release their contents all at once: histamine, tryptase, leukotrienes and prostaglandins. These chemicals make blood vessels dilate and leak fluid, so blood pressure drops sharply (distributive shock) and tissues swell, including the lips, tongue and larynx. They also cause bronchospasm (wheeze), itching, hives and gut symptoms like vomiting. Swelling of the upper airway and collapse of the circulation can kill within minutes. People with asthma are at higher risk of a severe reaction.
explain.confirm: Anaphylaxis is a clinical diagnosis: sudden onset after a likely trigger with airway, breathing or circulation problems, usually with skin or mucosal changes such as hives or swelling. A raised mast cell tryptase taken soon after the reaction supports it. Later, an allergy clinic confirms the trigger with skin-prick or specific IgE blood tests.
explain.treat: Intramuscular adrenaline into the outer thigh straight away is the key treatment, repeated if there is no improvement, alongside calling for help, lying the patient flat with legs raised (or sitting up if breathing is the main problem), high-flow oxygen and intravenous fluids. Nebulised bronchodilators help wheeze; antihistamines help itching but do not treat the life-threatening parts. He needs observation for a delayed second reaction, adrenaline auto-injectors to carry with training on using them, an allergy clinic referral and an action plan.

near.acute asthma: He's wheezing, but the hives, swollen lips, stridor and collapsed blood pressure after eating point to a whole-body reaction.
near.angioedema: Swelling is part of it, but low blood pressure and wheeze after a trigger make this a full systemic reaction.
near.vasovagal syncope: Fainting fits, but a simple faint has a slow pulse and no rash, swelling or wheeze.

cases.pearl: Adrenaline first, everything else second: antihistamines and steroids don't save lives in anaphylaxis.

cases.complaint: A 59-year-old man with poorly controlled high blood pressure collapses at work with sudden, severe chest pain that goes straight through to his back.

clues.history: The pain came on suddenly at full strength, described as 'tearing', in the front of his chest and then between the shoulder blades, and it seems to be moving downward. He has had high blood pressure for years and often forgets his tablets. No exertional chest pain before. He briefly felt his left arm go weak and tingly.
clues.vitals: Temp 36.6 °C, HR 110/min, BP 182/96 mmHg in the right arm and 128/74 mmHg in the left arm, RR 22/min, SpO2 96% on room air.
clues.exam: Sweaty and in severe pain. Left radial pulse weaker than the right. A soft early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge (aortic regurgitation). Chest clear. Abdomen soft, femoral pulses present.
clues.labs: High-sensitivity troponin T 18 ng/L (borderline). D-dimer markedly raised. Haemoglobin 136 g/L, creatinine 101 µmol/L, lactate 2.4 mmol/L. Group and crossmatch sent.
clues.imaging: ECG: left ventricular hypertrophy, no ST elevation. Chest X-ray: widened mediastinum and an abnormal aortic knuckle. CT angiogram: an intimal flap splits the ascending aorta into a true and a false channel, extending around the arch into the descending aorta and into the origin of the left subclavian artery; small pericardial effusion.

explain.patho: The aortic wall has three layers: intima, media and adventitia. Years of high blood pressure (or weak connective tissue, as in Marfan syndrome) damage the media. A tear in the intima lets blood under high pressure force its way into the media, splitting the wall and creating a false lumen that can travel along the aorta in seconds, causing pain that moves. As the flap spreads it can block branch arteries, cutting blood flow to an arm (unequal pulses), the brain (stroke), the spinal cord, kidneys or gut. Dissection near the heart can stretch the aortic valve ring (regurgitation), block a coronary artery or rupture into the pericardium, causing tamponade. Stanford type A involves the ascending aorta and is a surgical emergency; type B starts beyond the left subclavian artery.
explain.confirm: CT angiography is the main test and shows the intimal flap and true and false lumens and how far the dissection extends. Transoesophageal echo is used if the patient is too unstable for CT. A widened mediastinum on X-ray and a raised D-dimer support the diagnosis but cannot rule it in or out alone.
explain.treat: Immediate control of heart rate and blood pressure, usually with intravenous beta-blockers first and then vasodilators, plus strong pain relief, to reduce the force on the torn wall. Type A dissection needs emergency open-heart surgery to replace the ascending aorta. Uncomplicated type B dissection is usually managed with blood pressure control, and complicated type B with an endovascular stent graft. Clot-busting and antiplatelet drugs must be avoided.

near.stemi: The ECG has no ST elevation and the arm blood pressures differ a lot, which a heart attack wouldn't cause.
near.pulmonary embolism: The raised D-dimer fits, but tearing pain to the back, unequal arm pulses and a widened mediastinum point to the main artery itself.
near.pericarditis: There is a small effusion, but that may be the sign of something far more dangerous leaking into the sac.

cases.pearl: Always check both arms: a blood-pressure gap of more than 20 mmHg with chest pain is a dissection until proven otherwise, and giving clot-busters by mistake can be fatal.

cases.complaint: An 82-year-old man fainted while walking up a hill with his grandson, his second dizzy spell on exertion this month.

clues.history: He blacked out for a few seconds near the top of a steep hill and came round quickly with no confusion afterwards. For six months he has had chest tightness and breathlessness when walking briskly, which settle with rest. He was told years ago he had a 'heart murmur'. He has high blood pressure and high cholesterol. No tongue biting, no palpitations before the faint.
clues.vitals: Temp 36.6 °C, HR 72/min and regular, BP 112/88 mmHg (narrow pulse pressure), RR 16/min, SpO2 96% on room air.
clues.exam: A loud, harsh, crescendo-decrescendo (ejection) systolic murmur loudest at the right upper sternal edge, spreading up into both carotid arteries. The second heart sound is quiet. The pulse at the wrist and neck is weak and slow to rise (slow-rising, low-volume pulse). The apex beat is sustained but not displaced. Chest clear.
clues.labs: Haemoglobin 132 g/L, creatinine 104 µmol/L, potassium 4.3 mmol/L, glucose 5.6 mmol/L. Troponin T 18 ng/L, stable. NT-proBNP moderately raised. Bloods otherwise normal: no anaemia and no electrolyte cause for the faint.
clues.imaging: ECG: sinus rhythm with left ventricular hypertrophy and strain. Echocardiogram: heavily calcified aortic valve that barely opens; valve area 0.7 cm², peak jet velocity 4.6 m/s, mean gradient 52 mmHg (all severe); thick left ventricle with good squeeze. CT shows heavy calcium on the valve, and coronary angiography shows only mild coronary disease.

explain.patho: With age, the aortic valve leaflets undergo a process similar to atherosclerosis: lipid deposits, inflammation and then calcium build up, making the leaflets thick, stiff and unable to open fully (a two-leaflet bicuspid valve calcifies decades earlier). The left ventricle has to generate much higher pressure to push blood through the narrow opening, so its muscle thickens (concentric hypertrophy). Thick muscle needs more oxygen but its blood supply doesn't grow to match, causing angina even with normal coronaries. On exertion, the muscles' blood vessels dilate but the fixed narrow valve stops cardiac output rising, so blood pressure drops and the brain is starved of blood, causing syncope. Eventually the overloaded ventricle fails, causing breathlessness. Once angina, syncope or heart failure appear, survival without treatment is short, so symptoms are the trigger to replace the valve.
explain.confirm: Echocardiography confirms it, grading severity by valve area (severe under about 1 cm²), peak jet velocity (severe above 4 m/s) and mean pressure gradient (severe above 40 mmHg). CT calcium scoring helps when the numbers disagree. A dobutamine stress echo can help in patients with a weak ventricle and low flow.
explain.treat: There is no medicine that slows the valve narrowing; the treatment for severe symptomatic aortic stenosis is valve replacement. Options are surgical aortic valve replacement or transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI), where a new valve is passed up from the leg artery, which is often preferred in older patients. Until then, strenuous exertion is avoided and high blood pressure, heart failure and coronary disease are managed carefully, as some drugs that drop blood pressure quickly can be dangerous.

near.hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: The murmur is similar, but this one spreads up into the carotids, the pulse is slow-rising and the patient is 82 with a calcified valve.
near.vasovagal syncope: Simple faints happen with standing or emotion, not mid-climb with chest tightness and a loud murmur.
near.complete heart block: A slow rhythm can cause faints, but his pulse is regular at a normal rate.

cases.pearl: The classic triad of severe aortic stenosis is angina, syncope and breathlessness on exertion, and once symptoms start, the valve needs replacing.

cases.complaint: A 12-year-old boy is brought in by his parents with tummy pain since yesterday evening that is now worst low on the right side.

clues.history: The ache started as a dull, hard-to-pin-down pain around his belly button about a day ago and over several hours settled in the lower right. He has not wanted to eat anything since, felt sick, and vomited once after the pain began. The car ride in hurt every time they went over a bump. He has had no diarrhoea and no pain passing urine.
clues.vitals: Temp 37.9 °C, HR 108/min, BP 112/70 mmHg, RR 20/min, SpO2 99% on room air.
clues.exam: He lies still with his knees drawn up and refuses to hop. Maximal tenderness two-thirds of the way from the umbilicus to the right anterior superior iliac spine (McBurney's point) with guarding and rebound tenderness. Pressing on the left lower quadrant causes pain on the right (Rovsing sign), and extending his right hip hurts (psoas sign).
clues.labs: WBC 15.8 ×10^9/L with neutrophils 12.9 ×10^9/L (normal total 4–11). CRP clearly raised. Urine dipstick: no blood, no nitrites, no leucocytes. Sodium, potassium and creatinine (52 µmol/L) are normal.
clues.imaging: Ultrasound of the right lower quadrant: a blind-ending tubular structure 8 mm across that does not compress under the probe, with bright, inflamed fat around it and a small amount of free fluid. No abscess is seen.

explain.patho: Something blocks the narrow opening of the appendix, most often a hardened lump of stool (a faecolith) or, in children, swollen lymphoid tissue after a viral illness. The appendix keeps secreting mucus, so pressure inside rises until it squeezes the veins and then the small arteries in its wall. The starved, stretched wall lets gut bacteria invade, producing pus and inflammation. Early pain is felt vaguely around the umbilicus because the appendix sends visceral pain signals through the same spinal segment (about T10) as the skin there. When the inflammation reaches the parietal peritoneum, which has precise somatic nerves, the pain becomes sharp and fixed in the right lower quadrant. If the wall dies it can perforate, spreading infection through the abdomen (peritonitis) or walling off as an abscess.
explain.confirm: Diagnosis is mainly clinical: migrating pain, anorexia, focal RLQ tenderness and raised inflammatory markers. Risk scores (Alvarado, Paediatric Appendicitis Score) help sort low, medium and high risk. Ultrasound is first choice in children because it avoids radiation; CT is used in adults or when ultrasound is unclear.
explain.treat: Nil by mouth, intravenous fluids, pain relief and intravenous antibiotics. The usual definitive treatment is keyhole removal of the appendix (laparoscopic appendicectomy). Some uncomplicated cases settle with antibiotics alone, though a proportion come back. A perforated appendix with an abscess may be drained by a radiologist first and operated on later.

near.mesenteric adenitis: Also causes right lower quadrant pain in kids after a virus, but it rarely gives guarding, rebound and a non-compressible tube on ultrasound.
near.gastroenteritis: Here vomiting came after the pain and there's no diarrhoea; tummy bugs usually start with vomiting and diarrhoea and the pain stays vague.
near.constipation: Constipation doesn't cause fever, raised white cells and peritoneal signs like rebound and Rovsing.

cases.pearl: Pain first, then vomiting suggests a surgical abdomen; vomiting first, then pain suggests gastroenteritis.

cases.complaint: A 31-year-old man woke up this morning with the right side of his face drooping. Coffee dribbled out of the corner of his mouth.

clues.history: Yesterday he had an ache behind his right ear. This morning he couldn't close his right eye or smile on that side, food collects in his right cheek, sounds seem painfully loud in his right ear and food tastes odd. No weakness or numbness anywhere else, no headache, no rash, no ear discharge, no tick bites.
clues.vitals: Temp 36.8 °C, HR 74/min, BP 122/76 mmHg, RR 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air.
clues.exam: Complete weakness of the whole right side of the face, INCLUDING the forehead (he can't wrinkle it or raise the eyebrow). When he tries to close the right eye, the eyeball rolls upward (Bell's phenomenon). Ear canal and eardrum normal with no blisters; parotid gland normal. All other cranial nerves, limb strength, sensation and coordination are normal.
clues.labs: Glucose 5.2 mmol/L (diabetes is a risk factor). Full blood count normal. Lyme serology negative. No other tests are needed in a typical case.
clues.imaging: No imaging is needed for a typical presentation. Imaging is reserved for atypical features or no recovery after a few months; if MRI were done it might show enhancement of the facial nerve inside the temporal bone and would exclude a tumour. Otoscopy normal.

explain.patho: Bell's palsy is a sudden lower motor neuron palsy of the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII), thought to be caused mainly by reactivation of the cold sore virus (HSV-1) in the geniculate ganglion. The inflamed, swollen nerve gets squeezed inside its narrow bony tunnel in the temporal bone, especially the tight labyrinthine segment, causing ischaemia and loss of myelin. Because the whole nerve is affected, every muscle of facial expression on that side weakens, forehead included. Branches given off inside the canal explain the extras: the nerve to stapedius (no damping of loud sounds), the chorda tympani (taste from the front of the tongue) and the greater petrosal nerve (tears). A stroke, by contrast, spares the forehead, because the forehead's motor neurons receive input from both cerebral hemispheres.
explain.confirm: It is a clinical diagnosis of exclusion: sudden onset over less than three days, one-sided, lower motor neuron weakness including the forehead, and no other neurological signs. Doctors check the ear for blisters (Ramsay Hunt syndrome), the parotid for a mass and ask about tick bites (Lyme disease). Imaging is only needed if features are atypical or recovery doesn't happen.
explain.treat: Oral corticosteroids started early improve the chance of full recovery; antivirals are sometimes added alongside, though their benefit is uncertain. Protecting the eye is crucial because it can't close: lubricating drops, ointment and taping the eyelid shut at night prevent corneal damage. Most people recover fully over weeks to months.

near.stroke: A stroke spares the forehead; his whole half-face, forehead included, is weak, which means the nerve itself.
near.ramsay hunt syndrome: That comes with a painful blistering rash in the ear canal; his ear is clear.
near.lyme disease: Good thought for a facial palsy, but there's no tick bite and his serology is negative.
near.parotid tumour: A tumour causes gradually worsening weakness and a lump; this came on overnight with a normal parotid.

cases.pearl: Forehead spared = brain (upper motor neuron); forehead involved = the facial nerve itself (lower motor neuron).

cases.dx: Cauda equina syndrome (central lumbar disc herniation)
aliases: lumbar disc herniation with cauda equina
cases.complaint: A 42-year-old warehouse worker has severe low back pain shooting down both legs since lifting a heavy box two days ago, and now he can't pass urine.

clues.history: He has had back trouble for years, but this pain is far worse and goes down the backs of both legs. Since this morning the skin of his buttocks and inner thighs feels numb (it felt strange sitting on the toilet), and he hasn't passed urine for 12 hours without much urge to go. His legs feel weak and he is tripping over his feet. No fever, no weight loss, no history of cancer.
clues.vitals: Temp 36.9 °C, HR 92/min, BP 142/86 mmHg, RR 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air.
clues.exam: Weakness of ankle plantarflexion and big-toe extension on both sides. Ankle reflexes absent on both sides, knee reflexes normal; plantars downgoing. Reduced pinprick sensation over the buttocks and inner thighs in a 'saddle' distribution. Reduced anal sphincter tone. A full bladder can be felt above the pubic bone. Straight leg raise painful on both sides.
clues.labs: Bladder scan after attempting to void: 950 mL left in the bladder (painless urinary retention). Full blood count, CRP and ESR normal (makes infection or an abscess unlikely). Urinalysis normal. Creatinine 86 µmol/L.
clues.imaging: Urgent MRI lumbar spine: a large central disc extrusion at L4/5 filling most of the spinal canal and squashing the bundle of nerve roots (cauda equina). The spinal cord itself ends normally at L1 and is not compressed.

explain.patho: The spinal cord ends around the L1–L2 vertebrae; below that, the lumbar and sacral nerve roots continue down the spinal canal as a bundle that looks like a horse's tail (cauda equina). A large central disc herniation pushes back into the canal and compresses many roots on both sides at once, instead of one root as in ordinary sciatica. The sacral roots S2 to S4 carry sensation from the saddle area and the parasympathetic nerves that make the bladder muscle contract, so their compression causes saddle numbness and painless retention, with overflow later. These are peripheral nerve roots, so the signs are lower motor neuron: weakness, lost ankle reflexes and reduced tone, not brisk reflexes. Nerve roots tolerate compression poorly, and the longer they are squashed the more likely the damage, especially to bladder control, becomes permanent.
explain.confirm: This is a clinical emergency diagnosis confirmed by urgent MRI of the lumbar spine. A post-void bladder scan showing retention and reduced saddle sensation and anal tone strongly support it. Anyone with back pain plus saddle numbness or new bladder problems needs same-day MRI.
explain.treat: He needs emergency surgical decompression (discectomy, often with laminectomy) as soon as possible to relieve pressure on the nerve roots. A urinary catheter drains the bladder, and pain relief is given while he waits for theatre. Afterwards he needs physiotherapy and follow-up of bladder function; outcome is best when surgery happens before complete retention sets in.

near.sciatica: Ordinary sciatica affects one root on one side; he has both legs, saddle numbness and urinary retention.
near.spinal cord compression: So close, but the compression is below where the cord ends, and his reflexes are reduced, not brisk. Name the bundle of nerve roots.
near.guillain-barre syndrome: GBS doesn't cause saddle numbness and retention with a huge disc on MRI.
near.mechanical back pain: Simple back pain never causes saddle numbness, bladder retention or lost ankle reflexes.

cases.pearl: Back pain plus saddle numbness or new bladder trouble is cauda equina syndrome until an MRI says otherwise, at any hour of the day or night.

cases.complaint: A 46-year-old woman comes to the ED with constant pain under her right ribs since last night, now with a fever.

clues.history: The pain began about an hour after a large fried dinner and has not let up for 14 hours, unlike her previous attacks, which faded within a couple of hours. It sits in the right upper abdomen and spreads round to the tip of her right shoulder blade. She has vomited twice. Her urine and stools are a normal colour and her skin is not yellow.
clues.vitals: Temp 38.4 °C, HR 102/min, BP 134/82 mmHg, RR 18/min, SpO2 98% on room air.
clues.exam: Tender in the right upper quadrant with guarding. When the examiner presses below the right costal margin and she breathes in deeply, she stops mid-breath because of pain (Murphy's sign); the same test on the left side is painless. No jaundice. The rest of the abdomen is soft.
clues.labs: WBC 15.1 ×10^9/L with neutrophilia; CRP markedly raised. Bilirubin 19 µmol/L (normal under 21), ALT 48 U/L and ALP 140 U/L, both only slightly raised. Lipase normal, which makes pancreatitis unlikely.
clues.imaging: Right upper quadrant ultrasound: several gallstones, one stuck in the gallbladder neck. The gallbladder wall is thickened to 6 mm with a rim of fluid around it, and pressing the probe directly over the gallbladder reproduces her pain (sonographic Murphy sign). The common bile duct is normal width with no stones seen.

explain.patho: Gallstones form when bile holds more cholesterol (or bilirubin pigment) than it can keep dissolved, so crystals grow into stones. After a fatty meal the hormone cholecystokinin makes the gallbladder contract, which can jam a stone into its outlet, the cystic duct. Brief blockage causes biliary colic that fades when the stone falls back. If the stone stays stuck, trapped concentrated bile irritates the wall chemically, the gallbladder distends and its blood supply suffers, and bacteria from the gut often join in. The inflamed gallbladder touches the parietal peritoneum and diaphragm, giving localised pain and pain referred to the right shoulder via the phrenic nerve. Untreated, the wall can become gangrenous or perforate.
explain.confirm: Ultrasound is the key test: gallstones plus a thickened wall, fluid around the gallbladder and a sonographic Murphy sign, together with fever and raised white cells (the Tokyo criteria). A HIDA scan, which shows the gallbladder failing to fill, can help when ultrasound is unclear.
explain.treat: Admission, intravenous fluids, pain relief, nil by mouth at first and intravenous antibiotics. The definitive treatment is laparoscopic cholecystectomy, ideally early, during the same admission. Patients too unwell for surgery can have the gallbladder drained through the skin (cholecystostomy) until they recover.

near.biliary colic: Very close, but colic settles within a few hours and doesn't cause fever, high white cells or a thick-walled gallbladder.
near.acute pancreatitis: Pain here is under the right ribs, not boring through to the back, and the lipase is normal.
near.ascending cholangitis: That's a stone in the common bile duct with jaundice; her bilirubin and duct are normal.

cases.pearl: Biliary colic fades in hours; pain that lasts more than about six hours plus fever means the gallbladder itself is inflamed.

cases.complaint: An 11-year-old girl is seen in clinic because she has dropped down the growth chart and is always tired and bloated.

clues.history: Over two years she has fallen from the 50th to the 9th centile for height and weight. She has loose, pale, smelly stools that are hard to flush, a bloated tummy after meals and frequent tummy aches. Teachers say she gets exhausted easily. Her mother has type 1 diabetes and an aunt follows a special diet for a 'gut problem'.
clues.vitals: Temp 36.8 °C, HR 92/min, BP 98/60 mmHg, RR 18/min, SpO2 99% on room air.
clues.exam: Thin limbs with reduced muscle bulk and buttock wasting, and a distended, soft, non-tender abdomen. Pale conjunctivae. Small, painless mouth ulcers. A few itchy, blistering bumps on her elbows.
clues.labs: Haemoglobin 98 g/L with small, pale red cells (MCV 71 fL) and very low ferritin; folate also low. Albumin 33 g/L, slightly low. Tissue transglutaminase IgA antibody (tTG-IgA) more than ten times the upper limit of normal, with a normal total IgA (so the result can be trusted); anti-endomysial antibody positive. Thyroid tests normal.
clues.imaging: Upper GI endoscopy: the duodenal lining looks flattened with a scalloped pattern of folds. Biopsies of the duodenum show total loss of the finger-like villi, deepened crypts and many lymphocytes packed into the surface lining (Marsh 3 changes).

explain.patho: Coeliac disease is an autoimmune reaction to gluten, a protein in wheat, barley and rye, in people who carry the immune genes HLA-DQ2 or DQ8. Gluten fragments called gliadin resist digestion; the enzyme tissue transglutaminase modifies them so they fit tightly onto these HLA molecules. Immune T cells then attack, and the inflammation flattens the villi, the folds that give the small intestine its huge absorbing surface. With less surface, fat (pale floating stools), iron and folate (anaemia), and calories and protein (poor growth, low albumin) are poorly absorbed. The body also makes antibodies against tissue transglutaminase, which is why that antibody is such a useful blood test. Other autoimmune conditions, such as type 1 diabetes and thyroid disease, often cluster in the same families.
explain.confirm: Blood test for tTG-IgA, checked alongside total IgA, while the person is still eating gluten. In adults, and most children, the diagnosis is confirmed by duodenal biopsies showing villous atrophy. Some children with a very high tTG and a positive endomysial antibody can be diagnosed without a biopsy under paediatric guidelines.
explain.treat: A strict, lifelong gluten-free diet, which allows the villi to regrow and symptoms to resolve, with help from a specialist dietitian. Nutritional deficiencies such as iron and folate are corrected with supplements. Follow-up checks that antibodies fall and growth catches up, and screens for related conditions.

near.irritable bowel syndrome: IBS doesn't cause growth failure, iron deficiency and flattened villi; this is an immune reaction to something she eats.
near.crohn's disease: Crohn's also causes poor growth and anaemia, but the antibody result here points to a reaction to a dietary protein.
near.lactose intolerance: That causes bloating and diarrhoea after dairy, but not falling centiles, anaemia or positive autoantibodies.

cases.pearl: Always check total IgA with a coeliac antibody test: people with IgA deficiency (more common in coeliac disease) can have a falsely negative tTG-IgA.

cases.complaint: A 67-year-old man has had a cough, fever and shivering for three days and is now breathless.

clues.history: Three days of fever with shaking chills, a cough that started dry and now brings up rust-coloured sputum, and a sharp pain on the right side of his chest when he breathes in. He feels weak and has barely eaten. He has type 2 diabetes. No recent hospital stay, no travel.
clues.vitals: Temp 39.2 °C, HR 112/min, BP 104/62 mmHg, RR 28/min, SpO2 90% on room air.
clues.exam: Flushed and breathless but fully alert. Reduced chest movement on the right with a dull note when tapped over the right lower zone. Over the same area: bronchial breathing, coarse crackles and increased vocal resonance. Left lung clear. Heart sounds normal.
clues.labs: WBC 18.4 ×10^9/L with neutrophilia, CRP markedly raised. Urea 7.9 mmol/L (raised), creatinine 118 µmol/L, sodium 132 mmol/L, glucose 13.1 mmol/L. Lactate 1.8 mmol/L. Urine pneumococcal antigen positive. Blood cultures grow Streptococcus pneumoniae.
clues.imaging: Chest X-ray: dense white consolidation filling the right lower lobe with dark branching air bronchograms inside it; the right heart border is still visible. No effusion. ECG: sinus tachycardia.

explain.patho: Bacteria such as Streptococcus pneumoniae are breathed in or aspirated from the throat and get past the airway's defences (mucus, cilia and cough) into the alveoli. They multiply and trigger an intense inflammatory response: capillaries leak fluid, then neutrophils, red cells and fibrin flood the air sacs. The alveoli fill with this exudate instead of air, so the lung becomes solid (consolidation), which shows as a white area on X-ray with dark air-filled bronchi running through it. Blood still flows through lung that isn't ventilated, so oxygen falls. Solid lung transmits sound better, causing bronchial breathing and increased vocal resonance, and inflamed pleura over it causes pleuritic pain. Rust-coloured sputum comes from red blood cells in the exudate. Cytokines released into the blood cause fever, chills and, in severe cases, sepsis.
explain.confirm: New consolidation on chest X-ray in someone with symptoms of a lower respiratory infection confirms pneumonia. Sputum and blood cultures and urine antigen tests identify the organism. Severity is scored with CURB-65 (confusion, urea, respiratory rate, blood pressure, age), which guides whether to treat at home, on a ward or in intensive care.
explain.treat: Antibiotics are chosen by severity and local guidelines (for example a penicillin-type antibiotic, with a macrolide added in moderate or severe cases), started promptly. Supportive care includes oxygen to keep saturations up, intravenous fluids, fever control and early mobilisation. Severe cases may need high-flow oxygen, ventilation or treatment for sepsis; pneumococcal and flu vaccines help prevent it.

near.pulmonary embolism: He has a high fever, rusty sputum and signs of solid lung, which point to infection rather than a clot.
near.acute heart failure: Crackles fit, but they're on one side only with bronchial breathing and fever.
near.tuberculosis: A fair thought for a cough, but this came on over days with a high fever and a lower-lobe consolidation, not weeks of weight loss and an upper-lobe cavity.

cases.pearl: Bronchial breathing over a dull area means solid lung transmitting sound: the classic sign of consolidation.

cases.complaint: A 72-year-old woman with a long smoking history comes in with three days of worsening breathlessness and more sputum than usual.

clues.history: She smoked 25 cigarettes a day for 45 years and stopped two years ago. Normally she gets breathless walking 100 m. Three days ago she caught a cold, and since then her breathing has got much worse, her cough is more frequent and her sputum has turned thick and green. She uses inhalers daily and has had two similar flare-ups this year.
clues.vitals: Temp 37.8 °C, HR 106/min, BP 142/84 mmHg, RR 26/min, SpO2 85% on room air.
clues.exam: Breathing through pursed lips and using neck muscles. Barrel-shaped chest, reduced chest expansion and a hyperresonant note. Quiet breath sounds with a widespread wheeze and some crackles at both bases. No ankle swelling. Slight nicotine staining of fingers but no clubbing. Alert and orientated.
clues.labs: Arterial gas on air: pH 7.31, PaO2 6.9 kPa, PaCO2 7.8 kPa (high), bicarbonate 31 mmol/L (raised, showing chronic CO2 retention with an acute rise on top). WBC 12.6 ×10^9/L, CRP moderately raised. Haemoglobin 158 g/L. Sputum culture grows Haemophilus influenzae.
clues.imaging: Chest X-ray: hyperinflated lungs with flat diaphragms, more than seven ribs visible in front, a long thin heart and few blood vessels in the upper zones (emphysema); no consolidation and no pneumothorax. ECG: sinus tachycardia with tall P waves (right atrial strain). Previous spirometry: FEV1/FVC 0.52, FEV1 41% predicted, not reversible.

explain.patho: Years of breathing in cigarette smoke cause chronic inflammation in the lungs. In the airways, mucus glands enlarge and small airways scar and narrow (chronic bronchitis); in the lung tissue, enzymes released by inflammatory cells break down the elastic walls of the alveoli, merging them into large, floppy air spaces (emphysema). With less elastic recoil, small airways collapse on breathing out, trapping air and hyperinflating the chest. An infection or other trigger adds swelling, mucus and bronchospasm on top of this, so airflow falls further. The lungs can't clear carbon dioxide well enough, so CO2 rises and the blood becomes acidic (respiratory acidosis); the kidneys had already kept extra bicarbonate to compensate for her chronic CO2 retention. Some patients rely partly on low oxygen to drive their breathing, which is why oxygen is given carefully.
explain.confirm: An exacerbation is a clinical diagnosis: a sustained worsening of breathlessness, cough or sputum beyond normal day-to-day variation in someone with COPD. The underlying COPD is confirmed by spirometry showing a post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.7. A blood gas shows how severe it is, and the X-ray excludes pneumonia, pneumothorax or heart failure.
explain.treat: Controlled oxygen with a lower saturation target to avoid worsening carbon dioxide retention, nebulised bronchodilators, a short course of oral steroids and antibiotics when sputum becomes purulent. If the blood stays acidic from high carbon dioxide despite treatment, non-invasive ventilation (BiPAP) helps her breathe out carbon dioxide. Long term: inhaled bronchodilators and sometimes steroids, pulmonary rehabilitation, flu and pneumococcal vaccines and staying smoke-free.

near.asthma: Wheeze fits, but she's an older ex-smoker with fixed airflow limitation and chronic CO2 retention.
near.pneumonia: She has a fever and green sputum, but the X-ray shows no consolidation.
near.acute heart failure: No raised JVP, no leg swelling and a thin heart on X-ray; the problem is the airways.

cases.pearl: In COPD, a raised bicarbonate in the blood gas tells you the CO2 has been high for a long time; oxygen is titrated to a lower target rather than turned up to maximum.

cases.complaint: A 17-year-old boy has had months of diarrhoea, cramping pain in his lower right abdomen and weight loss.

clues.history: For five months he has had loose stools four to six times a day, sometimes waking him at night, with cramping lower-right abdominal pain after meals. He has lost 7 kg and feels constantly drained. He gets painful mouth ulcers and recently noticed tender red lumps on his shins. There has been no travel and nobody at home is unwell.
clues.vitals: Temp 37.6 °C, HR 96/min, BP 118/72 mmHg, RR 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air.
clues.exam: Thin and pale. Several aphthous ulcers inside the cheeks. A tender, firm, sausage-shaped mass in the right iliac fossa. Raised, tender, reddish-purple nodules on both shins (erythema nodosum).
clues.labs: Haemoglobin 104 g/L, platelets 520 ×10^9/L (high, reacting to inflammation), CRP raised, albumin 29 g/L (low). Faecal calprotectin very high, showing inflammation in the bowel wall itself. Stool cultures negative for infection; coeliac antibody negative.
clues.imaging: MR enterography: the last 15 cm of the small intestine (terminal ileum) has a thick, inflamed wall with a narrowed segment, and there is a second, separate inflamed patch higher up with normal bowel between. Colonoscopy: patchy deep ulcers in the terminal ileum giving a cobblestone look; biopsies show inflammation through the full thickness with non-caseating granulomas.

explain.patho: Crohn's disease is a chronic inflammatory bowel disease caused by an abnormal immune response to the normal gut bacteria in a genetically susceptible person (for example with NOD2 gene variants), influenced by environment. The immune reaction is driven by T-helper cells and TNF-alpha and goes through the whole thickness of the bowel wall (transmural), which is why it can cause strictures, fistulas between loops and abscesses. It can affect anywhere from mouth to anus but most often the terminal ileum, and in characteristic 'skip lesions' with normal bowel in between. The terminal ileum absorbs vitamin B12 and recycles bile acids, so disease there causes B12 deficiency and bile-acid diarrhoea. Granulomas, organised clusters of immune cells, are a hallmark under the microscope. The same immune activity can affect the skin, eyes and joints.
explain.confirm: Diagnosis combines symptoms, raised inflammatory markers and faecal calprotectin, with ileocolonoscopy and biopsies (transmural inflammation, granulomas, skip lesions). MR enterography maps small-bowel disease and complications such as strictures without radiation. Infections are excluded with stool tests.
explain.treat: Flares are calmed with corticosteroids, or in children often with exclusive liquid enteral nutrition, which avoids steroid side effects on growth. Long-term control uses immunomodulators (such as azathioprine) and biologic drugs (anti-TNF antibodies and newer agents). Surgery is used for strictures, fistulas or abscesses, but it does not cure the disease. Nutrition, iron and vitamin levels, growth and bone health are all monitored.

near.ulcerative colitis: Also an IBD, but that is continuous, starts in the rectum and stays in the colon; here the ileum is involved with skip lesions and granulomas.
near.appendicitis: The right iliac fossa is right, but five months of diarrhoea and weight loss is not an acute appendix.
near.coeliac disease: Diarrhoea and weight loss fit, but the antibody is negative and the ileum shows granulomas.
near.inflammatory bowel disease: Right family! Now be specific: which type of IBD causes skip lesions and granulomas?

cases.pearl: Crohn's: skip lesions, transmural, granulomas, anywhere from mouth to anus. UC: continuous, mucosal, rectum outward.

cases.dx: Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) of the leg
cases.complaint: A 46-year-old man notices his left calf is swollen and aching three days after a long flight home from Australia.

clues.history: He flew 14 hours from Sydney, mostly sitting in a window seat and sleeping. Two days later his left calf began aching, especially when walking, and the leg looks bigger. No injury. He had treatment for bowel cancer last year. No chest pain, no breathlessness, no coughing up blood.
clues.vitals: Temp 37.2 °C, HR 84/min, BP 132/82 mmHg, RR 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air.
clues.exam: Left calf 4 cm larger in circumference than the right, measured 10 cm below the kneecap. Pitting oedema of the left lower leg. Warmth and tenderness along the course of the deep veins behind the knee and in the calf. Superficial veins slightly more visible. No skin break, no red streaks. Pulses normal. Chest clear.
clues.labs: D-dimer raised. Full blood count normal (platelets 248 ×10^9/L, haemoglobin 141 g/L). Creatinine 79 µmol/L. Clotting screen normal before treatment. CRP mildly raised.
clues.imaging: Compression ultrasound of the left leg: the popliteal vein and calf veins do not squash flat under the probe and contain echogenic clot, with no flow on Doppler; the femoral vein is clear. Chest X-ray not needed, as there are no lung symptoms. Wells score: 'DVT likely'.

explain.patho: Virchow's triad sums up why clots form in veins: slow flow (stasis), damage to the vessel wall, and blood that clots more easily (hypercoagulability). Sitting still for hours on a flight makes blood pool in the calf veins because the calf muscle pump isn't squeezing it back up. A history of cancer makes the blood more prone to clotting. A clot usually starts in the pockets behind the valves in the calf veins and grows upward toward the knee and thigh. The blocked vein stops blood draining from the leg, so the leg swells and aches, and inflammation around the vein causes warmth and tenderness. The biggest danger is that part of the clot breaks off and travels to the lungs as a pulmonary embolism; longer-term, damaged valves can cause post-thrombotic syndrome, with chronic swelling and skin changes.
explain.confirm: The Wells score estimates how likely a DVT is. If unlikely, a normal D-dimer rules it out; if likely or the D-dimer is raised, a compression ultrasound is the key test, and a vein that will not compress confirms the clot.
explain.treat: Anticoagulation, usually with a direct oral anticoagulant or low-molecular-weight heparin, is given for months to stop the clot growing and prevent a pulmonary embolism while the body dissolves it. The length of treatment depends on whether there was a clear temporary trigger or an ongoing risk such as cancer. Walking is encouraged, and on future long flights he should move around, flex his calves and stay well hydrated.

near.cellulitis: Cellulitis gives a hot red skin infection, often with a break in the skin and fever; here the ultrasound finds the problem inside a vein.
near.baker's cyst: A burst cyst behind the knee can mimic this, but the ultrasound shows clot in the vein, not fluid.
near.pulmonary embolism: That's the complication to watch for, but he has no breathlessness, chest pain or low oxygen yet.

cases.pearl: A swollen, tender calf after a long flight or operation is a clot until an ultrasound says it isn't.

cases.complaint: A 13-year-old girl is brought to the ED drowsy, vomiting and breathing fast after a few weeks of feeling unwell.

clues.history: For three weeks she has been drinking huge amounts, getting up several times a night to pass urine, and has lost weight despite eating well; her jeans are loose. Over the last day she developed tummy pain and vomiting and has become sleepy and hard to wake fully. Her grandmother has thyroid disease. She has not been ill with anything else recently.
clues.vitals: Temp 36.9 °C, HR 128/min, BP 100/62 mmHg, RR 32/min (deep, sighing breaths), SpO2 99% on room air.
clues.exam: Drowsy but rousable and talking (GCS 14). Dry mouth, sunken eyes and slow capillary refill. Deep, regular, laboured breathing (Kussmaul breathing) and a sweet, fruity smell on her breath. The abdomen is diffusely tender without guarding.
clues.labs: Venous blood gas: pH 7.08 (normal 7.35–7.45), bicarbonate 7 mmol/L, pCO2 2.6 kPa (low, as she blows off CO2). Glucose 29.4 mmol/L, blood ketones (beta-hydroxybutyrate) 6.2 mmol/L. Sodium 131 mmol/L, potassium 5.6 mmol/L, anion gap high. Urea 8.5 mmol/L, creatinine 92 µmol/L.
clues.imaging: ECG: sinus tachycardia with slightly tall T waves, consistent with the raised potassium. Chest X-ray normal, no infection. No head scan was needed because her conscious level improves with treatment and there are no signs of brain swelling.

explain.patho: In type 1 diabetes the immune system destroys the insulin-making beta cells of the pancreas. Without insulin, cells cannot take up glucose, so glucose builds up in the blood and spills into the urine, dragging water with it (thirst, frequent urination, dehydration). The body behaves as if it is starving: fat is broken down and the liver turns the fatty acids into ketone bodies, which are acids. As ketones accumulate, bicarbonate is used up and the blood becomes acidic; the brain responds by driving deep, fast breathing to blow off carbon dioxide (Kussmaul breathing). Acidosis and lack of insulin push potassium out of cells, so blood potassium can look high even though total body potassium is depleted by urine losses. Once insulin is given, potassium rushes back into cells and can fall dangerously low.
explain.confirm: Diagnosis requires all three: high blood glucose (or known diabetes), raised blood ketones, and acidosis (low pH or low bicarbonate). Autoantibodies (such as GAD and IA-2) and a low C-peptide later confirm type 1 diabetes.
explain.treat: Careful intravenous fluid replacement and an intravenous insulin infusion to switch off ketone production, with potassium added to the fluids and glucose added once blood sugar falls. Electrolytes, ketones, glucose and conscious level are checked frequently. Children are watched closely for cerebral oedema, the most feared complication, which is why fluids are given more cautiously than in adults. After recovery she moves to long-term insulin, with education from a diabetes team.

near.gastroenteritis: Vomiting and tummy pain fit, but weeks of thirst, weight loss and a glucose near thirty point elsewhere.
near.hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state: That's usually older people with type 2 diabetes and a sky-high glucose without much ketone or acid; she is very acidotic with high ketones.
near.appendicitis: Abdominal pain can be part of this metabolic emergency; check the blood gas and the breath.

cases.pearl: Thirst, frequent urination, weight loss and tiredness in a child: check a finger-prick glucose the same day; delay can mean DKA.

cases.complaint: A 16-year-old boy is brought in two hours after being hit on the side of the head by a hockey puck. He seemed fine at first but is now vomiting and very drowsy.

clues.history: The puck struck his left temple; he was knocked out for under a minute, then got up, said he was fine and sat on the bench chatting for about an hour (a lucid interval). Over the last 40 minutes he has developed a worsening headache, vomited three times and become hard to keep awake. No other medical problems.
clues.vitals: Temp 36.9 °C, HR 52/min, BP 172/92 mmHg, RR 10/min and irregular, SpO2 94% on room air (high blood pressure, slow pulse and irregular breathing: the Cushing response to raised intracranial pressure).
clues.exam: GCS 9 (opens eyes to pain, incomprehensible sounds, localises to pain). Boggy swelling over the left temple. Left pupil dilated and sluggish, right pupil normal. Weakness of the right arm and leg with an upgoing right plantar.
clues.labs: Haemoglobin 142 g/L, platelets 255 ×10^9/L, INR and APTT normal. Glucose 6.0 mmol/L, sodium 140 mmol/L. Blood group and crossmatch sent for theatre.
clues.imaging: Non-contrast CT head: a lens-shaped (biconvex) bright collection of blood over the left temporal lobe that stops at the suture lines, compressing the brain with 8 mm of midline shift and effacement of the basal cisterns. Bone windows: a linear fracture of the thin left temporal bone crossing the groove of the middle meningeal artery.

explain.patho: The pterion, where four skull bones meet at the temple, is thin, and the middle meningeal artery runs just underneath it. A blow there fractures the bone and tears the artery. High-pressure arterial blood peels the dura away from the inner skull, but the dura is glued tightly at the sutures, so the clot bulges inward as a lens shape. At first the skull compensates by squeezing out CSF and venous blood (the Monro–Kellie doctrine), so the patient can seem fine. Once that reserve is used up, pressure climbs steeply and the temporal lobe's uncus is pushed over the edge of the tentorium, compressing the third nerve (a blown pupil on the same side) and the cerebral peduncle (weakness on the opposite side). The brainstem reacts with the Cushing triad of hypertension, bradycardia and irregular breathing, a sign of imminent herniation.
explain.confirm: An urgent non-contrast CT head shows the biconvex collection that respects the sutures, usually with an overlying skull fracture. Head injury rules (such as the Canadian CT Head rule) flag who needs scanning.
explain.treat: This is a neurosurgical emergency: he needs an urgent craniotomy to remove the clot and stop the bleeding artery. While theatre is prepared he is intubated to protect his airway, his head is raised, and hyperosmolar therapy (mannitol or hypertonic saline) can buy time by drawing water out of the brain. Small epidural haematomas in alert patients are sometimes watched with repeat scans, but with a blown pupil surgery cannot wait.

near.subdural haematoma: Close, but this clot is lens-shaped and stops at the sutures, from a torn artery in a young person, not a crescent from torn veins.
near.concussion: Concussion doesn't make you deteriorate after a good spell, blow a pupil or slow your heart.
near.subarachnoid haemorrhage: The blood isn't in the cisterns around the brain; it's a lens-shaped clot between skull and dura.

cases.pearl: 'Talk and die': someone chatting after a head blow can still have an expanding arterial bleed, which is why a skull fracture near the temple gets a scan and close watch.

cases.complaint: A 58-year-old woman arrives by ambulance with severe upper abdominal pain that started suddenly this morning and is boring through to her back.

clues.history: Pain began in the upper middle abdomen over about an hour and now feels like it is going straight through to her back. Sitting up and leaning forward helps a little. She has vomited repeatedly. Last year she was told she had gallstones after an episode of right-sided pain, but she was waiting for surgery. She takes no regular medicines.
clues.vitals: Temp 37.8 °C, HR 112/min, BP 108/68 mmHg, RR 22/min, SpO2 95% on room air.
clues.exam: She looks unwell and is lying very still. The upper abdomen is markedly tender with guarding, and bowel sounds are quiet. Her eyes are slightly yellow. No bruising of the flanks or around the umbilicus yet.
clues.labs: Lipase 2,600 U/L (more than three times the upper limit of normal). ALT 320 U/L and bilirubin 42 µmol/L; an ALT this high strongly points to a gallstone cause. WBC 16.5 ×10^9/L, urea 9.8 mmol/L, glucose 9.1 mmol/L. Calcium 2.28 mmol/L and triglycerides normal, ruling out those two causes.
clues.imaging: Abdominal ultrasound: multiple gallstones in the gallbladder and a common bile duct widened to 8 mm. The pancreas is partly hidden by gas. A CT done later shows a swollen pancreas with fluid around it but no areas of dead tissue.

explain.patho: The pancreas makes powerful digestive enzymes that are normally stored in an inactive form and switched on only inside the intestine. A small gallstone passing down the common bile duct can lodge at the ampulla, where the bile duct and pancreatic duct share an exit, blocking pancreatic outflow. Pressure and reflux cause trypsinogen to be activated to trypsin inside the pancreas itself, and trypsin then activates the other enzymes: the gland starts digesting itself. This releases inflammatory signals that make blood vessels leaky, so fluid shifts out of the circulation into the tissues, causing a fast heart rate, low blood pressure and raised urea. In severe cases the inflammation spreads to the whole body, damaging the lungs and kidneys and causing parts of the pancreas to die (necrosis).
explain.confirm: Two of three criteria are needed: typical pain, lipase or amylase above three times the upper limit of normal, and imaging showing pancreatitis. Ultrasound looks for gallstones as the cause; a high ALT supports a biliary origin. CT is reserved for unclear diagnosis or for checking complications after a few days, and severity is graded by organ failure.
explain.treat: Supportive care is the core: careful intravenous fluids, good pain relief, oxygen if needed and early feeding by mouth or tube rather than prolonged fasting. ERCP to clear the duct is done if there is cholangitis or a persistently blocked duct. To stop it happening again, the gallbladder is removed, ideally during the same admission once the attack settles.

near.acute cholecystitis: Gallstones are involved, but the lipase is sky high and the pain goes through to the back; think about the organ that drains beside the bile duct.
near.perforated peptic ulcer: That gives free air under the diaphragm and a rigid abdomen, not a lipase in the thousands.
near.myocardial infarction: Always worth an ECG for upper abdominal pain, but the enzyme pattern here points below the diaphragm.

cases.pearl: In pancreatitis the height of the lipase tells you the diagnosis, not the severity; severity is judged by organ failure.

cases.complaint: A 61-year-old man's wife says that over six weeks he has become irritable and withdrawn, gets morning headaches and struggles to find words. Last week his right arm jerked uncontrollably for a minute.

clues.history: Headaches are worst on waking and with coughing, and sometimes he vomits in the morning. He keeps losing his thread mid-sentence and calls things by the wrong name. His wife says he has lost interest in things he used to love. Last week his right arm jerked rhythmically for about a minute while he stayed awake (a focal seizure). No fever, no weight loss, no known cancer anywhere else.
clues.vitals: Temp 36.8 °C, HR 64/min, BP 150/86 mmHg, RR 14/min, SpO2 98% on room air.
clues.exam: Mild expressive dysphasia (hesitant speech, word-finding errors). Mild right lower-face weakness and a right pronator drift. Right-sided reflexes slightly brisker. Early swelling of both optic discs (papilloedema). Sensation and coordination are normal.
clues.labs: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver tests and calcium normal. CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis shows no tumour elsewhere (makes a metastasis unlikely). After surgery, pathology: a highly cellular astrocytic tumour with necrosis surrounded by palisading tumour cells and proliferating small vessels; molecular testing shows IDH-wildtype and a methylated MGMT promoter.
clues.imaging: MRI brain with contrast: a 5 cm mass in the left frontal and temporal lobes with a thick, irregular rim that lights up with contrast around a dark necrotic centre. A large surrounding area of bright T2 signal (oedema and infiltrating tumour) causes 6 mm of midline shift. MR perfusion shows high blood volume in the rim and MR spectroscopy shows high choline and low N-acetylaspartate, typical of an aggressive tumour.

explain.patho: Glioblastoma is the most common primary malignant brain tumour in adults, arising from astrocyte-like glial cells; most are IDH-wildtype, the most aggressive kind. It grows fast, and its cells don't stay in one lump: they crawl along white-matter tracts and blood vessels far beyond the visible edge, so surgery can't remove every cell. The tumour outgrows its blood supply, so its centre dies (necrosis) and the surviving hypoxic cells pump out VEGF, driving leaky new vessels; these leak contrast (the enhancing rim) and fluid (vasogenic oedema). The growing mass and oedema raise intracranial pressure, causing morning headaches, vomiting and papilloedema. Irritation of the cortex causes seizures, and damage to the dominant frontal and temporal lobes explains personality change and language problems. MGMT is a DNA repair enzyme; when its gene is silenced by methylation, the tumour can't repair damage from chemotherapy as well.
explain.confirm: MRI with contrast strongly suggests the diagnosis, but it's confirmed only by tissue from a biopsy or resection, examined under the microscope and by molecular testing (IDH status, MGMT methylation and other markers in the WHO classification). Body imaging helps rule out metastases from elsewhere.
explain.treat: Treatment begins with maximal safe surgical removal, often with awake craniotomy and brain mapping to protect speech, and fluorescent dye guidance to see tumour tissue. This is followed by radiotherapy combined with temozolomide chemotherapy, then further chemotherapy cycles. Corticosteroids (dexamethasone) reduce the brain swelling, antiseizure medicines control seizures, and some patients use tumour-treating fields. Palliative care is involved early because the outlook remains poor.

near.brain abscess: An abscess also rings, but he has no fever, normal markers, and MR perfusion shows high blood volume typical of tumour.
near.brain metastasis: Metastases are common, but his body scans are clear and the pathology shows a primary glial tumour.
near.stroke: A stroke starts suddenly; this crept up over weeks with headaches, seizures and a mass on MRI.
near.meningioma: Meningiomas sit outside the brain on the dura and enhance evenly; this one is inside the brain with a necrotic centre.

cases.pearl: Glioblastoma is always bigger than it looks: tumour cells are found centimetres beyond the enhancing rim on the MRI.
