cases.complaint: A 16-year-old girl is referred because she has lost weight, feels jittery all the time and her friends say her eyes look 'starey'.

clues.history: Over four months she has lost 6 kg despite eating more than usual. She feels hot when others are cold, sweats a lot, and her heart pounds even at rest. Her hands shake so much her handwriting has got messy, she has loose stools a few times a day, and she struggles to sleep and concentrate. Her aunt has an underactive thyroid.
clues.vitals: Temp 37.4 °C, HR 118/min (regular), BP 132/58 mmHg (wide pulse pressure), RR 18/min, SpO2 99% on room air.
clues.exam: Fine tremor of the outstretched hands and warm, moist skin. A smooth, evenly enlarged, non-tender thyroid with a soft whooshing sound over it on listening (a bruit). Both eyes bulge forward with white visible above the iris (proptosis and lid retraction), and the upper lids lag behind when she looks down. Brisk reflexes.
clues.labs: TSH below 0.01 mU/L (normal 0.4–4.0), free T4 52 pmol/L (normal 12–22) and free T3 also high. TSH-receptor antibodies (TRAb) strongly positive. Full blood count normal. Mildly raised ALP from increased bone turnover.
clues.imaging: Thyroid ultrasound: a diffusely enlarged gland with greatly increased blood flow throughout ('thyroid inferno') and no nodules. A radioactive uptake scan (if done) shows high, evenly spread uptake across the whole gland. ECG: sinus tachycardia.

explain.patho: Graves' disease is an autoimmune condition in which the immune system makes antibodies that mimic TSH, the pituitary hormone that normally tells the thyroid to work. These TSH-receptor antibodies switch the thyroid on continuously, so it grows (goitre) and pours out thyroid hormones T4 and T3. Thyroid hormone sets the body's metabolic rate and increases sensitivity to adrenaline, causing weight loss, heat intolerance, tremor, fast heart rate, sweating and anxiety. The high hormone levels feed back to the pituitary, shutting TSH production down almost to zero. The same immune process inflames the muscles and fat behind the eyes, pushing the eyeballs forward (thyroid eye disease), which is specific to Graves'.
explain.confirm: A suppressed TSH with high free T4 and/or T3 confirms hyperthyroidism. Positive TSH-receptor antibodies confirm Graves' as the cause, and eye signs make it almost certain. A radionuclide uptake scan separates Graves' (diffuse high uptake) from thyroiditis (low uptake) or toxic nodules (patchy uptake).
explain.treat: Beta-blockers quickly calm the tremor and racing heart. Antithyroid drugs (such as carbimazole or methimazole) reduce hormone production and many patients enter remission after a long course. If it relapses, definitive options are radioactive iodine or surgical removal of the thyroid, after which lifelong thyroid hormone replacement is needed. Eye disease is managed with an eye specialist and may need anti-inflammatory treatment.

near.anxiety: Anxiety can make you shaky with a fast heart, but it doesn't cause a goitre, bulging eyes or a suppressed TSH.
near.toxic multinodular goitre: That causes an overactive thyroid in older people with lumpy glands; she's young with a smooth gland, eye signs and antibodies.
near.hashimoto's thyroiditis: Right organ, also autoimmune, but that usually makes the thyroid underactive; her hormones are sky high.
near.hyperthyroidism: Yes, her thyroid is overactive. Now name the specific autoimmune cause that also makes the eyes bulge.

cases.pearl: Eye bulging (proptosis) plus an overactive thyroid points to Graves' disease specifically; other causes of hyperthyroidism don't cause it.

cases.complaint: A 34-year-old man has had tingling in his feet and hands for four days and now can't climb the stairs; this morning he struggled to lift a cup.

clues.history: Two weeks ago he had a few days of severe diarrhoea and cramps after a barbecue with undercooked chicken. The tingling started in his toes and fingertips; then weakness crept up from his legs to his hips and now his arms. He has an aching lower back. Today his face feels 'heavy' and he feels short of breath lying flat.
clues.vitals: Temp 37.0 °C, HR 118/min swinging down to 60/min at times, BP 158/96 mmHg varying a lot between readings, RR 22/min and shallow, SpO2 95% on room air. He can only count to 12 in one breath.
clues.exam: Symmetric flaccid weakness, worse in the legs than the arms. All tendon reflexes absent. Mild glove-and-stocking loss of light touch and vibration. Weak face on both sides (can't puff out cheeks or close eyes tightly). No sensory level on the trunk, normal bladder function, no muscle tenderness.
clues.labs: Sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, CK normal (rules out muscle disease), glucose 5.4 mmol/L. Bedside spirometry: forced vital capacity 1.6 L (predicted 4.8 L) and falling on repeat measurement. CSF: protein 1.8 g/L with white cells 2 ×10^6/L (high protein, normal cells). Stool culture from his illness: Campylobacter jejuni. Anti-ganglioside antibodies positive.
clues.imaging: Nerve conduction studies: slowed conduction velocities, prolonged distal latencies, conduction block and absent F waves (a demyelinating pattern). MRI spine: enhancement of the cauda equina nerve roots, no spinal cord compression.

explain.patho: GBS is an autoimmune attack on peripheral nerves, usually triggered by an infection a few weeks earlier. Campylobacter's outer coat carries sugar molecules that look almost identical to gangliosides on human nerve membranes, so antibodies made against the bacterium cross-react with nerves (molecular mimicry). Antibodies and complement mark the myelin, and macrophages strip it off, slowing or blocking conduction; longer nerves are hit first, so symptoms start in the feet and climb. Because the damage is in peripheral nerves, the signs are lower motor neuron: floppy weakness and lost reflexes. Inflamed nerve roots leak protein into the CSF without drawing in white cells. Autonomic nerve involvement causes heart rate and blood pressure swings, and weakness of the diaphragm and chest muscles can cause respiratory failure. Schwann cells can remyelinate, so most people recover over months.
explain.confirm: The diagnosis is clinical: progressive, fairly symmetric weakness with reduced or absent reflexes. It is supported by high CSF protein with a normal cell count (albuminocytological dissociation, which may be absent in the first week) and nerve conduction studies showing demyelination or axonal damage.
explain.treat: He needs immunotherapy with intravenous immunoglobulin or plasma exchange, which are equally effective; corticosteroids do not help. Vital capacity is measured regularly, and he goes to intensive care for ventilation if it keeps falling, with heart monitoring for autonomic instability. Clot prevention, pain control, physiotherapy and rehabilitation support recovery.

near.myasthenia gravis: Myasthenia keeps reflexes and sensation; here reflexes are gone and there's tingling.
near.spinal cord compression: A cord problem gives brisk reflexes and a sensory level on the trunk; he has neither.
near.hypokalaemia: His potassium is normal, and low potassium doesn't raise CSF protein.
near.transverse myelitis: That would give a sensory level and bladder trouble; his problem is in the peripheral nerves.

cases.pearl: Watch the vital capacity, not the oxygen saturation: sats stay normal until the breathing muscles are already failing.

cases.complaint: A 44-year-old woman sees her GP because she is exhausted, has gained weight and feels cold all the time.

clues.history: Over the past year she has gained 8 kg without eating more. She is always cold, even in summer, her skin is dry and her hair has become coarse and thin, and she is constipated. She feels slow and foggy and her voice has become hoarse. Her mother has vitiligo and her sister has type 1 diabetes.
clues.vitals: Temp 36.1 °C, HR 54/min, BP 136/88 mmHg, RR 14/min, SpO2 98% on room air.
clues.exam: Puffy face and eyelids, dry and cool skin, thinning of the outer third of the eyebrows. A firm, slightly enlarged, non-tender, bumpy thyroid. Ankle reflexes contract normally but relax very slowly. Mild non-pitting swelling of the shins.
clues.labs: TSH 42 mU/L (normal 0.4–4.0), free T4 6 pmol/L (normal 12–22). Anti-thyroid peroxidase (anti-TPO) antibodies strongly positive. Total cholesterol 7.4 mmol/L (raised), sodium 133 mmol/L (slightly low). Haemoglobin 118 g/L with normal-sized red cells.
clues.imaging: Thyroid ultrasound: a diffusely enlarged gland with a patchy, darker (hypoechoic) texture typical of chronic autoimmune inflammation, and no nodules needing biopsy. ECG: sinus bradycardia with small complexes.

explain.patho: Hashimoto's thyroiditis is the commonest cause of hypothyroidism where iodine intake is adequate. Lymphocytes and antibodies against thyroid proteins, especially thyroid peroxidase, the enzyme that builds thyroid hormone, gradually destroy the gland. As output of T4 and T3 falls, the pituitary detects the shortage and raises TSH, which is why TSH is the most sensitive test. Low thyroid hormone slows the body's metabolism: less heat is produced (cold intolerance), heart rate slows, the gut slows (constipation), and fats are cleared less efficiently (high cholesterol). Water-binding substances called glycosaminoglycans build up in the skin and tissues, causing puffiness and a hoarse voice. Like many autoimmune diseases it is commoner in women and runs in families with other autoimmune conditions.
explain.confirm: A raised TSH with a low free T4 confirms primary hypothyroidism. Positive anti-TPO antibodies identify Hashimoto's as the cause. A raised TSH with normal T4 is called subclinical hypothyroidism and is usually rechecked before treating.
explain.treat: Lifelong replacement with levothyroxine, a synthetic form of thyroxine, taken daily on an empty stomach. The amount is adjusted gradually according to repeat TSH tests until TSH returns to the normal range and symptoms resolve. Older patients or those with heart disease are started more cautiously.

near.depression: Tiredness and low mood fit, but depression doesn't cause a slow pulse, slowly relaxing reflexes and a TSH this high.
near.graves' disease: Right gland and also autoimmune, but she is slowed down, not sped up; her TSH is high, not suppressed.
near.secondary hypothyroidism: In pituitary failure TSH is low or normal; here the pituitary is shouting with a very high TSH.

cases.pearl: In primary hypothyroidism TSH goes up, because the pituitary keeps shouting at a thyroid that can't answer.

cases.complaint: A 74-year-old man is brought from home because he has become increasingly confused and weak over several days.

clues.history: He has type 2 diabetes treated with tablets. His daughter says that for about a week he has been very thirsty and passing a lot of urine, and for three days he has had a cough with green sputum. He has barely eaten and seems muddled, not recognising where he is today. There has been no vomiting or abdominal pain.
clues.vitals: Temp 38.2 °C, HR 118/min, BP 98/56 mmHg, RR 22/min, SpO2 93% on room air.
clues.exam: Drowsy and disorientated (GCS 12) but with no one-sided weakness. Very dry tongue and skin that stays tented when pinched. Crackles at the right lung base. Breathing is not deep or sighing and there is no fruity breath smell.
clues.labs: Glucose 46.8 mmol/L. Sodium 148 mmol/L, urea 22 mmol/L; calculated serum osmolality about 365 mOsm/kg (normal 275–295). Blood ketones 0.8 mmol/L (only slightly raised). Venous pH 7.34, bicarbonate 21 mmol/L. Creatinine 165 µmol/L (baseline 85). WBC 15.4 ×10^9/L and CRP raised.
clues.imaging: Chest X-ray: consolidation in the right lower lobe, consistent with pneumonia. CT head: no bleed or stroke, so the confusion is not from a structural brain problem. ECG: sinus tachycardia only.

explain.patho: In type 2 diabetes the body still makes some insulin, but not enough to control blood sugar, especially during an illness such as pneumonia, which raises stress hormones that push glucose up further. The small amount of insulin present is enough to stop fat breakdown and ketone production, so severe acidosis does not develop. Instead glucose climbs very high over days, causing massive urine losses and profound dehydration, often greater than in DKA. The blood becomes highly concentrated (hyperosmolar), and water is drawn out of brain cells, causing confusion, drowsiness and sometimes seizures or coma. Thick, concentrated blood and immobility greatly increase the risk of clots.
explain.confirm: Diagnosis rests on a very high glucose (usually above 30 mmol/L), high serum osmolality (above 320 mOsm/kg) and marked dehydration, without significant ketosis or acidosis. A trigger such as infection should always be looked for.
explain.treat: Fluids are the main treatment, replaced steadily rather than too fast, because rapid shifts in sodium and osmolality can harm the brain. Insulin is added only if glucose stops falling with fluids alone or if ketones are significant. Electrolytes are monitored closely, clot prevention is given, and the trigger (here pneumonia, with antibiotics) is treated.

near.diabetic ketoacidosis: Close cousin, but his ketones are barely up and his pH is nearly normal; the problem here is concentration, not acid.
near.stroke: Confusion in an older person should make you think stroke, but there's no focal weakness and the CT is clear.
near.sepsis: There is an infection driving this, but the extreme glucose and osmolality are the main problem to name.

cases.pearl: DKA develops over hours to a day; HHS creeps up over days, with worse dehydration and more confusion.

cases.complaint: A 35-year-old woman is brought in by her partner because over two days she has become feverish, confused and 'not herself', and this morning she had a fit.

clues.history: Three days ago she had a fever and headache like flu. Since yesterday she has been acting oddly: she keeps repeating questions, can't find words, and says she smells burning rubber that nobody else can smell. This morning she had a seizure lasting about two minutes. She gets occasional cold sores. No travel, no rash, no recent illness in contacts.
clues.vitals: Temp 38.9 °C, HR 110/min, BP 128/76 mmHg, RR 18/min, SpO2 98% on room air.
clues.exam: GCS 13: disoriented, unable to form new memories during the conversation and struggling to name objects (word-finding difficulty). Mild neck stiffness. No rash, no focal limb weakness, no papilloedema.
clues.labs: WBC 11.0 ×10^9/L, CRP mildly raised, sodium 131 mmol/L, glucose 6.2 mmol/L. CSF: clear, opening pressure mildly raised, white cells 120 ×10^6/L (mostly lymphocytes), red cells 350 ×10^6/L, protein 0.9 g/L, glucose 3.6 mmol/L (normal ratio to blood), Gram stain negative. CSF PCR: HSV-1 DNA detected.
clues.imaging: MRI brain: swelling and bright T2/FLAIR signal in the left medial temporal lobe and insula with restricted diffusion and small spots of bleeding; the right side is less affected. EEG: periodic sharp discharges over the left temporal region.

explain.patho: After a childhood cold sore, HSV-1 (the cold sore virus) hides dormant in the trigeminal ganglion. In encephalitis it reactivates (or arrives freshly) and travels along nerve fibres, possibly via the olfactory or trigeminal pathways, to the base of the brain. It has a striking preference for the medial temporal and orbitofrontal lobes and the insula, the limbic system that handles memory, emotion and smell. The virus kills cells directly and triggers intense inflammation, producing haemorrhagic necrosis; that's why red cells appear in the CSF and seizures are common. Temporal lobe damage explains the memory loss, odd behaviour, language trouble and smell hallucinations. Untreated, most patients die and survivors are often left with severe memory problems, so treatment speed is everything.
explain.confirm: CSF PCR for HSV DNA is the key test; it can be falsely negative in the first day, so it is repeated if suspicion is high. The CSF shows a lymphocytic pattern with normal glucose, often with red cells. MRI temporal lobe changes and EEG temporal discharges support the diagnosis.
explain.treat: Intravenous antiviral treatment (aciclovir) is started immediately on suspicion, without waiting for the PCR result, and continued for a full course. Supportive care includes seizure control with antiseizure medicines, management of brain swelling and low sodium, and intensive care if needed. Survivors often need rehabilitation for memory and behaviour.

near.bacterial meningitis: The CSF has lymphocytes and a normal glucose, and the brain tissue itself is affected, especially one temporal lobe.
near.viral meningitis: Meningitis gives headache and neck stiffness, but confusion, memory loss and seizures mean the brain itself is inflamed.
near.psychosis: New odd behaviour with fever, seizures and abnormal CSF is a brain infection until proven otherwise.
near.autoimmune encephalitis: Good thinking, it can look similar, but the PCR has found a virus.

cases.pearl: Fever plus confusion, odd behaviour or smell hallucinations: start the antiviral first and prove the diagnosis later.

cases.complaint: A 17-year-old boy collapses suddenly during a soccer match and is revived by a defibrillator on the sideline.

clues.history: He was sprinting when he fell to the ground without warning. A coach started CPR and the shock from the sideline defibrillator brought him back. He now admits to a few months of chest tightness and light-headedness during hard training. His uncle died suddenly at 32 while jogging, 'heart problem, no one knew why'. No illness or medicines.
clues.vitals: Temp 36.7 °C, HR 78/min, BP 124/72 mmHg, RR 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air.
clues.exam: Alert and orientated after recovering. A harsh systolic murmur at the left sternal edge that does NOT spread to the neck: it gets louder when he stands up or strains (Valsalva) and quieter when he squats. A double-pulse feel at the carotid. Forceful, sustained apex beat. Chest clear.
clues.labs: Troponin T mildly raised at 46 ng/L after the arrest and shock, then falling. Potassium 4.1 mmol/L, magnesium 0.86 mmol/L, calcium normal. TSH normal. Glucose 5.8 mmol/L. Genetic testing (sent later) finds a disease-causing variant in the MYBPC3 sarcomere gene.
clues.imaging: ECG: very tall QRS complexes showing left ventricular hypertrophy, deep inverted T waves across the chest leads and narrow, deep Q waves in the lateral leads. Echo: the septum is 24 mm thick (normal under 12), much thicker than the back wall; during systole the mitral valve leaflet is pulled forward into the outflow tract (systolic anterior motion), creating a large outflow gradient that rises on straining. Cardiac MRI: patchy scarring (late gadolinium enhancement) in the thickened septum. The defibrillator recording shows ventricular fibrillation.

explain.patho: HCM is usually inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern from a mutation in a sarcomere gene (such as MYH7 or MYBPC3), the proteins that make heart muscle contract. The heart muscle cells become enlarged and disorganised (myocyte disarray), with scarring in between, and the walls thicken, most often the septum. The thick, stiff ventricle relaxes poorly so it fills badly (diastolic dysfunction). In many patients the bulging septum narrows the outflow path, and fast blood flow sucks the mitral valve leaflet forward, blocking the outflow further during systole; anything that shrinks the ventricle (standing, straining, dehydration) worsens this, which is why the murmur gets louder. The disarray and scar are an unstable electrical substrate, so intense exercise can trigger ventricular fibrillation and sudden death. It is one of the commonest causes of sudden cardiac death in young athletes.
explain.confirm: Echocardiography or cardiac MRI showing an unexplained thick left ventricular wall (classically at least 15 mm in adults) that is not due to high blood pressure or a valve problem confirms HCM. The ECG is abnormal in most patients, genetic testing finds the mutation in many, and first-degree relatives are screened with ECG and echo.
explain.treat: Anyone who has survived a cardiac arrest gets an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) to shock dangerous rhythms. Beta-blockers or certain calcium channel blockers relax the heart and lower the outflow gradient, newer cardiac myosin inhibitors reduce excessive contraction, and dehydration is avoided. If obstruction still causes symptoms, part of the septum can be removed surgically (septal myectomy) or shrunk with a catheter procedure, and decisions about competitive sport are made individually with a specialist.

near.aortic stenosis: The murmur sounds similar, but it doesn't reach the neck and gets louder when he stands or strains; also, he's seventeen.
near.commotio cordis: That's a blow to the chest at the wrong moment; here nothing hit him and the echo shows a thick septum.
near.long qt syndrome: Another cause of sudden death in the young, but the ECG shows a thick-walled heart rather than a long QT.

cases.pearl: A systolic murmur that gets louder on standing or straining and softer on squatting is hypertrophic obstruction until proven otherwise.

cases.dx: Hypoglycaemia in type 1 diabetes after exercise
cases.complaint: A 15-year-old boy with type 1 diabetes is brought off the football pitch after the match because he is sweaty, shaky and acting strangely.

clues.history: He injected his usual insulin before lunch and then played a full, intense match in the afternoon. He ate less than normal because he was nervous. Teammates say he became pale, irritable and started slurring his words and missing easy passes near the end. He has had type 1 diabetes since he was eight.
clues.vitals: Temp 36.5 °C, HR 118/min, BP 132/70 mmHg, RR 18/min, SpO2 99% on room air.
clues.exam: Pale, clammy and trembling. He is confused and slow to answer questions but can swallow safely (GCS 14). Pupils equal and reactive, no weakness of the limbs. His insulin pen and glucose meter are in his kit bag.
clues.labs: Capillary glucose 2.3 mmol/L (normal fasting about 4–7). Blood ketones 0.2 mmol/L (normal). Sodium, potassium and creatinine normal. After treatment, glucose rises to 6.8 mmol/L within 15 minutes.
clues.imaging: No imaging was needed: he improved completely once glucose was raised, which rules out a head injury from the match as the cause. ECG: sinus tachycardia only. If confusion had not improved after glucose, a CT head would have been the next step.

explain.patho: In type 1 diabetes, injected insulin keeps acting whatever the body's needs are, because the pancreas can no longer switch insulin off. Exercise makes muscles take up glucose even without insulin and increases insulin sensitivity for many hours afterwards, so glucose can fall fast during and after sport. When blood glucose drops, the body releases adrenaline, causing sweating, shaking, a racing heart and hunger (warning symptoms). The brain depends almost entirely on glucose, so as levels fall further it starts to fail: confusion, slurred speech, odd behaviour and eventually seizures or loss of consciousness. Repeated hypos can blunt the adrenaline warning response (hypoglycaemia unawareness).
explain.confirm: A blood glucose below about 4 mmol/L in someone with diabetes is a hypo, and symptoms that resolve when glucose is raised (Whipple's triad) confirm it. A finger-prick test should always be checked in anyone with diabetes who becomes unwell or confused.
explain.treat: If he can swallow safely, a fast-acting sugar such as glucose tablets, gel or a sugary drink, then a longer-acting carbohydrate snack once glucose recovers. If he cannot swallow or is unconscious, glucagon is given by injection or nasal spray, or glucose into a vein in hospital. Prevention means planning: extra carbohydrate and adjusted insulin around sport, checking glucose before, during and after exercise, and continuous glucose monitors with alarms.

near.concussion: Sport-related, but his symptoms disappear completely once his blood sugar goes up.
near.diabetic ketoacidosis: That's the opposite problem: high glucose and high ketones; his ketones are normal and his glucose is very low.
near.dehydration: Thirst and tiredness are common after a match, but slurred speech and a reading this low point to the brain's fuel supply.

cases.pearl: Anyone with diabetes who becomes confused, slurred or unusually aggressive has a low blood sugar until proven otherwise; check the glucose first.

cases.dx: Cushing syndrome from long-term steroid treatment
cases.complaint: A 15-year-old boy with severe asthma is reviewed because his face has become round, he has gained weight around his middle and he has stopped growing taller.

clues.history: His asthma has been hard to control, and over the past 18 months he has needed long courses of steroid tablets almost continuously, often restarting soon after stopping. He has gained 12 kg, mostly around his tummy and face, bruises easily and has new purple stretch marks. His height has hardly changed in a year and he feels moody and his muscles tire on the stairs. His friends tease him about his acne.
clues.vitals: Temp 36.7 °C, HR 84/min, BP 142/90 mmHg (high for his age), RR 16/min, SpO2 97% on room air.
clues.exam: Rounded, red face ('moon face') and a fat pad at the back of the neck; slim arms and legs with central obesity. Wide purple stretch marks (striae) across the abdomen and thighs, thin skin and bruises on the forearms. Weak thigh muscles: he needs his hands to rise from a squat. Acne on his face and back.
clues.labs: Fasting glucose 7.6 mmol/L (raised), potassium 3.4 mmol/L (slightly low), white cells 12.8 ×10^9/L with high neutrophils and low eosinophils, a typical steroid effect. Morning cortisol and ACTH are both low: his own adrenal glands have been switched off because the medicine is doing their job.
clues.imaging: DEXA bone scan: bone density below expected for his age (low Z-score). Wrist X-ray: bone age delayed compared with his real age. Eye check: early cataracts at the back of the lens (posterior subcapsular), another steroid effect.

explain.patho: Cortisol, and steroid medicines that copy it, raise blood glucose by making the liver produce sugar and making tissues resistant to insulin. They break down protein in muscle, skin and bone, causing weak thigh muscles, thin skin that bruises, wide purple stretch marks and thin bones. Fat is redistributed to the face, neck and trunk while the limbs thin. Steroids raise blood pressure and suppress the immune response, and in children they slow growth by blocking growth plates and growth hormone signalling. Because the pituitary senses plenty of glucocorticoid, it stops making ACTH, and over months the adrenal glands shrink; if the medicine is suddenly stopped, the body cannot make its own cortisol and an adrenal crisis can follow.
explain.confirm: The diagnosis is clinical: typical features in someone taking long-term steroids, with the drug history as the key. Low morning cortisol and ACTH confirm suppression of the body's own axis (in contrast, Cushing's disease from a pituitary tumour has high cortisol and normal or high ACTH). Bone density, eyes, blood pressure, glucose and growth are checked for complications.
explain.treat: Steroids are reduced slowly under medical supervision, never stopped suddenly, so the adrenal glands can recover. Asthma control is moved to steroid-sparing treatments such as inhaled preventers, better inhaler technique, and biologic antibody therapies for severe asthma. Complications are treated: bone protection with calcium and vitamin D, and management of blood pressure and glucose. He carries a steroid alert card and needs extra steroid cover during serious illness until his own adrenal function returns.

near.cushing's disease: Close! That's the pituitary tumour version with a high ACTH; here ACTH is low and the cause is something he takes.
near.obesity: Simple obesity doesn't cause purple stretch marks, thin bruising skin, weak thighs and stunted growth.
near.hypothyroidism: That can cause weight gain and slow growth, but not moon face, purple striae and high blood sugar.

cases.pearl: Never stop long-term steroids suddenly: the body's own adrenal glands have been asleep and need time to wake up.

cases.complaint: A 24-year-old woman has had daily headaches for two months and has started seeing double.

clues.history: The headache is worse in the morning and when lying down, and worse with coughing or bending. She hears a whooshing sound in time with her heartbeat in both ears. Her vision goes grey for a few seconds when she stands up or bends over. Over the last week, things side by side look doubled. She has gained about 12 kg over the past year. No fever, no weakness and she takes no regular medicines.
clues.vitals: Temp 36.7 °C, HR 76/min, BP 128/80 mmHg, RR 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air. BMI 36.
clues.exam: Both optic discs are swollen with blurred margins and no venous pulsations (bilateral papilloedema). Her left eye won't turn outwards fully (left sixth nerve palsy). Visual field testing shows enlarged blind spots. Otherwise the neurological exam is normal and she is fully alert.
clues.labs: Full blood count, kidney function and electrolytes normal. Lumbar puncture lying on her side with legs relaxed: opening pressure 34 cmH2O (high; normal adults are under about 25). CSF white cells 1 ×10^6/L, protein 0.30 g/L, glucose 3.4 mmol/L, all normal.
clues.imaging: MRI brain with MR venography: no mass, no hydrocephalus and no venous sinus thrombosis. Indirect signs of high pressure: a flattened 'empty' sella, flattening of the back of both eyeballs, fluid-distended optic nerve sheaths and narrowing of both transverse venous sinuses.

explain.patho: In IIH the pressure of the cerebrospinal fluid rises without any tumour, blockage or infection to explain it. The exact cause is unclear, but impaired absorption of CSF into the venous system, narrowed transverse venous sinuses that raise venous pressure, and metabolic and hormonal effects of obesity all seem to play a part. The high pressure is transmitted along the fluid sleeve around each optic nerve, squeezing the axons where they enter the eye and blocking axoplasmic flow, so the optic discs swell. Ongoing papilloedema can permanently damage the optic nerve and cause blindness, which is the real danger. The sixth cranial nerve has a long course inside the skull and gets stretched by raised pressure, so it's a 'false localising' sign rather than a sign of a lesion at a specific spot. The pulsatile whooshing comes from turbulent blood flow through the narrowed venous sinuses.
explain.confirm: The diagnosis needs papilloedema, a normal neurological exam apart from sixth nerve palsy, MRI with venography showing no mass, hydrocephalus or venous thrombosis, normal CSF contents and a raised opening pressure (the modified Dandy criteria). Imaging must come before the lumbar puncture.
explain.treat: Weight loss is the main treatment that changes the disease, supported by dietitians and sometimes weight-loss medicines or surgery. Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (acetazolamide) reduce CSF production, and headache treatment avoids painkiller overuse. Vision is checked regularly with visual fields and eye exams; if vision is threatened, options include CSF shunting, optic nerve sheath fenestration or stenting of a narrowed venous sinus.

near.brain tumour: Right to think of raised pressure, but the MRI shows no mass, and that's the point of the name.
near.venous sinus thrombosis: An essential mimic to exclude, but the MR venogram shows narrowing without clot.
near.migraine: Migraine never causes papilloedema or a raised opening pressure.
near.hydrocephalus: Pressure is high, but the ventricles are normal-sized or small.

cases.pearl: Every headache with papilloedema needs a scan before a lumbar puncture, and a venogram before you call it idiopathic.

cases.complaint: A 17-year-old rugby player has had a severe sore throat, fever and crushing tiredness for a week and wants to know if he can play this weekend.

clues.history: It started with feeling washed out, then a very sore throat and swollen glands in his neck. He is sleeping 14 hours a day and can barely finish training. His GP gave him amoxicillin for presumed tonsillitis three days ago, and he then developed an itchy red rash all over. Several teammates had a similar illness last month; they share water bottles in the changing room.
clues.vitals: Temp 38.6 °C, HR 102/min, BP 118/70 mmHg, RR 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air.
clues.exam: Enlarged tonsils covered with a greyish-white coating, and tiny red spots on the roof of the mouth. Tender, enlarged lymph nodes in the neck, especially at the back of the neck behind the sternocleidomastoid muscles. Puffy eyelids. The spleen tip is felt below the left ribs and the liver edge is slightly tender. A widespread pink, raised rash on the trunk.
clues.labs: WBC 13.5 ×10^9/L with lymphocytes making up 65%, many of them large 'atypical' lymphocytes on the blood film. Heterophile antibody test (Monospot) positive. EBV viral capsid antigen IgM positive. ALT 140 U/L (mildly raised, as the liver is involved). Platelets 132 ×10^9/L (slightly low). Throat swab negative for group A strep.
clues.imaging: Abdominal ultrasound: the spleen is enlarged at 16 cm long (normal up to about 12 cm) with a smooth outline and no tear or bleeding around it. The liver is mildly enlarged with normal texture.

explain.patho: Glandular fever is usually caused by Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), which spreads through saliva and close contact, such as sharing drinks or cutlery. The virus first infects cells in the throat and then B lymphocytes, the antibody-making white cells, which carry it through the lymph nodes, spleen and liver. The body fights back with a huge army of cytotoxic T cells; these activated T cells are the 'atypical lymphocytes' seen on the film, and their expansion causes the swollen glands, tonsils, spleen and liver. Most symptoms come from this immune response rather than the virus itself, which is why fatigue can last weeks. The enlarged spleen has a stretched, thin capsule, so a hit in contact sport can rupture it and cause dangerous internal bleeding. Infected B cells also make unusual antibodies (heterophile antibodies), the basis of the Monospot test.
explain.confirm: A typical picture with lymphocytosis and atypical lymphocytes plus a positive heterophile (Monospot) test confirms it. If Monospot is negative early, or in younger children, EBV-specific antibodies (VCA IgM) confirm recent infection. A throat swab excludes strep throat.
explain.treat: Treatment is supportive: rest, fluids, and paracetamol or anti-inflammatories for fever and sore throat. Antibiotics don't help a virus, and amoxicillin-type antibiotics commonly cause a rash in glandular fever. He must avoid contact sports and heavy lifting until the spleen has returned to normal size and he is fully recovered, usually several weeks. Steroids are used only for complications such as tonsils swelling enough to threaten the airway.

near.strep throat: The tonsils look similar, but the strep swab is negative and strep doesn't usually enlarge the spleen or cause atypical lymphocytes.
near.tonsillitis: His tonsils are inflamed, but name the virus behind it that also swells the spleen and liver.
near.leukaemia: A high white count, big spleen and low platelets can worry you, but these are reactive lymphocytes and the virus antibody test is positive.

cases.pearl: A rash after amoxicillin for a 'sore throat' in a teenager is a classic clue to glandular fever, and athletes with it must not play contact sport until the spleen settles.

cases.complaint: A 52-year-old man with a known heart murmur has had fevers, night sweats and tiredness for three weeks.

clues.history: Fevers and drenching night sweats for three weeks, with aching joints, poor appetite and 3 kg weight loss. About five weeks ago he had two teeth pulled for an abscess. He was told as a child he had rheumatic fever, and he has a known mitral valve murmur. No cough, no urinary symptoms, no recent travel.
clues.vitals: Temp 38.6 °C, HR 104/min, BP 128/68 mmHg, RR 18/min, SpO2 97% on room air.
clues.exam: Pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the armpit, louder than in his old notes. Thin dark red lines under several fingernails (splinter haemorrhages). Painless flat red spots on both palms (Janeway lesions) and a tender red bump on a fingertip (Osler node). Spleen tip palpable. Retina shows small haemorrhages with pale centres (Roth spots).
clues.labs: Haemoglobin 108 g/L, WBC 13.6 ×10^9/L with neutrophilia, CRP and ESR raised. Creatinine 112 µmol/L. Urine dipstick: blood present (microscopic haematuria). Three sets of blood cultures taken from separate sites over hours: all grow viridans-group streptococci.
clues.imaging: Transthoracic echo: a mobile, irregular mass 11 mm long attached to the mitral valve leaflet with moderate-to-severe mitral regurgitation. Transoesophageal echo confirms the vegetation and shows no abscess. Chest X-ray normal. ECG: sinus tachycardia, normal PR interval.

explain.patho: Damaged heart valves (here from childhood rheumatic fever) have rough surfaces and turbulent blood flow, which lets platelets and fibrin build tiny sterile clumps on them. A dental extraction can briefly release mouth bacteria such as viridans streptococci into the bloodstream, and they stick to these clumps and multiply. Layers of bacteria, fibrin and platelets build up into a vegetation that the immune system struggles to reach, so bacteria keep seeding the blood and causing fever. The infection eats into the valve, worsening regurgitation and sometimes causing heart failure or an abscess. Bits of vegetation can break off as emboli to the brain, kidneys, spleen and skin (Janeway lesions, splinter haemorrhages). Immune complexes cause Osler nodes, Roth spots and kidney inflammation.
explain.confirm: The modified Duke criteria are used: the two major criteria are persistently positive blood cultures with a typical organism and echo evidence of a vegetation, abscess or new valve leak. Minor criteria include a predisposing heart condition, fever, embolic signs and immune signs. Multiple blood cultures must be taken before any antibiotics.
explain.treat: Prolonged courses of intravenous bactericidal antibiotics chosen from culture results, usually given over weeks, often with part of the course at home. Heart surgery to repair or replace the valve is needed for heart failure, uncontrolled infection, abscess or a large vegetation with high risk of embolism. Good dental hygiene and regular dental check-ups lower the risk of it happening again.

near.rheumatic fever: He had that as a child, which damaged the valve, but now positive blood cultures and a valve vegetation point to an active infection on it.
near.lymphoma: Night sweats and weight loss fit, but positive blood cultures and nail and palm signs point to the heart.
near.sepsis: He is septic, but ask where the bacteria are coming from: listen to that changed murmur.

cases.pearl: Fever plus a new or changed murmur is endocarditis until proven otherwise; take three sets of blood cultures before the first antibiotic.

cases.complaint: A 62-year-old woman develops a sudden headache and vomiting while gardening, and within half an hour her left side has gone weak and she is getting drowsy.

clues.history: She has had high blood pressure for 15 years but stopped her tablets months ago because she 'felt fine'. The weakness got steadily worse over the first 30 minutes rather than appearing all at once. No head injury, no blood thinners, no known bleeding disorder.
clues.vitals: Temp 37.0 °C, HR 72/min regular, BP 222/118 mmHg, RR 18/min, SpO2 96% on room air.
clues.exam: GCS 13 (eyes open to voice, confused). Dense left-sided weakness of the face, arm and leg equally, with left-sided loss of sensation. Eyes deviated to the right. Left plantar upgoing. Fundoscopy shows narrowed arteries with AV nicking (long-standing hypertension).
clues.labs: Glucose 7.1 mmol/L. Platelets 260 ×10^9/L, INR 1.0 and APTT normal, which rules out a clotting problem as the cause. Creatinine 110 µmol/L. Troponin normal.
clues.imaging: Non-contrast CT head: a bright (hyperdense) blood clot about 35 mL in volume centred on the right putamen with a dark rim of surrounding oedema, a little blood spilling into the right lateral ventricle and 3 mm of midline shift. ECG: left ventricular hypertrophy from chronic hypertension.

explain.patho: Years of high pressure damage the small penetrating arteries (the lenticulostriate branches of the MCA) that dive straight off a large vessel into deep brain. Their walls thicken and degenerate (lipohyalinosis) and can form tiny weak bulges called Charcot–Bouchard microaneurysms. When one ruptures, arterial blood tears into brain tissue, forming a clot that compresses and destroys the surrounding neurons. The haematoma often keeps growing for the first few hours, which is why symptoms worsen gradually and why early blood pressure control matters. Swelling around the clot and blood in the ventricles raise intracranial pressure and can block CSF flow, causing drowsiness. Classic hypertensive sites are the putamen, thalamus, pons and cerebellum; the putamen sits right beside the internal capsule, so face, arm and leg are all weakened together.
explain.confirm: A non-contrast CT shows fresh blood as bright white within the brain substance. CT angiography looks for an underlying vascular malformation or aneurysm and can show a 'spot sign' of active leaking. MRI later can look for other causes such as a tumour or amyloid angiopathy, especially in lobar bleeds in older people.
explain.treat: Treatment is in a stroke or neuro-intensive care unit: rapid but careful blood pressure lowering with intravenous antihypertensives, reversal of any blood-thinning drug, and measures for raised intracranial pressure such as head elevation. Neurosurgery drains hydrocephalus with an external ventricular drain and removes clots in the cerebellum or selected large lobar bleeds. Clot-dissolving drugs are absolutely contraindicated. Long-term blood pressure control and rehabilitation follow.

near.ischaemic stroke: The symptoms fit, but the CT shows bright fresh blood, not a blocked artery.
near.subarachnoid haemorrhage: The blood is inside the brain tissue itself, not spread through the sulci and cisterns around it.
near.brain tumour: Too sudden; a tumour grows over weeks and this bleed came on in minutes in someone with very high blood pressure.

cases.pearl: You can't tell a bleed from a clot at the bedside, which is why every suspected stroke gets a CT before any clot-busting drug.

cases.complaint: A 2-year-old boy is brought to his doctor because he looks very pale, is grumpy and tired, and has been chewing on odd things.

clues.history: He is a 'fussy eater' who refuses meat and vegetables but drinks a lot of cow's milk, about six or seven big cups a day from a bottle, which fills him up. His parents have noticed him eating paper and licking the wall. He tires quickly when playing and is more irritable than before. There is no blood in his nappies and no recent illness.
clues.vitals: Temp 36.8 °C, HR 132/min (fast for his age), BP 92/56 mmHg, RR 26/min, SpO2 99% on room air.
clues.exam: Very pale skin, lips and inside of the lower eyelids. A soft flow murmur from the fast circulation. No jaundice, no enlarged liver, spleen or lymph nodes, and no bruising, which makes a bone marrow cancer unlikely. Growth is on the 50th centile for weight.
clues.labs: Haemoglobin 76 g/L (normal for age about 105–135), MCV 58 fL (small red cells), MCH low (pale cells). Ferritin very low, transferrin saturation 4% (low), total iron-binding capacity high. Red cell distribution width (RDW) raised. White cells and platelets normal (platelets slightly high, common in iron deficiency). Stool test for hidden blood negative.
clues.imaging: Blood film: small, pale (microcytic, hypochromic) red cells with a pale centre, varying in size, and some long thin 'pencil cells'. No blast cells. No imaging was needed; the red cell pattern, the low iron stores and the diet together explain everything.

explain.patho: Iron is the centre of the haem molecule in haemoglobin, the protein that carries oxygen in red cells. Cow's milk is very low in iron, its calcium and casein reduce iron absorption from other foods, and large volumes fill a toddler up so he eats few iron-rich foods. Over months the body's iron stores (measured by ferritin) run out, and the bone marrow cannot build enough haemoglobin. The marrow responds by making red cells smaller and paler, which shows as a low MCV and MCH. Less oxygen reaches the tissues, causing tiredness and pallor, and the heart pumps faster to compensate. Pica, craving non-food items, is a curious but classic symptom of iron deficiency, and lack of iron can also affect brain development in young children.
explain.confirm: A low haemoglobin with small, pale red cells and a low ferritin confirms iron-deficiency anaemia; ferritin is the most useful single test (though it can be falsely normal during inflammation). The underlying cause must always be found: diet in this toddler, but in adults, especially older adults, a slow bleed from the gut has to be investigated with endoscopy.
explain.treat: Oral iron supplements, best absorbed on an empty stomach or with vitamin C, continued for a while after haemoglobin normalises to refill stores. Fix the cause: cut down cow's milk, stop the bottle and add iron-rich foods (meat, beans, leafy greens, fortified cereals), with help from a dietitian. A blood count is rechecked to make sure haemoglobin rises; failure to respond suggests poor adherence, ongoing loss or a different diagnosis.

near.thalassaemia trait: Also gives small red cells, but iron stores are normal; here ferritin is very low and the diet explains it.
near.leukaemia: Pallor and tiredness are worrying, but white cells and platelets are normal, there are no blasts and no enlarged organs.
near.anaemia of chronic disease: That also lowers iron in the blood, but ferritin is normal or high in it; here ferritin is very low and there's no chronic illness.

cases.pearl: A toddler who drinks lots of milk and eats little else is the classic setup for iron deficiency: milk fills the tummy but not the iron stores.

cases.complaint: A 68-year-old man is brought in by ambulance after his wife found he suddenly couldn't move his right arm or get his words out at breakfast.

clues.history: He was last seen normal at 07:30 and the symptoms were there by 07:45; he arrived at 08:20. He has high blood pressure and an irregular heartbeat found on a check-up last year that he never followed up. Ex-smoker. No headache, no vomiting, no seizure, no head injury, and he takes no blood thinners.
clues.vitals: Temp 36.8 °C, HR 96/min and irregularly irregular, BP 178/96 mmHg, RR 16/min, SpO2 97% on room air.
clues.exam: Right-sided face weakness affecting the lower face but sparing the forehead. Right arm much weaker than the right leg. He understands commands but speech is halting and effortful with few words (expressive aphasia). Right homonymous visual field loss and eyes deviated to the left. NIH Stroke Scale score 14.
clues.labs: Capillary glucose 6.4 mmol/L (rules out low sugar as a stroke mimic). Platelets 240 ×10^9/L, INR 1.0, APTT normal. Creatinine 92 µmol/L, sodium 139 mmol/L. Troponin 9 ng/L (normal).
clues.imaging: Non-contrast CT head: no blood. Bright, dense left middle cerebral artery (hyperdense artery sign) and subtle loss of grey-white distinction in the left insula. CT angiogram: abrupt cut-off of the left MCA M1 segment. ECG: atrial fibrillation, no acute ST changes.

explain.patho: In atrial fibrillation the left atrium quivers instead of contracting, so blood pools in the left atrial appendage and a clot forms. A fragment breaks off, travels up the left internal carotid and lodges in the middle cerebral artery. Neurons have almost no energy reserve: within minutes ATP runs out, the sodium-potassium pump fails, cells swell (cytotoxic oedema) and glutamate floods out, killing neighbouring cells (excitotoxicity). The dead core is surrounded by a 'penumbra' of stunned but salvageable tissue fed by collateral vessels, which is what emergency treatment races to save. The left MCA supplies the lateral frontal, parietal and temporal lobes, including Broca's area and the motor strip for the face and arm, which explains aphasia and face-arm-more-than-leg weakness on the right. Eyes look toward the side of the lesion because the frontal eye field pushing them right is knocked out.
explain.confirm: A non-contrast CT is done first to rule out bleeding. CT angiography shows the blocked large vessel, and CT perfusion or MRI can map core versus penumbra. MRI diffusion-weighted imaging shows the infarct as bright restricted diffusion within minutes.
explain.treat: If there's no bleed and he is within the time window, a clot-dissolving drug (thrombolysis with alteplase or tenecteplase) is given. A large-vessel blockage like this one is pulled out with a catheter (mechanical thrombectomy). He then goes to a stroke unit for monitoring, swallow assessment and early rehabilitation, with antiplatelet treatment at first, then long-term anticoagulation for the atrial fibrillation, blood pressure control and a statin.

near.transient ischaemic attack: The deficit hasn't gone away and the CT already shows signs of tissue injury.
near.haemorrhagic stroke: Good thought, but the CT shows no blood at all, just a blocked artery.
near.bell's palsy: The forehead is spared and the arm and speech are involved too, which points to the brain, not the facial nerve.
near.hypoglycaemia: Low sugar can mimic this, but his glucose is normal.

cases.pearl: Time is brain: in a large-vessel stroke roughly 1.9 million neurons are lost every minute that the artery stays blocked.

cases.dx: Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (first generalised tonic-clonic seizure)
cases.complaint: A 16-year-old boy collapsed and shook all over at breakfast the morning after staying up almost all night revising for exams.

clues.history: His sister saw him go stiff with a cry, fall, then jerk all four limbs rhythmically for about two minutes; he bit the side of his tongue and wet himself, then was confused and sleepy for half an hour. On careful questioning he admits that for months he has had sudden jerks of his arms in the first hour after waking: he drops his toothbrush and flicks his cereal across the table, and thought he was just clumsy. A cousin has epilepsy. No head injury, no fever, no recent illness.
clues.vitals: Shortly after the seizure: Temp 37.3 °C, HR 108/min, BP 138/82 mmHg, RR 20/min, SpO2 96% on room air.
clues.exam: Drowsy for 30 minutes after the event, then fully alert and oriented. Bite mark on the side of the tongue. No neck stiffness, no rash, no focal neurological signs, normal fundi.
clues.labs: Glucose 5.8 mmol/L, sodium 140 mmol/L, calcium 2.35 mmol/L (all normal, so no metabolic cause). Lactate 6.2 mmol/L straight after the seizure, normal two hours later. CK the next day 900 U/L (muscle strain from the convulsion). ECG normal, with a normal QT interval (helps exclude a cardiac cause of collapse).
clues.imaging: CT head and MRI brain: normal. EEG: bursts of generalised fast spike-and-wave and polyspike-and-wave discharges over both hemispheres, triggered by flashing lights (a photoparoxysmal response), especially after sleep deprivation.

explain.patho: Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy is a genetic generalised epilepsy that usually starts in the teenage years. The problem is a network that is too excitable, linking the cortex and thalamus on both sides, so seizures involve both hemispheres at once from the very first moment. Myoclonic jerks are brief bursts of synchronised firing that make muscles twitch, typically just after waking, when the brain's excitability is highest. Sleep deprivation, stress and flashing lights lower the seizure threshold further, so a sleepless exam night is a classic trigger for the first big convulsion. In a tonic-clonic seizure, the tonic phase is sustained contraction of all muscles (the cry is air forced past closed vocal cords), and the clonic phase is rhythmic jerking as inhibition repeatedly breaks through. Afterward the exhausted brain causes a period of confusion, and intense muscle work raises lactate and CK.
explain.confirm: The diagnosis comes from the history, especially asking about morning myoclonic jerks, plus an EEG showing generalised polyspike-and-wave discharges, often with a photoparoxysmal response. MRI is normal. A cardiac cause is excluded with an ECG, and blood tests rule out metabolic causes.
explain.treat: Broad-spectrum antiseizure medicines such as valproate, levetiracetam or lamotrigine are used; narrow-spectrum drugs such as carbamazepine can make myoclonic jerks and absences worse. Regular sleep and avoiding sleep deprivation matter a lot. Treatment is usually lifelong, and he needs advice on seizure first aid, safety around water and heights, and driving rules.

near.syncope: A faint is brief with quick recovery; a bitten tongue side, prolonged confusion and months of morning jerks point elsewhere.
near.focal epilepsy: His EEG shows generalised discharges across both hemispheres at once and his MRI is normal.
near.febrile seizure: He is a teenager with no fever, so think of a lifelong epilepsy syndrome.
near.absence epilepsy: Close family of syndromes, but his key clue is morning jerks plus a convulsion.

cases.pearl: Ask every teenager with a first convulsion whether they drop things or jerk in the first hour after waking; the answer often reveals juvenile myoclonic epilepsy.

cases.complaint: A 3-year-old boy has had a high fever for six days that won't come down, and he is very irritable.

clues.history: Fever up to 40 °C every day for six days, not helped much by fever medicine. Two days ago both eyes went red without any discharge, and his lips became bright red and cracked. Yesterday a blotchy rash appeared on his trunk and his hands and feet became red and puffy, so he won't walk. A GP thought it was a virus. No sick contacts, no foreign travel, vaccinations up to date.
clues.vitals: Temp 39.8 °C, HR 168/min, BP 96/58 mmHg, RR 30/min, SpO2 98% on room air.
clues.exam: Miserable and very irritable. Both eyes red with the whites around the iris spared and no pus. Red, dry, cracked lips and a red, bumpy 'strawberry' tongue. Widespread blotchy red rash on the trunk with no blisters. Red, firm, swollen palms and soles. A single enlarged, tender lymph node of about 2 cm on the right side of the neck. Heart: fast with a soft flow murmur. Throat swab negative for strep.
clues.labs: WBC 17.8 ×10^9/L with neutrophilia, CRP and ESR markedly raised. Haemoglobin 102 g/L (mild anaemia). Platelets 480 ×10^9/L (they will climb higher in the second week). Albumin 28 g/L (low). ALT 82 U/L (mildly raised). Urine: white cells but no bacteria (sterile pyuria). Blood cultures negative.
clues.imaging: Echocardiogram: the left anterior descending and right coronary arteries are enlarged for his body size (z-scores just above 2.5, which counts as small aneurysms), with smooth walls; small pericardial effusion; normal heart squeeze. ECG: sinus tachycardia. A week later the skin around his fingertips and toes begins to peel.

explain.patho: Kawasaki disease is an acute inflammation of medium-sized arteries (a vasculitis) that mostly affects children under five, especially of East Asian background. The cause is unknown, but the leading theory is that an unidentified trigger, possibly an infection breathed in, sets off an exaggerated immune response in genetically susceptible children. Immune cells infiltrate the walls of arteries throughout the body, and the coronary arteries are particularly vulnerable: inflammation weakens their walls so they balloon out into aneurysms. Inflamed vessels everywhere cause the red eyes, red mouth, rash and swollen hands and feet, while the cytokine storm causes fever and high inflammatory markers. Aneurysms can later fill with clot or narrow as they heal, which can cause a heart attack even in a young child. Kawasaki disease is the commonest cause of acquired heart disease in children in developed countries.
explain.confirm: The diagnosis is clinical: fever for five days or more plus at least four of five features: red eyes without discharge, mouth and lip changes, rash, changes in the hands and feet, and a neck lymph node larger than 1.5 cm. Children with fewer features but high inflammatory markers or echo changes can have 'incomplete' Kawasaki disease. An echocardiogram looks for coronary artery dilation or aneurysms and is repeated over the following weeks.
explain.treat: Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) given early dramatically lowers the risk of coronary aneurysms, together with aspirin, which is one of the few times aspirin is used in children, under specialist supervision. Steroids or other immune-calming drugs are added for high-risk or treatment-resistant cases. Children are followed with repeat echocardiograms, and those with aneurysms need long-term cardiology care and sometimes anticoagulation.

near.scarlet fever: A strawberry tongue and rash fit, but the strep swab is negative and red eyes plus swollen hands and feet with a week of fever point to a vasculitis.
near.measles: Fever, rash and red eyes fit, but measles has a cough, runny nose and spots inside the cheeks, and he is vaccinated.
near.viral infection: Six days of fever with these specific features and dilated coronary arteries is far more than a virus.

cases.pearl: Any child with five or more days of unexplained fever deserves a check for Kawasaki features: the danger is in the coronary arteries.

cases.complaint: A 10-year-old boy has a spreading red rash on his thigh and feels feverish and achy, a week and a half after a family camping trip.

clues.history: The family camped in the woods of Connecticut in June, hiking through long grass. His mother pulled a tiny dark 'speck' off the back of his thigh after the trip but thought nothing of it. Five days ago a red patch appeared at the same spot and has grown steadily bigger. He has felt tired, with headaches, mild fever and aching muscles and joints, but no stiff neck, facial droop or chest symptoms.
clues.vitals: Temp 37.9 °C, HR 96/min, BP 104/64 mmHg, RR 18/min, SpO2 99% on room air.
clues.exam: An oval red patch 11 cm across on the back of the left thigh with a clearer centre and a redder outer ring (a 'bull's-eye' pattern); it is warm but barely itchy or painful, and there is a tiny dark mark at its centre. A slightly enlarged lymph node in the left groin crease. Full facial movement, no neck stiffness, normal heart sounds and no swollen joints.
clues.labs: Full blood count, kidney and liver tests essentially normal (ALT 38 U/L). Lyme antibody blood test (ELISA): negative at this stage, which is common in the first weeks because the immune system hasn't yet made enough antibodies. A repeat test in a few weeks, if done, would be expected to turn positive.
clues.imaging: ECG: normal sinus rhythm with a normal PR interval, so there is no sign of Lyme carditis (heart block). No other imaging needed: the diagnosis rests on the rash and the tick exposure.

explain.patho: Lyme disease is caused by the spiral-shaped bacterium Borrelia burgdorferi, carried by blacklegged (Ixodes) ticks that live in woodland and long grass in the northeastern and upper midwestern US and parts of Europe. The tick usually has to stay attached for more than a day to pass the bacteria on, which is why tiny young ticks (nymphs), easily missed, cause most cases. At the bite site the bacteria spread outward through the skin, producing the expanding erythema migrans rash, with the immune reaction strongest at the advancing edge. Weeks later, if untreated, they can spread through the blood to other organs: the nerves (facial palsy, meningitis), the heart (heart block) and, months later, the large joints (arthritis, often the knee). Antibodies take several weeks to develop, so blood tests are often negative early on.
explain.confirm: In early localised Lyme disease, a typical erythema migrans rash (usually at least 5 cm and expanding) in someone with possible tick exposure in an area where Lyme occurs is enough to diagnose and treat; blood tests are not needed and are often negative. For later stages, two-tier antibody testing (ELISA, then a confirmatory immunoblot) is used.
explain.treat: Oral antibiotics, usually doxycycline (now considered suitable for short courses in children) or amoxicillin, for a short course; this cures most early infections and prevents spread. Later complications such as heart block, meningitis or arthritis may need antibiotics through a drip and monitoring. Prevention is key: insect repellent, long clothing, daily tick checks and removing ticks promptly with fine tweezers.

near.cellulitis: Cellulitis is hot, painful and spreads fast with a fever; this patch is barely tender, has a clear centre and followed a tick bite.
near.ringworm: Ringworm is also a ring, but it's scaly and itchy and doesn't come with fever and aches after a woodland trip.
near.rocky mountain spotted fever: Also tick-borne, but that gives a spotty rash starting on the wrists and ankles, not one expanding bull's-eye at the bite.

cases.pearl: A negative Lyme blood test in the first weeks doesn't rule it out; an expanding bull's-eye rash after a tick bite is the diagnosis.

cases.complaint: A 17-year-old boy who lives in a school boarding house is brought in with a fever, a pounding headache and spots appearing on his legs.

clues.history: He felt fluey and achy 14 hours ago, then developed a severe headache, vomiting, neck pain and could not stand bright light. His legs ached and his hands and feet felt cold. His roommate noticed purple spots on his shins an hour ago. He has not had his meningococcal booster.
clues.vitals: Temp 39.4 °C, HR 126/min, BP 92/54 mmHg, RR 24/min, SpO2 96% on room air. Capillary refill 4 seconds.
clues.exam: GCS 14, irritable. Neck stiffness; Kernig sign positive (extending the knee with the hip flexed causes pain) and Brudzinski sign positive. Purple, non-blanching purpuric spots on the legs and trunk that don't fade under a pressed glass. Cold hands and feet. No focal neurological signs, no papilloedema.
clues.labs: WBC 22.5 ×10^9/L with neutrophilia, platelets 88 ×10^9/L, CRP very high, lactate 4.1 mmol/L, prolonged clotting times. Blood cultures: Gram-negative diplococci. CSF (after resuscitation): cloudy, opening pressure 32 cmH2O, white cells 2400 ×10^6/L (95% neutrophils), protein 2.1 g/L, glucose 1.2 mmol/L with blood glucose 6.5 mmol/L (ratio well under 0.4), Gram-negative diplococci on Gram stain; PCR positive for Neisseria meningitidis.
clues.imaging: CT head (done because of reduced consciousness before the lumbar puncture): no mass, no hydrocephalus, no cerebral swelling. Chest X-ray clear.

explain.patho: Neisseria meningitidis lives harmlessly in the nose and throat of many teenagers and spreads by respiratory droplets and close contact, which is why shared living spaces matter. In a few people it invades the bloodstream; its polysaccharide capsule helps it dodge complement and white cells. It crosses into the CSF, where there are few defences, and its outer-membrane endotoxin (lipooligosaccharide) triggers a massive cytokine storm. Inflammation breaks down the blood-brain barrier, causing brain swelling and raised pressure, and the neutrophil-rich pus consumes glucose while barrier damage blocks its transport, so CSF glucose falls and protein rises. In the blood, endotoxin damages vessel walls and switches on clotting everywhere (disseminated intravascular coagulation), using up platelets and causing the purpuric rash and shock.
explain.confirm: Blood cultures and PCR for meningococcus are taken quickly, ideally before antibiotics but never delaying them. The lumbar puncture shows the classic bacterial pattern of high neutrophils, high protein and low glucose with organisms on Gram stain. A CT is needed before the lumbar puncture only if there are signs of raised pressure or reduced consciousness.
explain.treat: Intravenous antibiotics (a third-generation cephalosporin such as ceftriaxone) are given immediately, even before tests if needed, along with corticosteroids (dexamethasone) in suspected bacterial meningitis. He needs aggressive sepsis care with fluids, oxygen and intensive care support. Close contacts get preventive antibiotics, and public health is notified. Vaccines (MenACWY and MenB) prevent most cases.

near.viral meningitis: Viral CSF is mostly lymphocytes with normal glucose, and it doesn't cause a purpuric rash and shock.
near.subarachnoid haemorrhage: The stiff neck fits, but this built up over hours with a high fever and a rash.
near.influenza: Flu doesn't give a non-blanching rash, neck stiffness and low CSF glucose.
near.sepsis: Yes, but there's a specific infection affecting the brain's coverings here.

cases.pearl: Fever plus a non-blanching rash means antibiotics within minutes; never wait for the lumbar puncture.

cases.complaint: A 15-year-old girl sees zigzag shimmering lights spreading across her vision in a maths lesson, then gets a throbbing headache and has to go home.

clues.history: The lights started as a small sparkling spot near the centre of her vision and slowly spread outward over 20 minutes, then faded. Next, tingling crept from her right fingers up to her face over 10 minutes. Then came a throbbing left-sided headache with nausea; light and noise made it worse and she wanted to lie in a dark room. She has had three similar attacks this year, usually after skipped meals or late nights. Her mother gets migraines.
clues.vitals: Temp 36.7 °C, HR 82/min, BP 112/68 mmHg, RR 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air.
clues.exam: Seen the next day: full neurological examination normal, including visual fields and fundoscopy (sharp optic discs, no papilloedema). No neck stiffness. Blood pressure normal.
clues.labs: No blood tests are needed. Full blood count and glucose were normal when checked.
clues.imaging: No imaging is needed: there are no red flags, the attacks are stereotyped, she has a family history and the examination is normal. Scanning would be considered for a sudden thunderclap onset, an aura that doesn't resolve, an abnormal exam or a change in pattern.

explain.patho: The aura is caused by cortical spreading depression: a slow wave of intense neuronal firing followed by silence that creeps across the cortex at a few millimetres per minute. When it travels through the visual cortex it produces sparkling lights that move and grow, followed by a blind patch; through the sensory cortex it causes tingling that marches up the limb. The headache comes from the trigeminovascular system: trigeminal nerve fibres around the blood vessels of the meninges get activated and release neuropeptides, especially CGRP, causing inflammation and widening of those vessels. Pain pathways in the brainstem and thalamus then become sensitised, so normal light, sound and movement feel unbearable. Migraine has a strong genetic tendency, and triggers like skipped meals, poor sleep and stress lower the threshold for an attack.
explain.confirm: It is a clinical diagnosis using the International Classification of Headache Disorders: at least two attacks with fully reversible aura symptoms that spread gradually over several minutes, each lasting up to an hour, usually followed by headache. A normal examination and no red flags mean no tests are needed.
explain.treat: Attacks are treated early with simple painkillers or anti-inflammatories, triptans and anti-sickness medicines, resting in a dark, quiet room. Using painkillers on too many days a month causes medication-overuse headache, so frequency is tracked with a headache diary. Regular sleep, meals, hydration and exercise reduce attacks, and frequent migraines can be prevented with daily preventive medicines or newer CGRP-blocking antibodies.

near.transient ischaemic attack: TIA symptoms come on suddenly and remove function; hers spread slowly with sparkles and tingling in a healthy teenager.
near.seizure: Seizure auras last seconds to a couple of minutes; hers spread over 20 minutes and were followed by a classic headache.
near.subarachnoid haemorrhage: This headache built up gradually after a spreading aura; it wasn't a thunderclap.
near.tension headache: Tension headaches are band-like and don't come with zigzag lights, nausea and light sensitivity.

cases.pearl: Aura creeps, stroke strikes: migraine symptoms spread over minutes and are 'positive' (sparkles, tingling), while stroke and TIA symptoms are sudden and 'negative' (loss of function).

cases.complaint: A 27-year-old woman has had blurred vision in her left eye for four days, with an ache when she moves the eye.

clues.history: Colours look 'washed out' in the left eye, especially reds. Eye movement makes the ache worse. Two years ago she had three weeks of tingling and numbness in both legs up to the waist that went away on its own and was never investigated. She notices an electric shock down her spine when she bends her neck forward. Symptoms got worse after a hot shower.
clues.vitals: Temp 36.8 °C, HR 72/min, BP 118/74 mmHg, RR 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air.
clues.exam: Left visual acuity 6/36, right 6/6. Left relative afferent pupillary defect (both pupils dilate when the light swings to the left eye). Red desaturation and a central blind spot in the left eye. Optic disc looks normal. Brisk knee and ankle reflexes with an upgoing right plantar. Lhermitte sign positive.
clues.labs: Full blood count, vitamin B12, thyroid tests and inflammatory markers normal. Aquaporin-4 and MOG antibodies negative (rules out neuromyelitis optica and MOG antibody disease). CSF: white cells 6 ×10^6/L (lymphocytes), protein 0.45 g/L, and oligoclonal IgG bands present in the CSF but not in the blood.
clues.imaging: MRI brain and spine with contrast: multiple oval white-matter lesions next to and perpendicular to the lateral ventricles ('Dawson's fingers'), plus lesions just under the cortex, in the brainstem and in the cervical spinal cord. One lesion lights up with contrast (new) while the others don't (old). The left optic nerve is swollen and enhancing. Visual evoked potentials: delayed signal from the left eye.

explain.patho: In MS, autoreactive T cells and B cells get across the blood-brain barrier and attack myelin made by oligodendrocytes in the brain, optic nerves and spinal cord. Stripped of myelin, axons can no longer use fast saltatory conduction, so signals slow down or get blocked; that's why the visual evoked potential is delayed. Inflammation calms and some remyelination happens, so early attacks often recover, giving the relapsing-remitting pattern. Over time, axons themselves are lost, and disability accumulates. Heat further slows conduction in demyelinated fibres (Uhthoff phenomenon), and bending the neck stretches damaged dorsal column fibres in the cervical cord (Lhermitte sign). Genes, low vitamin D and earlier Epstein–Barr virus infection all raise risk.
explain.confirm: The McDonald criteria require evidence of damage in at least two separate CNS areas (dissemination in space) occurring at different times (dissemination in time), shown clinically or on MRI. Enhancing and non-enhancing lesions together prove dissemination in time, and CSF oligoclonal bands can substitute for it. Mimics such as neuromyelitis optica and B12 deficiency must be excluded.
explain.treat: Acute relapses such as optic neuritis are treated with a short course of high-dose corticosteroids to speed recovery, or plasma exchange if severe. Long-term disease-modifying therapies reduce relapses and new lesions: options range from interferon-beta and glatiramer to more powerful B-cell-depleting antibodies (such as ocrelizumab) and natalizumab. Symptom treatment, physiotherapy and support complete care.

near.optic neuritis: That's what happened to her eye, but the earlier leg episode and the MRI show the bigger diagnosis behind it.
near.neuromyelitis optica: Good thinking, but her aquaporin-4 and MOG antibodies are negative and the lesions sit next to the ventricles.
near.brain tumour: Multiple lesions of different ages in different places, coming and going over years, point to an immune disease.
near.migraine: Migraine doesn't cause a pupil defect, upgoing toes and oligoclonal bands.

cases.pearl: In optic neuritis 'the patient sees nothing and the doctor sees nothing': the inflammation is behind the eye, so the disc usually looks normal.

cases.complaint: A 29-year-old woman says her eyelids droop and she sees double by the evening, and lately she has started choking at the end of meals.

clues.history: She wakes up feeling fine, but as the day goes on her eyelids droop and she gets double vision, especially reading late. Her jaw gets tired chewing steak, liquids sometimes come out of her nose and her arms tire when she brushes her hair. Rest makes it better. No numbness, no pain, normal bladder, no recent infection.
clues.vitals: Temp 36.7 °C, HR 76/min, BP 116/72 mmHg, RR 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air. Forced vital capacity normal.
clues.exam: Both eyelids droop unevenly and droop further when she looks up for a minute (fatigability). An ice pack on the eyelids for two minutes improves the droop. Eye movements are limited in a pattern that fits no single nerve. Pupils are normal. Neck and shoulder muscles weaken with repeated testing. Reflexes and sensation are normal.
clues.labs: Acetylcholine receptor antibodies: strongly positive. Thyroid tests normal (autoimmune thyroid disease often travels with it). CK normal. Full blood count and electrolytes normal.
clues.imaging: Repetitive nerve stimulation: the muscle response drops by more than 10% over a train of stimuli (decremental response). Single-fibre EMG: increased 'jitter'. CT chest: a soft-tissue mass in the anterior mediastinum consistent with a thymoma.

explain.patho: In myasthenia gravis the immune system makes antibodies against the nicotinic acetylcholine receptors on the muscle side of the neuromuscular junction. The antibodies block receptors, cross-link them so they are pulled inside the cell, and activate complement that flattens the folded muscle membrane. With fewer working receptors, the normal 'safety margin' of transmission is lost. Even in healthy people the amount of acetylcholine released falls with repeated nerve firing, so with too few receptors, muscles fail more and more with use and recover with rest. Eye and eyelid muscles are affected first because they fire fast and have very small motor units. The thymus, where T cells learn not to attack the body, is abnormal in most patients and can harbour a thymoma.
explain.confirm: Positive acetylcholine receptor antibodies (or MuSK antibodies if those are negative) plus the typical fatigable weakness confirm it. Repetitive nerve stimulation shows a decrement and single-fibre EMG shows jitter. A CT of the chest looks for a thymoma.
explain.treat: Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (pyridostigmine) boost acetylcholine at the junction to relieve symptoms. Immunosuppression with corticosteroids and steroid-sparing drugs controls the disease, and newer complement and antibody-removing treatments are used in some patients. A thymoma must be surgically removed (thymectomy), which also helps many patients without one. A myasthenic crisis with breathing or swallowing failure is treated with intravenous immunoglobulin or plasma exchange and ventilatory support, and some antibiotics and other drugs that worsen weakness are avoided.

near.lambert-eaton syndrome: In that condition strength improves briefly with use and reflexes are reduced; here weakness gets worse with use and reflexes are normal.
near.guillain-barre syndrome: No tingling and normal reflexes; the weakness fluctuates through the day rather than climbing steadily.
near.third nerve palsy: A third nerve palsy involves the pupil and fits one nerve's pattern; here the pupils are normal and the pattern fits no single nerve.
near.thyroid eye disease: Her thyroid tests are normal and the weakness also involves swallowing and arms.

cases.pearl: Myasthenia never touches the pupil: a droopy lid with a big pupil is a third nerve problem.

cases.complaint: A 74-year-old man's family say that over the past year his walking has become shuffly, he leaks urine and he has become forgetful and slow.

clues.history: First his walking changed: he says his feet feel 'glued to the floor' and he has had several near-falls turning around. Then came urinary urgency and, for the last few months, accidents before he reaches the toilet. Lately he is slower to answer, loses interest and forgets appointments. Years ago he had a bad bout of meningitis. No tremor, no headache, no head injury.
clues.vitals: Temp 36.7 °C, HR 72/min, BP 136/80 mmHg, RR 14/min, SpO2 97% on room air.
clues.exam: Broad-based gait with short, shuffling, 'magnetic' steps; his feet barely leave the floor and turning takes many small steps. Arm swing is normal and there is no rest tremor or cogwheel rigidity. Thinking is slow, with poor attention and planning; cognitive screening score 22 out of 30. No papilloedema. Strength and sensation normal.
clues.labs: Vitamin B12, thyroid function, glucose, sodium and calcium normal (screening for reversible causes of cognitive decline). Urinalysis normal, no infection. Lumbar 'tap test': opening pressure 14 cmH2O (normal range); after removing a large volume of CSF, his walking speed the next day improved by about a third, with fewer steps when turning.
clues.imaging: MRI brain: lateral ventricles markedly enlarged, out of proportion to the size of the sulci (Evans index 0.36), a narrow callosal angle, tight sulci at the top of the brain with widened Sylvian fissures (a pattern called DESH), and no blockage of CSF flow. The cerebral aqueduct is open.

explain.patho: Normal pressure hydrocephalus is a communicating hydrocephalus: CSF can flow through all the ventricles, but it isn't absorbed properly into the venous system at the arachnoid granulations. It can follow damage to those granulations, for example after meningitis or a subarachnoid bleed, or arise without a clear cause in older people. The ventricles slowly enlarge; the pressure looks normal on a single measurement, but there are intermittent pressure waves and the brain's compliance is altered. The enlarged lateral ventricles stretch and starve nearby white-matter fibres: those running from the motor cortex to the legs and those controlling the bladder curve around the ventricles, and connections between the frontal lobes and deeper structures are disrupted. That gives the classic triad of gait disturbance (usually first), urinary incontinence and slowed thinking.
explain.confirm: The diagnosis is suggested by the triad with ventricles enlarged out of proportion to brain shrinkage on CT or MRI. It's supported by improvement in walking after a large-volume lumbar tap test or a few days of extended lumbar drainage, which also predicts who will benefit from a shunt.
explain.treat: The treatment is a ventriculoperitoneal shunt: a neurosurgeon places a tube with a programmable valve from a lateral ventricle under the skin to the abdomen, draining excess CSF.
