Walking improves the most and earliest, bladder control often improves, and thinking improves least. Risks include shunt infection, blockage and over-drainage causing subdural collections, so follow-up adjusts the valve setting.

near.parkinson disease: Shuffling fits, but he has normal arm swing, no rest tremor and huge ventricles that improve with a tap.
near.alzheimer disease: Memory problems fit, but the walking problem came first, with bladder trouble and large ventricles.
near.vascular dementia: It can look similar, but there's no stroke history and his gait improved after removing CSF.
near.obstructive hydrocephalus: The CSF pathways are open and the opening pressure is normal.

cases.pearl: Wet, wobbly and wacky (incontinence, gait, confusion): one of the few causes of dementia that a neurosurgeon can reverse.

cases.complaint: A 68-year-old woman comes to the ED with episodes of chest tightness over the past two days, the latest lasting 25 minutes at rest this morning.

clues.history: For two months she has had chest tightness when climbing stairs that settles within minutes of resting. Over the last two days it has come on with less effort and this morning it woke her and lasted 25 minutes, with breathlessness and nausea. She has type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure and chronic kidney disease. The pain has now eased.
clues.vitals: Temp 36.7 °C, HR 88/min, BP 156/88 mmHg, RR 18/min, SpO2 97% on room air.
clues.exam: Comfortable now. Heart sounds normal, no murmur, no rub. Chest clear and no raised JVP. Pulses equal. Chest wall is not tender.
clues.labs: High-sensitivity troponin I 48 ng/L on arrival (99th centile 16), rising to 310 ng/L at 3 hours. Creatinine 132 µmol/L, potassium 4.6 mmol/L, glucose 9.8 mmol/L, haemoglobin 128 g/L. D-dimer normal.
clues.imaging: ECG: sinus rhythm with 1–2 mm horizontal ST depression and T-wave inversion in V4–V6, I and aVL; no ST elevation anywhere. Echo: mild reduced movement of the lateral wall, normal valves, no pericardial fluid. Chest X-ray normal.

explain.patho: Like a STEMI, an NSTEMI starts with a coronary plaque that ruptures or erodes, triggering platelet clumping and a thrombus. The difference is that the clot only partly blocks the artery, or blocks it on and off, so blood flow is reduced rather than stopped. The innermost layer of heart muscle (the subendocardium) is furthest from the coronary arteries and suffers first, so injury is often not full-thickness. Subendocardial ischaemia shows up as ST depression or T-wave inversion instead of ST elevation. Enough cells die to release troponin, which is what separates NSTEMI from unstable angina, where the symptoms are the same but troponin does not rise. Crescendo angina (pain coming on with less and less effort) is the warning sign of an unstable plaque.
explain.confirm: A rise and/or fall of high-sensitivity troponin above the 99th centile on serial samples, with ischaemic symptoms and no persistent ST elevation, confirms NSTEMI. Risk scores such as GRACE guide how quickly to do coronary angiography, which shows the culprit narrowing.
explain.treat: Antiplatelet therapy (aspirin plus a second antiplatelet), an anticoagulant, nitrates and beta-blockers for pain, and a high-intensity statin. Most patients have coronary angiography within a day or so, with stenting or bypass surgery depending on the anatomy. Long-term care focuses on secondary prevention: blood pressure, diabetes and cholesterol control, exercise and cardiac rehab.

near.stemi: The ECG shows ST depression, not elevation, so the artery is not fully blocked.
near.stable angina: Stable angina is predictable and settles with rest; pain at rest with a rising troponin means something more.
near.pulmonary embolism: A normal D-dimer makes this very unlikely, and the ECG changes fit a coronary territory.

cases.pearl: Same symptoms, same ECG: if troponin rises it is NSTEMI, if it stays normal it is unstable angina.

cases.complaint: A 66-year-old man comes in because his wife has noticed his right hand shakes when he is sitting watching TV, and he seems to be slowing down.

clues.history: The tremor started a year ago in the right hand and is worse when he is relaxed or stressed. His handwriting has got smaller, his voice quieter and his walking slower. Years ago he lost his sense of smell, he has had constipation for a long time, and his wife says he shouts and punches in his sleep as if acting out dreams. He feels lightheaded standing up quickly. He takes no regular medicines.
clues.vitals: Temp 36.6 °C, HR 70/min, BP 132/80 mmHg lying and 110/68 mmHg after three minutes standing, RR 14/min, SpO2 98% on room air.
clues.exam: A slow 'pill-rolling' tremor of the right hand at rest that fades when he reaches for something, then returns. Ratchety 'cogwheel' stiffness in the right wrist. Finger taps get smaller and slower with repetition (bradykinesia). Reduced facial expression and blinking. He walks with short steps, a stooped posture and reduced right arm swing, and turns in several steps. Mild unsteadiness when pulled backwards.
clues.labs: Full blood count, thyroid function, vitamin B12, glucose and liver tests normal (screening for treatable mimics). He is not taking any medicine that blocks dopamine, such as some anti-sickness drugs or antipsychotics.
clues.imaging: MRI brain: age-appropriate, no strokes, no enlarged ventricles, no structural lesion. DaT scan (a SPECT scan of dopamine transporters): reduced uptake in the putamen, worse on the left, turning the normal 'comma' shape into a 'full stop'.

explain.patho: Parkinson disease is caused by the gradual death of dopamine-making neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta, with clumps of misfolded alpha-synuclein protein called Lewy bodies inside surviving cells. More than half these neurons are lost before movement symptoms appear. Dopamine normally drives the basal ganglia 'direct pathway' (via D1 receptors) that releases movement and dampens the 'indirect pathway' (via D2 receptors) that brakes it. Without dopamine the brakes win: the globus pallidus internus over-inhibits the thalamus, so movements become small and slow. Alpha-synuclein pathology often starts in the gut and the smell pathways and in brainstem sleep centres years earlier, explaining the long-standing constipation, loss of smell and dream-enactment. The left side of his brain is worse, so the symptoms are on the right.
explain.confirm: It is a clinical diagnosis: bradykinesia plus a rest tremor or rigidity, using the Movement Disorder Society criteria. A clear, lasting improvement on levodopa supports it. A DaT scan helps only when the picture is unclear, for example to separate it from essential tremor or drug-induced parkinsonism.
explain.treat: Levodopa, combined with a decarboxylase inhibitor (carbidopa) so more reaches the brain, is the most effective drug; dopamine agonists and MAO-B inhibitors are other options. Regular exercise, physiotherapy, and speech and occupational therapy are vital. In advanced disease with motor fluctuations, a neurosurgeon can implant deep brain stimulation electrodes in the subthalamic nucleus or globus pallidus.

near.essential tremor: Essential tremor shakes during action like holding a cup, not at rest, and doesn't cause slowness or stiffness.
near.normal pressure hydrocephalus: His MRI ventricles are normal, there's a rest tremor, and the signs are one-sided.
near.drug-induced parkinsonism: He takes no dopamine-blocking medicines and his DaT scan is abnormal.
near.multiple system atrophy: Possible as a mimic, but his signs are one-sided with a classic rest tremor and no early severe autonomic failure.

cases.pearl: Parkinson disease starts on one side and stays worse on that side; symmetric parkinsonism from day one should make you think of a mimic.

cases.dx: Upper GI bleed from a duodenal ulcer
cases.complaint: A 62-year-old man collapsed at home after vomiting dark material and passing black stools.

clues.history: He has had burning upper abdominal pain on and off for six weeks, often eased by eating. For his knee arthritis he has been taking ibuprofen most days for two months. This morning he vomited material like coffee grounds and later passed sticky, black, tar-like stool with a strong smell. He felt faint standing up and collapsed briefly in the bathroom.
clues.vitals: Temp 36.6 °C, HR 116/min, BP 96/58 mmHg (falls further on sitting up), RR 22/min, SpO2 97% on room air.
clues.exam: Pale, sweaty and cool hands with slow capillary refill. Mild tenderness in the upper middle abdomen but no guarding. Rectal examination shows black, tarry stool (melaena). No enlarged liver or other signs of liver disease.
clues.labs: Haemoglobin 79 g/L (normal 130–170; it was 142 g/L a year ago). Urea 19.5 mmol/L but creatinine only 96 µmol/L; the high urea comes from digested blood protein absorbed in the gut. Platelets and clotting normal. H. pylori biopsy urease test: positive.
clues.imaging: Upper GI endoscopy (within 24 hours): a 1.5 cm ulcer on the back wall of the first part of the duodenum with a visible blood vessel in its base and fresh clot. The stomach shows mild inflammation. No varices.

explain.patho: The stomach and duodenum are protected from their own acid by a mucus-bicarbonate layer, a good blood supply and prostaglandins, which keep that defence running. NSAIDs such as ibuprofen block cyclo-oxygenase, the enzyme that makes these protective prostaglandins, so the lining becomes vulnerable. H. pylori bacteria add to this by inflaming the lining and increasing acid output, which floods the duodenum. Acid digests a crater through the lining; if it erodes into an artery behind the duodenum (the gastroduodenal artery), it bleeds briskly. Blood exposed to acid turns into coffee-ground material when vomited, and blood digested on its way through the gut becomes black melaena. Losing blood quickly drops the circulating volume, so the heart races and blood pressure falls before the haemoglobin has had time to drop fully.
explain.confirm: Endoscopy is both the diagnostic test and the treatment, showing the ulcer and features that predict re-bleeding, such as a visible vessel. The Glasgow-Blatchford score before endoscopy and the Rockall score after help judge risk. H. pylori is checked by biopsy, breath or stool antigen test.
explain.treat: Resuscitation first: large-bore intravenous access, fluids and blood transfusion when needed. At endoscopy the bleeding vessel is treated with clips, heat or injection, and an acid-suppressing proton pump inhibitor is given afterwards. If endoscopy fails, a radiologist can block the artery (embolisation) or a surgeon can operate. Long term: stop the NSAID and eradicate H. pylori with a combination of antibiotics and acid suppression.

near.oesophageal varices: Varices bleed in people with liver disease; he has none, and endoscopy found the source further down past the stomach.
near.mallory-weiss tear: That tear follows forceful retching and usually bleeds bright red then stops, without weeks of meal-related pain.
near.gastric cancer: Also possible at his age, but the story of NSAIDs plus H. pylori and a crater in the duodenum points to something benign.

cases.pearl: A high urea with a normal creatinine is a quiet clue to an upper GI bleed: the gut digests the blood like a high-protein meal.

cases.complaint: A 24-year-old man comes in with sharp chest pain for two days that is worse when he lies flat.

clues.history: Sharp central chest pain that is worse on breathing in and lying back, and better when he sits up and leans forward. It sometimes goes to the top of his left shoulder. He had a cold with a sore throat and runny nose about ten days ago. No exertional pattern, no recent travel or surgery, no leg swelling.
clues.vitals: Temp 37.9 °C, HR 98/min, BP 124/78 mmHg, RR 18/min, SpO2 98% on room air.
clues.exam: A scratchy, high-pitched three-part sound is heard at the left lower sternal edge, loudest when he leans forward and breathes out (a friction rub). Heart sounds otherwise normal. JVP not raised, no pulsus paradoxus. Chest clear.
clues.labs: CRP and ESR raised. WBC 11.8 ×10^9/L. High-sensitivity troponin T 12 ng/L (normal). Creatinine 84 µmol/L, urea 5.1 mmol/L, TSH normal.
clues.imaging: ECG: widespread concave ('saddle-shaped') ST elevation in I, II, aVL, aVF and V2–V6 with PR-segment depression; ST depression and PR elevation only in aVR. Echo: a thin rim of pericardial fluid, normal heart squeeze, no signs of tamponade. Chest X-ray normal.

explain.patho: The pericardium is a two-layered sac around the heart with a small amount of lubricating fluid between the layers. Most acute cases are caused by viruses (such as coxsackievirus) or have no clear cause, and the immune response makes the layers inflamed and rough. The rough surfaces rubbing together create the friction rub and the sharp pain, which worsens when the heart and lungs press the layers together lying flat or breathing in. Pain can reach the shoulder tip because the phrenic nerve, which supplies part of the pericardium, shares nerve roots with the shoulder skin. Inflammation of the outer heart muscle beneath the pericardium causes ST elevation in almost every lead, not in one coronary territory. If fluid builds up fast it can squeeze the heart (tamponade).
explain.confirm: At least two of four criteria: typical pleuritic, positional chest pain; a friction rub; widespread ST elevation or PR depression on ECG; and a new or growing pericardial effusion. Raised CRP supports it, and echo checks for an effusion or tamponade. A raised troponin suggests the heart muscle is involved too (myopericarditis).
explain.treat: Anti-inflammatory treatment with NSAIDs (or aspirin) combined with colchicine, which reduces the chance of it coming back. Rest and avoiding strenuous exercise until symptoms and CRP settle; athletes are kept out of competitive sport for longer. Steroids are second-line, and a large effusion or tamponade is drained with a needle (pericardiocentesis).

near.stemi: An infarct's ST elevation stays in one coronary territory with reciprocal depression; here it is everywhere with PR depression and the troponin is normal.
near.pneumothorax: Pleuritic pain fits, but the positional relief leaning forward and the rub point at the sac around the heart.
near.pulmonary embolism: Pleuritic pain and tachycardia fit, but a rub plus widespread saddle ST elevation points elsewhere.

cases.pearl: Better leaning forward, worse lying flat, plus PR depression: think pericarditis.

cases.dx: Pre-renal acute kidney injury from dehydration
cases.complaint: A 79-year-old man is admitted feeling weak and dizzy after three days of diarrhoea and vomiting, and he has barely passed urine today.

clues.history: He caught a stomach bug from his grandchildren; he has had watery diarrhoea and vomiting for three days and has managed only sips of water. He takes ramipril and a water tablet (furosemide) for blood pressure and heart failure, and kept taking them. Today he has passed only a small amount of dark urine. He feels lightheaded when he stands.
clues.vitals: Temp 37.2 °C, HR 108/min, BP 96/54 mmHg lying, dropping to 78/46 mmHg on standing, RR 18/min, SpO2 96% on room air.
clues.exam: Dry tongue and lips, sunken eyes, cool hands with slow capillary refill, low neck veins. Chest clear with no ankle swelling. Abdomen soft with active bowel sounds; the bladder is not enlarged.
clues.labs: Creatinine 248 µmol/L (his baseline three months ago was 88). Urea 24.1 mmol/L, so urea has risen much more than creatinine. Sodium 146 mmol/L, potassium 5.8 mmol/L. Urine: concentrated, with a very low urine sodium of 9 mmol/L, meaning the kidneys are holding on to salt. Urine dipstick: no blood or protein.
clues.imaging: Renal ultrasound: two normal-sized kidneys with no swelling of the collecting systems (no hydronephrosis), which rules out a blockage; the bladder is nearly empty. ECG: sinus tachycardia, no changes from the potassium yet.

explain.patho: The kidneys filter blood at a rate set by the pressure in the glomerular capillaries. Losing fluid through vomiting and diarrhoea shrinks the circulating volume, so less blood reaches the kidneys and filtration falls; urea and creatinine are no longer cleared and build up. In pre-renal injury the kidney tissue is healthy and responds correctly: it holds on to sodium and water, producing small amounts of concentrated, low-sodium urine. The body normally protects filtration by constricting the outflow vessel from the glomerulus with angiotensin II; ACE inhibitors such as ramipril block this rescue, and diuretics remove more fluid, so both make the injury worse. Because urea is reabsorbed along with water when the kidney is conserving fluid, urea rises out of proportion to creatinine. If the low blood flow continues, the kidney tubules can be damaged (acute tubular necrosis), which no longer reverses quickly.
explain.confirm: AKI is defined by a rise in creatinine from baseline (for example by half again within a week) or a drop in urine output (KDIGO criteria). A pre-renal cause is supported by the history of fluid loss, signs of dehydration, a low urine sodium and a prompt improvement in creatinine with fluids. Ultrasound excludes obstruction.
explain.treat: Intravenous fluids to restore circulating volume, with close monitoring of urine output, fluid balance and blood tests. Drugs that strain the kidneys or lower blood pressure, such as ACE inhibitors, diuretics and anti-inflammatory painkillers, are paused ('sick day rules') and restarted when he recovers. High potassium is treated if it rises or changes the ECG. Dialysis is only needed if the kidneys fail to recover and complications become dangerous.

near.urinary retention: Low urine output can mean a blocked bladder, but his bladder is empty and the scan shows no blockage.
near.acute tubular necrosis: That's what this can become if it isn't fixed; right now his kidneys still hold on to sodium, so the tubules are working.
near.gastroenteritis: That's the trigger; name what it has done to his kidneys.

cases.pearl: When a patient with diarrhoea and vomiting takes ACE inhibitors or diuretics, pause them: they block the kidney's own defence against low blood pressure.

cases.complaint: A tall, thin 19-year-old man develops sudden sharp pain on the right side of his chest while sitting in class.

clues.history: The pain came on suddenly at rest, is sharp and worse on breathing in, and he feels mildly short of breath. No injury. He is 1.93 m tall and slim. No asthma or other lung disease. He doesn't smoke. His older brother had something similar at 20.
clues.vitals: Temp 36.8 °C, HR 96/min, BP 126/78 mmHg, RR 20/min, SpO2 96% on room air.
clues.exam: Mildly uncomfortable. Reduced breath sounds and reduced chest movement on the right with a hyperresonant note when tapped. Trachea central. No surgical emphysema. Neck veins normal.
clues.labs: Blood tests are rarely needed here. Full blood count normal (WBC 7.4 ×10^9/L, haemoglobin 152 g/L). Troponin, checked by the triage nurse, is normal at 4 ng/L. D-dimer was not sent because the X-ray explains the symptoms.
clues.imaging: Chest X-ray: a thin white line (the visceral pleura) separated from the right chest wall by a black space with no lung markings, with a 3 cm rim of air at the level of the hilum. No mediastinal shift. ECG: normal sinus rhythm. CT (if done later) shows small air blisters (blebs) at the top of both lungs.

explain.patho: A primary spontaneous pneumothorax happens in people without known lung disease, classically tall, thin young men. Tiny air-filled blisters called blebs or bullae form under the pleura at the lung apex, possibly because the lungs of tall people are stretched more at the top where pressure is most negative. When a bleb bursts, air escapes from the lung into the pleural space. The lung's natural elastic recoil then pulls it inward, partly collapsing it, while the chest wall springs outward. Less lung is ventilated, causing breathlessness, and the irritated pleura causes sharp, pleuritic pain. Smoking and a family history raise the risk, and it often recurs.
explain.confirm: An erect chest X-ray showing the visceral pleural line with no lung markings beyond it confirms the diagnosis; the size of the rim of air guides treatment. Ultrasound (absent lung sliding) and CT help in unclear cases.
explain.treat: Small pneumothoraces with mild symptoms can be watched with outpatient follow-up as the air is reabsorbed, or managed with a small one-way valve device. Larger or symptomatic ones are treated with needle aspiration or a small chest drain. Recurrent cases are treated with keyhole surgery (VATS) to remove the blebs and make the pleura stick together (pleurodesis); flying is avoided until the lung is fully healed, and scuba diving is permanently unsafe unless surgery has been done.

near.tension pneumothorax: Air is in the right place, but his blood pressure is normal and the trachea is central, so it's not under tension.
near.pulmonary embolism: Sudden pleuritic pain fits, but the hyperresonance and reduced breath sounds point to air outside the lung.
near.pericarditis: Sharp chest pain in a young man, but the lung signs on one side point to the pleural space.

cases.pearl: Tall, thin young man plus sudden one-sided pleuritic pain at rest: pneumothorax until the X-ray says otherwise.

cases.complaint: A 58-year-old man becomes suddenly short of breath with sharp chest pain eight days after a hip replacement.

clues.history: Sudden breathlessness this morning at home with a sharp pain on the right side of his chest that is worse on breathing in. He coughed up a small streak of blood. He had a right hip replacement eight days ago and has been mostly in a chair since. His right calf has felt tight and sore for two days. No fever, no previous heart or lung disease.
clues.vitals: Temp 37.4 °C, HR 118/min, BP 122/80 mmHg, RR 26/min, SpO2 89% on room air.
clues.exam: Anxious and breathless. Chest clear on listening, no wheeze. Heart sounds normal, JVP mildly raised. Right calf swollen (3 cm larger than left), warm and tender along the deep veins. Healing hip wound, no infection.
clues.labs: D-dimer strongly raised. Arterial gas on air: pH 7.48, PaO2 7.6 kPa (low), PaCO2 4.0 kPa (low). Troponin T 28 ng/L, BNP mildly raised. Haemoglobin 124 g/L, creatinine 86 µmol/L, platelets 260 ×10^9/L.
clues.imaging: ECG: sinus tachycardia with T-wave inversion in V1–V3; no ST elevation. Chest X-ray: near normal, small wedge-shaped shadow at the right base. CT pulmonary angiogram: filling defects (clots) in the right lower lobe artery and several left segmental arteries; the right ventricle is mildly enlarged. Leg ultrasound: non-compressible right popliteal vein with clot.

explain.patho: Virchow's triad explains why clots form: slow blood flow (immobility after surgery), damage to the vessel wall (the operation itself) and blood that clots more easily (surgery triggers a clotting response). A clot forms in the deep veins of the leg, then a piece breaks off, travels through the right side of the heart and lodges in the pulmonary arteries. The blocked lung segments are still ventilated but not perfused, so oxygen can't be picked up: this is ventilation–perfusion mismatch, causing hypoxia. The patient breathes fast to compensate, blowing off carbon dioxide (low PaCO2). The right ventricle suddenly has to pump against high resistance, so it strains and stretches, releasing troponin and BNP; a large clot can cause the right ventricle to fail and blood pressure to collapse. Lung tissue downstream can die (infarct), causing pleuritic pain and coughing up blood.
explain.confirm: Clinical probability is estimated first with the Wells score. If PE is unlikely, a normal D-dimer rules it out; if likely, CT pulmonary angiography is the key test and shows the clot directly. A V/Q scan is an alternative when CT contrast is unsafe, and echo shows right-heart strain in unstable patients.
explain.treat: Anticoagulation is the mainstay: usually a direct oral anticoagulant or low-molecular-weight heparin, continued for months, which stops the clot growing while the body breaks it down. Oxygen and pain relief are given. A massive PE causing shock is treated with clot-busting thrombolysis, or with catheter or surgical clot removal if thrombolysis is unsafe.

near.pneumonia: No fever, a clear chest and a swollen calf after surgery point elsewhere.
near.pneumothorax: Breath sounds are normal on both sides and the X-ray shows no collapsed lung.
near.stemi: No ST elevation; the T-wave changes in V1–V3 here reflect a strained right ventricle.

cases.pearl: A chest X-ray that looks surprisingly normal in a very hypoxic patient should make you think of PE.

cases.complaint: A 34-year-old man has had a cough for two months, with night sweats, weight loss and, this week, some blood in his sputum.

clues.history: His cough began about eight weeks ago and has not improved with a course of standard antibiotics from his GP. He wakes up drenched in sweat several nights a week, has lost 7 kg without trying and feels exhausted. This week he coughed up streaks of blood. He grew up in a country where TB is common and visited family there for three months last year; his grandfather was treated for 'a lung infection' at the time. He has type 2 diabetes.
clues.vitals: Temp 38.0 °C (evening), HR 98/min, BP 118/74 mmHg, RR 20/min, SpO2 95% on room air.
clues.exam: Thin, looks unwell. Crackles over the right upper chest at the front and back, with bronchial breathing over the same area. A few small, painless lymph nodes in the neck. No finger clubbing. Abdomen normal. Placed in a single room with the door closed while tests are done.
clues.labs: Haemoglobin 116 g/L, WBC 8.9 ×10^9/L, ESR and CRP raised. Albumin 31 g/L (low). Sodium 132 mmol/L. Glucose 12.4 mmol/L. Interferon-gamma release assay (blood TB test) positive. Three sputum samples: acid-fast bacilli seen on smear; a rapid PCR test (NAAT) detects Mycobacterium tuberculosis with no rifampicin-resistance mutation; culture confirms it weeks later.
clues.imaging: Chest X-ray: patchy shadowing in the right upper lobe with a thick-walled cavity (an air-filled hole) about 3 cm across, and swollen lymph nodes around the right hilum. CT chest: the cavity plus small 'tree-in-bud' nodules spreading through nearby airways, typical of active infection.

explain.patho: TB is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, a slow-growing bacterium with a thick, waxy cell wall that spreads through the air when someone with active lung TB coughs. Inhaled bacteria are swallowed by macrophages in the lungs but survive inside them. The immune system walls them off in granulomas, balls of immune cells with a cheese-like dead centre (caseous necrosis), and in most people the infection stays dormant for years (latent TB). If immunity weakens, for example with diabetes, poor nutrition, steroids or ageing, the bacteria reactivate, most often in the upper lobes, where oxygen levels are highest and the bacteria thrive. The caseous centre liquefies and empties into a bronchus, leaving a cavity full of bacteria that are coughed out, which makes the patient infectious and can erode blood vessels (blood in the sputum). Cytokines such as TNF cause fever, night sweats and weight loss.
explain.confirm: Active pulmonary TB is confirmed by finding M. tuberculosis in sputum: acid-fast bacilli on smear microscopy, a rapid nucleic acid amplification test (which also checks for rifampicin resistance), and culture, which is the gold standard and gives full drug-sensitivity results. A chest X-ray showing upper-lobe cavitation supports it. Blood (IGRA) or skin tests show TB infection but cannot distinguish latent from active disease.
explain.treat: Treatment is a combination of several antibiotics, classically rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol, started together, with fewer drugs continued for many months to kill slow-growing and dormant bacteria and prevent resistance. Taking every dose matters, so directly observed therapy and support are often used, along with checks of liver function and eyesight for side effects. He is isolated until no longer infectious, TB is a notifiable disease, and close contacts are traced and tested.

near.lung cancer: Weight loss and coughing blood fit, but fever, night sweats, a cavity and acid-fast bacilli in the sputum point to an infection.
near.community-acquired pneumonia: Ordinary pneumonia comes on over days and responds to standard antibiotics; this has smouldered for two months.
near.sarcoidosis: Granulomas and swollen hilar nodes fit, but sarcoid granulomas aren't cheesy, don't form cavities and won't grow bacteria.

cases.pearl: Weeks of cough plus night sweats and weight loss with an upper-lobe cavity: isolate the patient first, then send three sputum samples.

cases.complaint: A 26-year-old woman comes to the ED with fever, shivering and pain in her right side, after a few days of stinging when passing urine.

clues.history: Three days ago she noticed burning when passing urine and needing to go urgently and often. Yesterday she developed a high fever with uncontrollable shaking (rigors), pain in her right lower back and nausea, and she vomited twice today. She has had simple bladder infections before. No previous kidney problems.
clues.vitals: Temp 39.3 °C, HR 116/min, BP 112/68 mmHg, RR 20/min, SpO2 98% on room air.
clues.exam: Flushed and unwell. Marked tenderness when the right renal angle (between the lowest rib and the spine) is gently tapped. Mild tenderness above the pubic bone. The abdomen is otherwise soft with no guarding or rebound.
clues.labs: Urine dipstick: leucocytes +++, nitrites positive, blood +. Urine culture grows Escherichia coli above 10^8 colony-forming units per litre; blood cultures grow the same organism. WBC 18.2 ×10^9/L, CRP markedly raised. Creatinine 76 µmol/L, normal.
clues.imaging: Renal ultrasound: the right kidney is slightly swollen but there is no hydronephrosis, no stone and no abscess, so the infection is not trapped behind a blockage. CT with contrast (only if she fails to improve) would show wedge-shaped areas of reduced enhancement in the infected kidney.

explain.patho: Most urinary infections are caused by E. coli from the person's own gut, which reach the urinary opening and climb into the bladder; women's shorter urinary outlet tube makes this easier. Some strains have sticky hair-like projections (P fimbriae) that let them grip the lining of the ureter and climb up to the kidney against the flow of urine. In the kidney the bacteria invade the tubules and surrounding tissue, triggering intense inflammation with neutrophils, which produces fever, rigors and flank pain as the kidney swells and stretches its capsule. Nitrites appear because these bacteria convert dietary nitrate in urine to nitrite. Bacteria can enter the bloodstream from the kidney, causing sepsis. Blockages such as stones greatly worsen infection because stagnant urine cannot flush bacteria out.
explain.confirm: It is a clinical diagnosis: fever and flank pain with a positive urine dipstick, confirmed by urine culture, which also shows which antibiotics will work. Blood cultures are taken if she has a fever. Imaging is used if she doesn't improve quickly, has recurrent infections or might have a blockage.
explain.treat: Antibiotics that reach high levels in the kidney, given by mouth for milder cases or through a drip if she is vomiting or septic, then adjusted to the culture results. Fluids, pain relief and fever control. If imaging shows a blocked, infected kidney, urgent drainage is needed, and an abscess may need draining.

near.cystitis: She started with a bladder infection, but fever, rigors and flank tenderness mean it has climbed higher.
near.renal colic: Flank pain fits, but she has fever, high white cells and nitrites, and the scan shows no stone.
near.appendicitis: Right-sided pain with fever can fool you, but the urine is full of white cells and nitrites and the tenderness is in the back.

cases.pearl: Bladder infection = burning and frequency; kidney infection = add fever, rigors and flank pain.

cases.complaint: A 36-year-old man arrives at 4 a.m. with sudden, severe pain in his left side that he can't sit still with.

clues.history: The pain woke him two hours ago, starting in his left flank below the ribs and coming in waves that spread down towards his groin. He is pacing the room and cannot find a comfortable position. He has vomited once. He works outdoors in hot weather and admits he drinks very little water. His father had kidney stones.
clues.vitals: Temp 36.9 °C, HR 104/min, BP 148/92 mmHg (from pain), RR 20/min, SpO2 99% on room air.
clues.exam: Restless and writhing, unlike someone with peritonitis who lies still. Tender over the left flank and the angle between the lowest rib and the spine (renal angle). The abdomen is soft with no guarding. No pulsating mass in the abdomen.
clues.labs: Urine dipstick: blood ++, no nitrites, no leucocytes; microscopy confirms red cells. Creatinine 84 µmol/L (normal), calcium 2.38 mmol/L (normal), urate normal. WBC 9.8 ×10^9/L, CRP normal, so there is no sign of infection.
clues.imaging: Non-contrast CT of the kidneys, ureters and bladder (CT KUB): a 5 mm dense stone in the lower left ureter, just above where it joins the bladder (vesicoureteric junction). Mild swelling of the left ureter and kidney collecting system above it (hydroureter and mild hydronephrosis). The right kidney is normal.

explain.patho: Kidney stones form when urine becomes supersaturated with salts, most often calcium oxalate, so crystals come out of solution and grow. Low fluid intake and hot weather make urine concentrated, which favours stones, and family history matters. A stone sitting in the kidney is often painless, but when it moves into the narrow ureter it blocks urine flow. Pressure rises behind the blockage, and the ureter's smooth muscle squeezes hard in waves to push the stone along, which produces the colicky, waxing and waning pain. The pain follows the nerve supply of the ureter, from the flank down to the groin. The stone scrapes the lining, causing blood in the urine. Stones usually get stuck at narrow points: where the kidney joins the ureter, where the ureter crosses the pelvic brim, and where it enters the bladder.
explain.confirm: Non-contrast CT KUB is the gold standard, showing almost all stones, their size and position, and any blockage. Blood in the urine supports the diagnosis. Ultrasound is used in children to avoid radiation. Blood tests check kidney function, infection markers, calcium and urate.
explain.treat: Pain relief, with anti-inflammatory painkillers (NSAIDs) as first choice, and anti-sickness medicine. Small stones usually pass on their own; an alpha-blocker can relax the ureter and help a lower stone pass. Larger or stuck stones are removed by ureteroscopy or broken up by shock-wave lithotripsy. A blocked, infected kidney is an emergency that needs urgent drainage with a stent or a tube through the skin (nephrostomy), plus antibiotics.

near.pyelonephritis: That gives fever, white cells and nitrites in the urine; here the urine has blood only and no infection markers.
near.appendicitis: Patients with peritoneal pain lie still, but he can't stop moving and the pain comes in waves from his flank.
near.abdominal aortic aneurysm: Always consider a leaking aneurysm in an older man with flank pain, but he's 36 with a normal pulse in the belly and a stone on CT.

cases.pearl: Writhing patient = colic (stone, gallbladder); still patient = peritonitis.

cases.complaint: A 47-year-old woman gets a sudden, explosive headache while lifting shopping out of her car, 'like being hit with a bat', and collapses briefly.

clues.history: The headache hit full strength within seconds; she calls it the worst of her life. She vomited twice and passed out for about a minute. She has high blood pressure and smokes. Her mother died of 'a bleed in the brain' at 52. She has never had headaches like this before.
clues.vitals: Temp 37.4 °C, HR 58/min, BP 168/94 mmHg, RR 18/min, SpO2 98% on room air.
clues.exam: GCS 14 (slightly confused). Stiff neck and dislikes light. Right eyelid droops, the right pupil is large and doesn't react to light, and the right eye rests down and out (a pupil-involving right third nerve palsy). Limbs move normally.
clues.labs: Sodium 136 mmol/L (watch for falling sodium over the next days). Glucose 7.8 mmol/L. WBC 12.1 ×10^9/L. Troponin 46 ng/L, mildly raised from stress on the heart. Clotting normal. If the CT had been normal, a lumbar puncture done after 12 hours would show xanthochromia (yellow CSF from broken-down blood).
clues.imaging: Non-contrast CT head: bright blood filling the basal cisterns and both Sylvian fissures in a star shape, with early enlargement of the temporal horns (hydrocephalus). CT angiogram: a 7 mm saccular aneurysm at the junction of the right internal carotid and posterior communicating arteries.

explain.patho: Berry (saccular) aneurysms form at branch points in the circle of Willis, where the artery wall has a weak media and a broken internal elastic lamina and blood flow hammers the same spot. High blood pressure, smoking and family history make them grow and rupture. When one bursts, arterial blood sprays into the subarachnoid space around the brain and intracranial pressure briefly shoots up toward arterial pressure, cutting brain blood flow and causing collapse. Blood breakdown products irritate the meninges (neck stiffness) and clog the arachnoid granulations that absorb CSF (hydrocephalus). Days later, blood around the arteries triggers vasospasm, which can cause delayed strokes; damaged hypothalamic signalling can also cause low sodium. A posterior communicating aneurysm sits right next to the third nerve and presses on its outer pupil fibres first.
explain.confirm: Non-contrast CT is very sensitive in the first hours. If CT is normal but suspicion stays high, a lumbar puncture looks for xanthochromia. CT angiography or catheter angiography (digital subtraction angiography) then finds the aneurysm.
explain.treat: The aneurysm is secured as early as possible by endovascular coiling (platinum coils packed in through a catheter) or surgical clipping. A calcium channel blocker (nimodipine) is given to reduce delayed ischaemia from vasospasm, along with careful blood pressure control, pain relief and close monitoring in neuro-intensive care. Hydrocephalus is treated with an external ventricular drain, and sodium and fluid balance are watched closely.

near.migraine: Migraines build up; this one hit maximum in seconds and came with a blown pupil.
near.meningitis: The stiff neck fits, but the onset was a thunderclap during exertion, not an illness developing over hours.
near.intracerebral haemorrhage: There is a bleed, but look where the blood is: around the brain in the cisterns, not inside it.
near.tension headache: No ordinary headache peaks in seconds, causes collapse and dilates a pupil.

cases.pearl: A painful third nerve palsy with a dilated pupil is an aneurysm until proven otherwise: the pupil fibres run on the outside of the nerve, right where the aneurysm presses.

cases.complaint: A 67-year-old man has had cramping belly pain, a swollen abdomen and repeated vomiting for a day and a half.

clues.history: Waves of cramping central pain come every few minutes and then ease. He has vomited many times, first food and now green fluid. He has not passed any stool or wind since yesterday morning. Twenty years ago he had open abdominal surgery for a perforated bowel.
clues.vitals: Temp 37.3 °C, HR 104/min, BP 126/80 mmHg, RR 18/min, SpO2 97% on room air.
clues.exam: The abdomen is distended and drum-like on tapping, with a long healed midline scar. Bowel sounds are high-pitched and tinkling. It is mildly tender all over but there is no guarding or rebound. Hernia orifices are empty and the rectum is empty on examination. His mouth is dry.
clues.labs: Sodium 136 mmol/L, potassium 3.2 mmol/L, chloride 94 mmol/L, bicarbonate 31 mmol/L (a contraction alkalosis from vomiting). Urea 11.2 mmol/L and creatinine 118 µmol/L from dehydration. WBC 11.0 ×10^9/L. Lactate 1.6 mmol/L, which is reassuring against dead bowel.
clues.imaging: Abdominal X-ray: multiple dilated central loops of small bowel up to 4.5 cm across, with lines running fully across the bowel (valvulae conniventes), and very little gas in the colon. CT with contrast: dilated small bowel down to a sharp narrowing (transition point) in the lower abdomen with collapsed bowel beyond it and no visible cause other than a band; bowel walls enhance normally, so there is no sign of strangulation.

explain.patho: After any abdominal surgery, the healing peritoneum can lay down fibrous bands (adhesions) that tether loops of bowel together or to the abdominal wall. Years later a loop can kink or get caught under a band, blocking the passage of gut contents. Above the block, swallowed air and the litres of fluid the gut secretes each day pile up, stretching the bowel and triggering strong waves of peristalsis, which cause colicky pain and tinkling bowel sounds. Fluid lost into the bowel and through vomiting dehydrates the patient and lowers potassium and chloride. If the band twists the bowel or traps a closed loop, the blood supply can be cut off (strangulation), the wall dies and it can perforate.
explain.confirm: Suspected from the four cardinal features: colicky pain, vomiting, distension and absolute constipation, especially with a surgical scar. CT with contrast confirms it, shows the transition point and looks for danger signs such as a closed loop, poorly enhancing bowel wall or free fluid. Rising lactate and constant pain suggest ischaemia.
explain.treat: Most adhesional obstructions settle without surgery: nil by mouth, a nasogastric tube to drain the stomach ('drip and suck'), intravenous fluids with potassium replacement and careful monitoring. A water-soluble contrast drink can be both a test and a treatment, since contrast reaching the colon predicts resolution. Surgery to divide the adhesions is needed for strangulation, peritonitis or failure to improve.

near.large bowel obstruction: In large bowel obstruction the colon is the dilated part; here the colon is nearly empty of gas and the big loops are central with lines crossing the whole width.
near.gastroenteritis: Gastroenteritis gives diarrhoea, not a complete stop in stool and wind with a drum-like belly.
near.incarcerated hernia: A good thought, but his hernia openings are empty; look at his scar instead.

cases.pearl: In a patient with an abdominal scar and an obstructed bowel, adhesions are the commonest cause; with no scar, check carefully for a hernia.

cases.complaint: A 14-year-old boy is brought to the ED with severe pain in both thighs and his lower back that started overnight.

clues.history: He has a long-term blood condition diagnosed on newborn screening and has had similar pain episodes before, about twice a year. Yesterday he went swimming in a cold lake, got chilled, and then didn't drink much on a hot car journey home. The pain is deep, gnawing and 9/10, and his usual home painkillers haven't touched it. He has no cough, chest pain or breathlessness.
clues.vitals: Temp 37.7 °C, HR 112/min, BP 122/74 mmHg, RR 18/min, SpO2 97% on room air.
clues.exam: Distressed with pain. Tender over both thigh bones and the lower spine without swelling, redness or joint fluid. Mild yellow tinge to the whites of his eyes. The spleen cannot be felt. Chest clear on listening, with no new crackles.
clues.labs: Haemoglobin 74 g/L (his usual is about 80 g/L), reticulocytes 11% (high: the marrow is working hard to replace short-lived red cells). Bilirubin 48 µmol/L, mostly unconjugated, and LDH raised, both signs of red cell breakdown. WBC 14.0 ×10^9/L. Blood film: sickle-shaped cells, target cells and Howell-Jolly bodies (a sign the spleen no longer works). Haemoglobin electrophoresis on record: HbS with no HbA (HbSS).
clues.imaging: Chest X-ray: clear lungs, no new shadowing; this is important because new shadowing plus chest symptoms would mean acute chest syndrome, a more dangerous complication. Hip and spine X-rays were not needed for this typical episode. Ultrasound shows a small, shrunken spleen.

explain.patho: Sickle cell disease is inherited when a child gets an altered beta-globin gene from both parents: a single DNA change swaps one amino acid (valine for glutamic acid), producing haemoglobin S. When haemoglobin S gives up its oxygen, the molecules stick together into long rigid fibres that bend the red cell into a stiff sickle shape. Cold, dehydration, infection and low oxygen all encourage sickling. Sickled cells and sticky white cells jam in small blood vessels, especially in bone marrow, so the tissue beyond becomes starved of oxygen, causing intense pain. Sickled cells are also destroyed early, living only about two to three weeks instead of four months, which causes chronic anaemia, jaundice and a high reticulocyte count. Repeated blockages in the spleen destroy it in early childhood, leaving people vulnerable to certain bacterial infections.
explain.confirm: Sickle cell disease is confirmed by haemoglobin electrophoresis or HPLC, usually on newborn screening. A vaso-occlusive crisis is a clinical diagnosis: typical pain in a person with sickle cell disease after other causes such as infection, bone infection or acute chest syndrome have been excluded with examination, blood tests and a chest X-ray if needed.
explain.treat: Fast, effective pain relief is the priority, often with strong painkillers such as morphine given quickly and reviewed often, alongside paracetamol and anti-inflammatories when appropriate. Fluids, warmth, oxygen only if levels are low, and breathing exercises with an incentive spirometer to prevent acute chest syndrome. Long-term, hydroxyurea (hydroxycarbamide) increases fetal haemoglobin and reduces crises, along with vaccinations and preventive antibiotics. Regular transfusions are used for some patients, and stem cell transplant or gene therapy can be curative.

near.osteomyelitis: Bone infection is a real risk in sickle cell, but pain in several bones on both sides after cold and dehydration fits a different, commoner event.
near.acute chest syndrome: A feared complication of the same disease, but his chest is clear and he has no breathing symptoms; name the commoner event.
near.septic arthritis: There's no hot, swollen joint here; the pain is deep in the bones.

cases.pearl: In sickle cell disease, cold, dehydration and infection are the triggers; warmth, fluids and fast pain relief are the first moves.

cases.complaint: A 61-year-old man is brought in by ambulance with crushing central chest pain that started 50 minutes ago while he was shovelling snow.

clues.history: Heavy, pressing central chest pain radiating to the left arm and jaw, not relieved by rest. He is sweaty and nauseated and feels 'like something terrible is happening'. He has high blood pressure, high cholesterol and type 2 diabetes, and smoked for 30 years until last year. His father had a heart attack at 55.
clues.vitals: Temp 36.8 °C, HR 102/min, BP 148/92 mmHg, RR 22/min, SpO2 95% on room air.
clues.exam: Pale, clammy and anxious. Heart sounds normal with no murmur. Chest clear, no raised JVP, no leg swelling. Pulses equal in both arms. Pain is not reproduced by pressing on the chest wall.
clues.labs: High-sensitivity troponin T 640 ng/L (normal under 14), rising to 2,900 ng/L at 3 hours. Glucose 11.2 mmol/L. Potassium 4.1 mmol/L, creatinine 92 µmol/L, haemoglobin 148 g/L. Total cholesterol 6.4 mmol/L.
clues.imaging: ECG: ST elevation of 3–4 mm in leads V1–V5 with reciprocal ST depression in II, III and aVF; new Q waves starting in V2. Bedside echo: the front wall and tip of the left ventricle (apex) are barely moving; the rest contracts well. Chest X-ray: normal heart size, clear lungs.

explain.patho: A cholesterol-rich plaque inside a coronary artery ruptures, exposing its contents to the blood. Platelets stick to the tear and the clotting cascade builds a thrombus that completely blocks the artery. Here the blocked vessel is the left anterior descending (LAD) artery, which feeds the front wall of the left ventricle and most of the septum. Heart muscle without oxygen switches to anaerobic metabolism, loses its ability to contract within seconds and starts to die after about 20–30 minutes, spreading from the inner layer outward. Full-thickness injury causes ST elevation on the ECG in the leads that 'look at' that wall, and dying cells leak troponin into the blood. The longer the artery stays blocked, the more muscle is lost, which is why 'time is muscle'.
explain.confirm: The diagnosis is made on the ECG: new ST elevation in two or more neighbouring leads in someone with ischaemic symptoms. Treatment should not wait for troponin. Coronary angiography confirms the blocked artery and is the start of treatment.
explain.treat: Emergency reperfusion is the priority: primary percutaneous coronary intervention (balloon and stent) through the wrist or groin, or clot-busting thrombolytic drugs if a cath lab cannot be reached quickly. Patients get aspirin plus a second antiplatelet drug and an anticoagulant, with oxygen only if levels are low. Afterwards long-term secondary prevention includes statins, beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors, cardiac rehab and stopping smoking.

near.nstemi: Very close, but look at the ECG: the ST segments are elevated, not depressed, which means a fully blocked artery.
near.pericarditis: Pericarditis gives diffuse ST elevation in many territories with PR depression; this elevation is confined to one coronary territory with reciprocal changes.
near.aortic dissection: Always worth excluding, but the pulses are equal in both arms and the pain is crushing rather than tearing to the back.

cases.pearl: Reciprocal ST depression on the opposite side of the heart is one of the strongest clues that ST elevation is a true infarct and not pericarditis.

cases.dx: Subacute combined degeneration of the cord (vitamin B12 deficiency from pernicious anaemia)
aliases: subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord
cases.complaint: A 63-year-old woman has had tingling in her feet and hands for four months and feels unsteady, especially in the dark.

clues.history: The pins and needles started in her toes, then reached her fingers. She nearly fell in the shower when she closed her eyes to rinse her hair, and she uses a night light because she wobbles in the dark. She is very tired, gets breathless on the stairs, has a sore tongue and feels mentally foggy. She has vitiligo and an underactive thyroid treated with thyroxine. She eats a normal mixed diet including meat and dairy. No back pain.
clues.vitals: Temp 36.6 °C, HR 98/min, BP 124/72 mmHg, RR 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air.
clues.exam: Pale with a faint lemon-yellow tinge. Smooth, red, sore tongue (glossitis). Vibration sense lost to the knees and joint position sense lost in the toes. Romberg positive: steady with eyes open, sways and nearly falls with eyes closed. Mild stiffness and weakness in the legs. Ankle jerks absent, but knee jerks brisk and plantars upgoing (a mixed picture).
clues.labs: Haemoglobin 84 g/L, MCV 118 fL (large red cells), reticulocytes low, hypersegmented neutrophils on the blood film, mildly low white cells and platelets. Serum vitamin B12 very low; folate normal. Methylmalonic acid and homocysteine both raised. Intrinsic factor antibodies and gastric parietal cell antibodies positive. Unconjugated bilirubin 28 µmol/L and LDH raised (ineffective red cell production).
clues.imaging: MRI cervical and thoracic spine: symmetrical bright T2 signal in the dorsal columns, forming an 'inverted V' shape on cross-section. Nerve conduction studies: a mild sensory axonal neuropathy in the legs.

explain.patho: In pernicious anaemia, an autoimmune gastritis destroys the stomach's parietal cells, so they stop making intrinsic factor, the protein that carries vitamin B12 to be absorbed at the end of the small intestine (terminal ileum). B12 is a cofactor for two key enzymes. Methionine synthase is needed to make DNA building blocks, so without it the bone marrow makes large, immature red cells (megaloblastic anaemia). Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase is needed for normal fatty-acid handling, so without it abnormal fatty acids enter myelin and myelin breaks down. In the spinal cord this hits the dorsal columns (vibration and position sense, so a positive Romberg) and the lateral corticospinal tracts (weakness and upgoing toes), hence 'combined'. A peripheral neuropathy removes the ankle reflexes, which is why absent ankle jerks can sit beside upgoing plantars.
explain.confirm: Low serum B12 with raised methylmalonic acid and homocysteine confirms deficiency, and intrinsic factor antibodies confirm pernicious anaemia as the cause. The blood count shows macrocytic anaemia, and MRI shows the dorsal column signal change. Other autoimmune conditions such as thyroid disease often coexist.
explain.treat: Treatment is lifelong cobalamin replacement given by intramuscular injection (hydroxocobalamin), frequently at first and then as regular maintenance, because the gut can't absorb it normally. Folic acid must never be given alone, because it can correct the anaemia while the nerve damage keeps worsening. Physiotherapy helps balance, and nerve recovery is best when treatment starts early.

near.diabetic neuropathy: A neuropathy alone wouldn't cause brisk knees and upgoing toes, and she has a big-cell anaemia.
near.multiple sclerosis: MS doesn't cause a macrocytic anaemia or a sore smooth tongue; look at her blood count.
near.folate deficiency: Folate also causes big red cells, but her folate is normal and folate lack doesn't usually damage the cord like this.
near.iron deficiency anaemia: Iron deficiency gives small red cells; hers are large.

cases.pearl: Absent ankle jerks with upgoing toes is a short list worth knowing: B12 deficiency, Friedreich ataxia and lesions at the bottom of the cord (conus).

cases.complaint: An 82-year-old woman's daughter brings her in because over the past 10 days she has become increasingly muddled, sleepy and unsteady.

clues.history: Three weeks ago she tripped on a rug and bumped her forehead; it 'was nothing' and she didn't see a doctor. She takes warfarin for atrial fibrillation. Since then she has had headaches, and lately her confusion comes and goes, she drops things from her left hand and she has nearly fallen twice. Before this she lived alone and managed well.
clues.vitals: Temp 36.6 °C, HR 80/min irregularly irregular, BP 146/82 mmHg, RR 16/min, SpO2 96% on room air.
clues.exam: GCS 14 (confused, disoriented to date). Fading yellow bruise on the right forehead. Mild left pronator drift and slightly weaker left grip; left plantar upgoing. Attention fluctuates during the exam. No neck stiffness, no fever.
clues.labs: INR 3.4 (above her target range). Haemoglobin 124 g/L, platelets 210 ×10^9/L. Sodium 134 mmol/L, glucose 5.6 mmol/L, creatinine 84 µmol/L. CRP normal and urine dipstick clear, which makes an infection-driven delirium much less likely.
clues.imaging: Non-contrast CT head: a crescent-shaped collection over the right cerebral convexity, mostly darker than brain (old blood) with a few brighter streaks (fresh rebleeding), 18 mm thick. It crosses the suture lines, flattens the sulci and pushes the midline 7 mm to the left. The brain shows age-related shrinkage.

explain.patho: Bridging veins cross the subdural space from the brain surface to the dural venous sinuses. As the brain shrinks with age, these veins are stretched taut, so a minor jolt can tear them; blood thinners turn a tiny ooze into a growing collection. Because the bleeding is venous and slow, symptoms build over days to weeks. The clot becomes walled in by membranes full of fragile new vessels that keep rebleeding and leaking, so a chronic subdural can slowly enlarge. Blood in the subdural space isn't held by the sutures, so it spreads along the surface in a crescent until it meets the falx or tentorium. Pressure on the cortex causes confusion, headache and weakness on the opposite side of the body.
explain.confirm: A non-contrast CT shows a crescent that crosses sutures: bright when acute, darker when chronic, and mixed when there has been rebleeding. MRI helps if the CT is equivocal.
explain.treat: Her anticoagulation is reversed straight away (vitamin K and prothrombin complex concentrate). A symptomatic chronic subdural is drained through burr holes with a temporary drain; acute solid clots need a craniotomy. Middle meningeal artery embolisation is increasingly used to cut the membranes' blood supply and reduce recurrence. Small collections without symptoms can be watched with repeat scans.

near.epidural haematoma: This collection is a crescent that crosses sutures, from slow venous bleeding in an older person, not a lens-shaped arterial bleed.
near.dementia: Dementia creeps over months to years; this came on over days after a fall and has one-sided signs.
near.delirium: She is delirious, but her urine and CRP are clean; look for a cause inside the skull after that fall.
near.ischaemic stroke: A stroke starts suddenly; this crept up over days with a headache after a head bump.

cases.pearl: In an older person on blood thinners, new confusion weeks after a fall that 'was nothing' is a subdural until the CT says otherwise.

cases.complaint: A 24-year-old man is brought in after a motorbike crash, getting rapidly more breathless and confused in the resus bay.

clues.history: He came off his motorbike at speed and hit the left side of his chest on a barrier. Paramedics noted left chest pain and breathlessness. Over the last five minutes he has become more distressed, then drowsy. Wearing a helmet, no head injury seen.
clues.vitals: Temp 36.2 °C, HR 138/min, BP 78/44 mmHg, RR 36/min, SpO2 82% on high-flow oxygen.
clues.exam: Left side of the chest is barely moving, with no breath sounds and a drum-like (hyperresonant) note when tapped. The trachea is pushed to the right. Neck veins are distended. Bruising and crunchy crackling under the skin over left ribs (surgical emphysema). Peripheries cold and clammy.
clues.labs: Treatment must not wait for blood tests. Arterial gas taken during resuscitation: pH 7.21, PaO2 6.8 kPa on oxygen, PaCO2 6.9 kPa, lactate 5.2 mmol/L. Haemoglobin 138 g/L (no major blood loss yet). Group and crossmatch sent.
clues.imaging: This is a clinical diagnosis and should be treated before any X-ray. Bedside ultrasound (eFAST): no lung sliding on the left, with a 'barcode' pattern. Chest X-ray after decompression and a chest drain shows the re-expanded left lung, two fractured left ribs and the mediastinum back in the middle.

explain.patho: A rib fracture or a tear in the lung lets air leak into the pleural space between the lung and chest wall. In a tension pneumothorax the tear acts like a one-way valve: air gets in with each breath but cannot escape. Pressure in that side of the chest rises higher and higher, collapsing the lung completely and shoving the mediastinum (heart, trachea and great veins) toward the opposite side. Kinked and squashed great veins can't return blood to the heart, so cardiac output falls and blood pressure crashes, while the distended neck veins show blood backing up. Combined with the collapsed lung, the patient becomes profoundly hypoxic and can go into cardiac arrest within minutes. It is a form of obstructive shock.
explain.confirm: Tension pneumothorax is diagnosed clinically: respiratory distress, low blood pressure, absent breath sounds and hyperresonance on one side, a deviated trachea and distended neck veins. Bedside ultrasound showing absent lung sliding supports it, but treatment must never wait for an X-ray.
explain.treat: Immediate decompression to let the trapped air out: a needle placed through the chest wall on the affected side, or in trauma a finger thoracostomy. This is followed by a chest drain connected to an underwater seal to keep the lung expanded. High-flow oxygen and full trauma resuscitation run alongside it.

near.haemothorax: Blood in the chest is possible after trauma, but it would sound dull when tapped, not drum-like.
near.cardiac tamponade: Both cause low blood pressure and full neck veins, but the absent breath sounds, hyperresonance and pushed-over trachea point to the chest, not the heart sac.
near.simple pneumothorax: Air is there, but this one is crushing the heart's blood return: look at the blood pressure and the trachea.

cases.pearl: If you're waiting for a chest X-ray to diagnose a tension pneumothorax, you've waited too long.

cases.complaint: A 71-year-old man had 15 minutes of a weak, clumsy left hand and slurred speech this morning. By the time he reached the ED he felt completely normal.

clues.history: It came on suddenly while making coffee and faded over a quarter of an hour. Last week a 'grey curtain' came down over his RIGHT eye for a couple of minutes and lifted. He has type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure and high cholesterol, and smoked for 40 years. No headache, no jerking, no tingling that spread.
clues.vitals: Temp 36.7 °C, HR 78/min regular, BP 152/88 mmHg, RR 14/min, SpO2 97% on room air.
clues.exam: Neurological exam is now completely normal: strength, speech, visual fields and coordination. There is a soft whooshing bruit over the right carotid artery in the neck. Fundoscopy shows a tiny bright yellow fleck in a right retinal artery (a cholesterol embolus, Hollenhorst plaque).
clues.labs: Glucose 8.9 mmol/L, HbA1c 62 mmol/mol (poorly controlled diabetes). LDL cholesterol 3.9 mmol/L. Full blood count, clotting and creatinine (88 µmol/L) normal. ABCD2 score 6 (high early stroke risk).
clues.imaging: CT head: normal. MRI diffusion-weighted imaging: no area of infarction. Carotid Doppler ultrasound: about 80% narrowing of the right internal carotid artery with an irregular, ulcerated plaque. ECG and 24-hour heart monitor: sinus rhythm, no atrial fibrillation.

explain.patho: A TIA is a brief episode of focal brain or retinal ischaemia that resolves without leaving dead tissue, and today it is defined by a normal diffusion MRI rather than by a time limit. Here an atherosclerotic plaque at the carotid bifurcation has an ulcerated surface where platelets and fibrin clump. Small clumps break off and travel up the artery (artery-to-artery embolism), blocking a branch of the right MCA and causing left-hand weakness and slurred speech. The emboli are soft and get broken down or pushed through before neurons die, so symptoms resolve. The ophthalmic artery is the first branch of the internal carotid, so the same plaque also caused transient blindness in the right eye (amaurosis fugax). The same unstable plaque can throw a bigger clot at any time, so the stroke risk is highest in the first days.
explain.confirm: It is a clinical diagnosis based on a typical sudden, focal, 'negative' event that fully resolves. MRI diffusion imaging confirms no infarct has occurred. Carotid imaging, an ECG and heart rhythm monitoring look for the source.
explain.treat: Urgent specialist assessment, with antiplatelet treatment started straight away (often two antiplatelets for a short period), a high-intensity statin, and tight blood pressure and diabetes control plus stopping smoking. Because the narrowing caused symptoms and is severe, he should have carotid endarterectomy (surgically removing the plaque) or carotid stenting as soon as safely possible.

near.ischaemic stroke: Very close, but his symptoms resolved completely and the diffusion MRI shows no infarct.
near.migraine with aura: Migraine aura spreads gradually with positive symptoms like sparkles; this was sudden loss of function in an older man with a carotid bruit.
near.seizure: No jerking and no confusion afterwards; a weak limb after a seizure follows the fit, it doesn't stand alone.
near.hypoglycaemia: His sugar is high, not low, and the eye episode points to the carotid artery.

cases.pearl: Amaurosis fugax is a TIA of the eye: the ophthalmic artery is the first branch of the internal carotid, so a curtain over one eye sends you to look at that side's neck.

cases.complaint: A 58-year-old woman has sudden, stabbing electric-shock pains in her right cheek and jaw, many times a day, that stop her eating.

clues.history: Each jolt lasts a second or two and comes in bursts, dozens of times a day, sometimes with a dull ache between. Chewing, brushing her teeth, talking, a cold wind or lightly touching a spot beside her nose sets it off. Her dentist found nothing wrong and even removed a tooth, but the pain continued. Between attacks she feels normal. She has lost weight because eating is so painful.
clues.vitals: Temp 36.6 °C, HR 78/min, BP 134/82 mmHg, RR 14/min, SpO2 98% on room air.
clues.exam: She flinches and won't let the examiner touch her right cheek near the nose (a trigger zone). Facial sensation to light touch and pinprick is normal in all three trigeminal divisions, the corneal reflex is intact and jaw strength is normal. The rest of the cranial nerve and neurological exam is normal. Teeth and jaw joint are unremarkable.
clues.labs: Full blood count normal. ESR and CRP normal (giant cell arteritis is very unlikely, and its jaw pain is an aching on chewing, not shocks). Glucose 5.4 mmol/L.
clues.imaging: MRI brain with fine-cut sequences through the brainstem: a loop of the right superior cerebellar artery touches and indents the right trigeminal nerve where it enters the pons. No multiple sclerosis plaques and no tumour of the cerebellopontine angle.

explain.patho: Most classical trigeminal neuralgia is caused by a blood vessel, usually the superior cerebellar artery, pressing on the trigeminal nerve at its root entry zone, where myelin made by central oligodendrocytes changes to peripheral Schwann cell myelin. That transition zone is especially vulnerable. Years of pulsation wear away a patch of myelin, letting neighbouring axons short-circuit (ephaptic transmission) and making them fire spontaneously in bursts. As a result, signals from light-touch fibres jump onto pain fibres, so brushing the face triggers a jolt of severe pain. The maxillary (V2) and mandibular (V3) divisions are most often affected. When it occurs in younger people or on both sides, multiple sclerosis or a tumour pressing on the nerve must be considered.
explain.confirm: It is a clinical diagnosis from the classic pattern: brief, electric-shock-like pains in a trigeminal distribution, triggered by harmless stimuli, with a normal exam. MRI is done to look for a compressing vessel and to rule out secondary causes such as multiple sclerosis or a tumour, especially if there is numbness or the patient is young.
explain.treat: First-line treatment is a sodium-channel-blocking antiseizure medicine such as carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine, which calms the over-excitable nerve; ordinary painkillers don't work. If medicines fail or cause side effects, a neurosurgeon can perform microvascular decompression, opening the skull behind the ear and placing a small pad between the artery and the nerve. Other options are procedures that deliberately damage part of the nerve (percutaneous rhizotomy) or focused radiation (stereotactic radiosurgery).

near.dental abscess: Her dentist found nothing and pulling a tooth didn't help; the pain is brief shocks triggered by touch, not a constant throb.
near.cluster headache: Cluster pain is around the eye, lasts much longer and comes with a red, watering eye.
near.sinusitis: Sinus pain is a constant pressure with congestion, not split-second electric shocks.
near.giant cell arteritis: Her inflammatory markers are normal and the pain is shocks, not aching jaw fatigue.

cases.pearl: Microvascular decompression is one of the few operations that removes the cause of a pain syndrome rather than just blocking the pain.

cases.complaint: An 81-year-old woman from a care home is brought in because she has become confused and drowsy over the past day.

clues.history: Staff say she was her usual chatty self two days ago. Since yesterday she has been shivering, off her food and muddled, and today she is hard to wake. Her urine has been cloudy and smelly and she has been going more often. She had a kidney stone years ago. She has type 2 diabetes and mild memory problems.
clues.vitals: Temp 39.1 °C, HR 122/min, BP 82/48 mmHg (mean arterial pressure about 59), RR 26/min, SpO2 94% on room air.
clues.exam: Flushed and drowsy, opens eyes to voice, confused about where she is. Warm hands with fast capillary refill early on, now slowing. Tender in the right loin (renal angle) and above the pubic bone. Chest clear, no neck stiffness, no rash. Heart sounds normal, no murmur.
clues.labs: WBC 21.3 ×10^9/L with neutrophilia, CRP markedly raised. Lactate 4.4 mmol/L (high). Creatinine 182 µmol/L (her usual is 85), urea 14.6 mmol/L, potassium 5.1 mmol/L. Glucose 14.2 mmol/L. Platelets 96 ×10^9/L. Urine dipstick: leucocytes and nitrites positive. Urine and blood cultures both grow Escherichia coli.
clues.imaging: Chest X-ray: clear lungs. Renal ultrasound: right kidney mildly swollen with no hydronephrosis and no stone blocking the ureter. ECG: sinus tachycardia.

explain.patho: Bacteria from the gut, most often E. coli, climb the urethra into the bladder and then up the ureter into the kidney (pyelonephritis). From the inflamed kidney they enter the bloodstream. Sepsis is not the infection itself but the body's dysregulated response to it: immune cells release floods of cytokines that make blood vessels dilate and leak, so blood pressure falls (septic shock) despite a fast heart. Poor blood flow and damaged mitochondria force cells into anaerobic metabolism, raising lactate. Organs start to fail: the brain (confusion), kidneys (rising creatinine), clotting system (falling platelets) and sometimes the lungs. Older people often present with confusion rather than obvious urinary symptoms, and may not run a high fever at all.
explain.confirm: Sepsis is suspected infection plus organ dysfunction (an acute rise in SOFA score); quick bedside flags are confusion, fast breathing and low blood pressure. Septic shock is low blood pressure needing vasopressors with a raised lactate despite fluids. Blood and urine cultures identify the organism, and imaging looks for a blocked kidney, which would need urgent drainage.
explain.treat: The sepsis bundle is started immediately: blood cultures, then broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics within the first hour, intravenous fluids, oxygen if needed, lactate measurement and urine-output monitoring. Persistent low blood pressure is treated with vasopressors in intensive care. Antibiotics are narrowed once cultures return, and any blockage in the urinary tract is drained urgently (source control).

near.stroke: Sudden confusion in an older person is worth thinking about, but the fever, shock and abnormal urine point to infection.
near.pneumonia: A common source of sepsis in the elderly, but her chest is clear and the urine is the giveaway.
near.meningitis: Fever and confusion fit, but there's no neck stiffness or rash and the loin is tender.
near.pyelonephritis: The kidney is the source, but she is now in shock with failing organs: name the whole-body response, not just the local infection.

cases.pearl: In older people, new confusion may be the only sign of serious infection, and 'it's just a UTI' can become septic shock within hours.
